**Surah al-Zumar (The Troops)**

It is also called *Surat al-Ghuraf* (The Chambers), as mentioned in *al-Itqan* (a work on the sciences of the Qur'an by al-Suyuti) and *al-Kashshaf* (al-Zamakhshari's commentary), because of His words, exalted is He: ﴿For them are chambers, above them are chambers﴾. Ibn al-Durays, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it was revealed in Makkah, and he made no exception. Al-Nahhas narrated from him that he said: "Surat al-Zumar was revealed in Makkah except for three verses, which were revealed in Madinah concerning Wahshi, the slayer of Hamzah: ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾, up to the three verses." Some added: ﴿Say: O My servants who believe, fear your Lord﴾, the verse. This was mentioned by al-Sakhawi in *Jamal al-Qurra'* and related by Abu Hayyan from Muqatil. Others added ﴿God has sent down the best of speech﴾, which was related by Ibn al-Jawzi. What is mentioned in *al-Bahr* (Abu Hayyan's commentary, *al-Bahr al-Muhit*) from Ibn 'Abbas is the exception of ﴿God has sent down the best of speech﴾ and His words ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed﴾, etc. From some of them: "Except seven verses from His words, glorified is He, ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed﴾ to the end of the seven." Its number of verses is seventy-five according to the Kufan reckoning, three according to the Syrian, and two according to the rest. The details of the disagreement are in *Majma' al-Bayan* and elsewhere.

As for the connection between its beginning and the end of Surat Sad, it is that He, glorified is He, said there: ﴿It is nothing but a reminder to the worlds﴾, and said here, exalted is His majesty: ﴿The revelation of the Book is from God﴾. In this there is complete coherence, such that if the basmala were removed the speech would not be disjointed. Moreover, He, exalted is He, mentioned at the end of Sad the story of the creation of Adam, and mentioned at the beginning of this surah the story of the creation of his spouse from him, and the creation of all people from him. He mentioned their creation in the wombs of their mothers, creation after creation, then mentioned that they will die, then mentioned, glorified is He, the Resurrection, the Reckoning, Paradise, and the Fire. He concluded with His words, glorified is He: ﴿And it will be judged between them with truth, and it will be said: All praise is due to God, Lord of the worlds﴾. Thus He, exalted is His majesty, mentioned the states of creation from its beginning to the end of the return, connected to the creation of Adam, peace be upon him, mentioned in the surah before it. Between the two surahs there are other aspects of connection that become apparent upon reflection, so reflect.

﷽ (In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful)

﴿The revelation of the Book﴾. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: it is the subject (*mubtada'*), and His words ﴿from God, the Mighty, the Wise﴾ are its predicate (*khabar*), or the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "this mentioned thing is a revelation," and "from God" is connected to "revelation." The first view is better, as in *al-Kashf* (al-Zamakhshari's commentary, *al-Kashshaf*). "The Book" means the entire Qur'an, and the sentence in this case appears to be an explanation of its being a reminder to the worlds, or of His words ﴿and you will surely know its news after a while﴾. The apparent meaning, according to the second view, is that "the Book" refers to the surah, because it is in the position of being mentioned, and so it is closer in terms of the sense of presence that the demonstrative pronoun in it requires. "Revelation" is in the sense of "sent down" (*munazzal*), or it is intended for emphasis. Abu Hayyan assumed the subject to be "huwa" (it), referring to the reminder in "It is nothing but a reminder," and made the sentence a resumptive explanatory clause (*isti'naf bayani*), as if it were said: "What is this reminder?" Then it was said: "It is the revelation of the Book," and "the Book" here is the Qur'an. In "revelation" there are the two possibilities. It is also permitted, on the assumption that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, for "from God" to be a second predicate; and that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, also, i.e., "this, or it, is the revelation of the Book, this, or it, is from God." It is also permitted for it to be a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from "the Book," since the circumstantial clause may come from the genitive complement, because the genitive-governing noun functions like a verb. It is also permitted for it to be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun concealed in "revelation," on the assumption that it means "sent down," and for it to be a circumstantial clause from "revelation" itself, with the governing element being the sense of the demonstrative.

It has been objected that the meanings of verbs do not govern when what they govern is omitted. For this reason they refuted al-Mubarrad regarding his reading in the verse of al-Farazdaq: "And there is no human like them," that "like them" is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause, with its governing element being the omitted adverbial phrase, i.e., "there is in existence no human resembling them." They said that the adverbial phrase is a semantic governing element and does not govern when omitted. Ibn Abi 'Abla, Zayd ibn 'Ali, and 'Isa read "revelation" in the accusative, with an implied verb, such as "recite" or "adhere to."

The mention of the two attributes of might and wisdom is to signal the manifestation of their effects in the Book, through the operation of its rulings and the execution of its commands and prohibitions without any opponent or obstacle, and through the foundation of everything in it upon the basis of brilliant wisdoms.

[p. 233]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 39, verse 2:

The saying of He, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book in truth﴾ is an explanation that it was sent down with truth, and a preparation (tawti'ah) for what is mentioned after it. In Irshad al-Aql al-Salim (of Abu al-Su'ud) it is said that it is the beginning of an explanation of the one to whom it was sent down, and what is obligatory upon him, following on from the explanation of the status of what was sent down and that it is from Allah, exalted is He. Whichever it is, it does not repeat what preceded it. Indeed, the apparent meaning, on the assumption that the intended "Book" there is the Qur'an, would be to use its pronoun here; however, it is more evident in intending to magnify it and to give greater attention to its status.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "What appears to me is that the first "Book" is general to all that was sent down from Allah, exalted is He, and the second "Book" is specific to the Qur'an. So it is as if He informed, in a bare report, that the guiding, legislating books were sent down by Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and made this a preparation for His words, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book﴾." End of quote. And it is, as you see, [a weak view].

The "bi" (with) is connected to the sending down, and it is for causation, meaning: We sent it down because of the truth, that is, to establish and manifest it. Or it is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial state (hal) of the object, and it is for accompaniment, meaning: We sent it down accompanied by truth and rightness, and the intended meaning is that everything in it necessitates action and acceptance, definitively. It is also permitted that the omitted element be a circumstantial state of the subject, meaning: We sent it down while being accompanied by truth, that is, being correct in that. The "fa'" (so) in His words, exalted is He: ﴿So worship Allah, making the religion sincerely His﴾ is for the sequencing of the command to worship upon the sending down of the Book to him, upon him be prayers and peace, with truth; that is: worship Him, exalted is He, purifying the religion for Him from the admixtures of polytheism and showing-off, as clarified throughout what was sent down to you. The turn to the majestic Name is most fitting for this command. Ibn Abi 'Ablah recited "al-Dinu" (the religion) in the nominative, as narrated by the trustworthy transmitters, so there is no weight to al-Zajjaj's denial. Al-Farra' interpreted this as a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is the preceding prepositional phrase, for exclusivity or for emphasis of it. It was objected that this repeats with the words of He, exalted is He:

Al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, on Surah 39, verse 3:

﴿Is not sincere devotion (ad-din al-khalis) due to Allah alone?﴾ It has been answered that the first clause is a resumptive sentence (*istinaf*, a clause that begins a new statement) which serves as a justification (*ta'lil*) for the command to devote worship sincerely, and this clause is an emphasis (*ta'kid*) on the exclusivity of the religion to Him, the Exalted. That is: Is it not He, glorified is He, who must be singled out for sincere devotion to Him, the Exalted, because He alone possesses the attributes of divinity, among which is knowledge of the innermost secrets and hearts? According to the reading of the majority, it is a resumptive sentence that confirms what precedes it, namely the command to sincere devotion to Him, the Majestic, and the obligation to obey it. In the use of *ala* (is it not), the nominal form of the sentence, the explicit mention of the Name of Majesty (*al-Jalalah*, Allah) and of *ad-din*, the description of it as *al-khalis* (sincere), the fronting (*taqdim*) that conveys exclusivity together with the *lam* which some hold is for that purpose, there is evident indication of concern for the religion, which is the foundation of all good. It has been said: From this it is known that there is no harm in making the sentence an emphasis of the sentence before it according to the last reading, and this is the view of the author of *al-Taqrib*, who said: The two sentences differ in their meaning, one in summary and the other in detail. He thereby refuted the claim that this sentence cannot be an emphasis, based on the reading of al-Farra'.

The truth is that this is an interpretation that should not be relied upon. In *al-Kashshaf* (by al-Zamakhshari): When the Exalted's words ﴿To Allah belongs sincere devotion﴾ function as a justification for His words ﴿So worship Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾, the original would have been: "So to Allah belongs sincere devotion," but it was altered to ﴿Is not sincere devotion due to Allah alone?﴾ for emphasis, as you know that it is the stronger of the two connections. Then it was introduced with the particle of alerting (*harf al-tanbih*), adding emphasis upon emphasis and affirming that what is not sincere is as nothing. Hence, if the justifying resumptive sentence were assumed first without the required attribute that is the essence of the cause, and without the particle of alerting for the stated benefit, the sentence would be discordant, and there would be further discordance from describing the religion as sincere a second time, because this indicates vagueness in the first mention, since there is nothing in it that points to this attribute such that it could be taken as summary and detail. As for making it an emphasis, there is no justification for the attribute mentioned, and because the particle of alerting would not be fitting in that position, since it is used at the beginning of a resumptive sentence, which is contrary to the purpose of emphasis. End of quotation.

The second scholar (al-Allamah al-Thani, i.e. the author of *al-Kashshaf*'s commentator, Ibn al-Munir? — see note below) also stated that making the second sentence an emphasis of the first is invalid according to anyone with knowledge of the styles of speech and the formulation of meanings, for in it there is something that the context of emphasis rejects, and the emphasized element hardly accompanies it. However, in the words of the author of *al-Kashshaf*, that there is nothing in the first that points to the attribute of sincerity such that it could be taken as summary and detail, there is a matter for investigation, since one may say: ﴿lahu al-din﴾ (the religion belongs to Him) means the complete religion, and it is known that the completeness of religion is by its being sincere, so there is in the first clause something that points to this attribute. Yes, that justification has been weakened, whether or not it was accepted before this discussion.

Abu Hayyan said: *ad-din* is in the nominative case as the subject (*fa'il*) of *mukhlisan* (sincere), which is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*). The pronoun referring back to the one in the state (*dhu al-hal*) is omitted according to the view of the Basrans, meaning "the religion is from you." Or *al* (the definite article) in *ad-din* is a substitute for the pronoun, meaning "your religion." On this view, the description of the religion as sincere is the description of its possessor through metaphorical attribution (*al-isnad al-majazi*), like the saying "the poetry of a poet." The verse indicates the nobility of sincerity in worship, and how many verses indicate this.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Yazid al-Raqashi: "A man said: O Messenger of Allah, we give our wealth seeking reward and remembrance; is there reward for us? The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: No. He said: O Messenger of Allah, we give seeking only remembrance; is there reward for us? The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Allah, the Exalted, accepts only what is done sincerely for Him.' Then the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, recited this verse: ﴿Is not sincere devotion due to Allah alone?﴾"

[Page 235]

This is supported by the fact that the meaning of *ad-din* in the verse is obedience, not what was narrated from Qatadah, that it is the testimony that there is no god but Allah, nor what was narrated from al-Hasan, that it is Islam. The Exalted's words ﴿And those who take protectors besides Him﴾, etc., are a confirmation of the truth of monotheism through the falsity of polytheism, so that the truth of sincerity and the falsity of abandoning it may be known from it. In it is encouragement for the sincere and warning for others, which is evident. The relative pronoun refers to the polytheists of Quraysh and others, as narrated from Mujahid. Juwaybir narrated from Ibn Abbas that the verse was revealed concerning three tribes, Amir, Kinanah, and Bani Salimah, who used to worship idols and say: "The angels are daughters of Allah." So the relative pronoun is either a reference to them, or a reference to what includes them and similar worshippers of other than Allah, the Glorified, and this is the apparent meaning. Thus *al-awliya'* (protectors) refers to every false object of worship, such as the angels, Jesus, and idols, peace be upon them. The position of the relative clause is nominative as a subject, its predicate being the following sentence introduced by *anna*. The Exalted's words ﴿We only worship them so that they may bring us near to Allah in closeness﴾ are a circumstantial clause (*hal*) with an implied "saying" from the *waw* of ﴿took﴾, explaining the manner of their associating partners and the non-sincerity of their religion, meaning: they took them, saying so. It is permissible that the implied verb be "they said," and it be a substitute (*badal*) for ﴿took﴾, or that the implied element be that, and it be the predicate of the relative pronoun, and the following sentence a clarifying resumptive sentence (*istinaf bayani*), as if it were said after relating what was mentioned: "What does Allah, the Exalted, do with them?" So it is said: "Allah will judge between them," and so on. The first aspect is the one that comes to mind. Yes, Abdullah, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and Ibn Jubayr read: "They said: 'We worship them...'" etc., but this does not necessarily make it a substitute or predicate. The substitution has been objected to by the author of *al-Kashshaf*, on the grounds that the context is not one of substitution, since there is no repetition of the ruling, because the first is not sufficient for the purpose, out of concern for its importance, especially since omitting the substitute is weak; rather, it contradicts the purpose of mentioning it. The exception is a restrictive exception from the most general of causes. *Zulfa* (closeness) is a verbal noun (*masdar*) emphasizing a verb of different root, meaning: and those who did not devote worship sincerely to Allah, the Exalted, but mixed it with the worship of others besides Him, the Glorified, saying: "We do not worship them for anything except that they bring us near to Allah, the Exalted, in closeness."

It is read as "*nu'bidhum*" with a *damma* on the *nun*, following the vowel of the *ba'*. ﴿Indeed, Allah will judge between them﴾, meaning between them and their opponents, who are those sincere in religion. The object has been omitted, its being indicated by the situation, as in the Exalted's words ﴿We make no distinction between any of His messengers﴾, according to one of the two aspects, meaning between one of them and others. On this is the verse of al-Nabighah:

*Nothing came between the good, had Abu Hajar come safe, except a few brief nights.*

meaning: between the good and me. It has been said that the pronoun refers to the two groups that have been adopted, and the same applies to the plural pronouns in the Exalted's words ﴿concerning that about which they differ﴾. The meaning according to the first view is that He, the Exalted, decides the dispute between the polytheists and the sincere regarding what they differed about of monotheism and associating partners, and each claimed the validity of what he was characterized by, by admitting the sincere monotheists into Paradise and the polytheists into Hell. Or He, glorified is He, distinguishes them in a way from which the state of what they disputed is known. The meaning according to the second view is that He, the Exalted, judges between the worshippers and the worshipped regarding what they differ about, where the worshippers hope for their intercession while they disavow them and curse them, saying or in state, by admitting into Paradise whoever among the worshipped is fit to enter Paradise, and admitting the worshippers, and whoever among those worshipped is not fit to enter Paradise, such as idols, into the Fire. The admitting of the idols into the Fire is not for their punishment but for the punishment of their worshippers by them. What weakens this will come shortly, Allah willing.

Al-Zamakhshari permitted that the preceding relative pronoun refers to the worshipped, with the omission of its returning pronoun and the implicit mention of the polytheists without explicit reference, relying on the context to indicate them. The meaning would be: "And those whom the polytheists took as protectors, saying: 'We only worship them so that they may bring us near to Allah in closeness.' Indeed, Allah will judge between them and their worshippers regarding what the two groups differ about, where the worshippers hope for their intercession while they curse them, by admitting into Paradise whoever among them is fit for Paradise, and admitting the worshippers with their idols into the Fire." It has been criticized: after overlooking what it contains of forced interpretations, it is far from correct. How could it be otherwise, when there is no matter, in what was mentioned of seeking intercession and cursing, about which the two groups differ in a way that requires judgment and decision? Rather, that refers to the difference between the group of monotheists and the group of polytheists in the world concerning religion, which continues until the Day of Resurrection. So reflect, and do not be heedless.

It is also read: "*ma na'buduku-m illa li-tuqarribuna-na*" (We do not worship you except that you bring us near), as a report of what they addressed to their gods. ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide﴾, meaning does not grant success to the guidance which is the way of salvation from what is disliked and the attainment of what is sought, ﴿one who is a liar, a disbeliever﴾ in his very essence, and whose inherent readiness (*isti'dad*) is corrupt, because he is not receptive to guidance. Allah, the Exalted, does not bestow upon receptacles except according to their capacities, as His words indicate: ﴿Our Lord is He who gave everything its creation, then guided it﴾, and His words: ﴿Say: Each acts according to his manner﴾, and His words, Exalted is He: ﴿We did not wrong them, but they were wronging themselves﴾. This is what He, exalted is His state, decreed for one whose readiness is corrupt, by his dying upon misguidance. This was said by some of the eminent scholars. Al-Tabarsi said: He does not guide to Paradise, that is, on the Day of Resurrection, whoever is a liar and disbeliever in this world.

Ibn Atiyyah said: The meaning is that He does not guide the liar and disbeliever while he is in his lying and disbelief. This is nothing at all. The meaning of "one who is a liar, a disbeliever" has been said to include those spoken of and others; and it has been said that they are those spoken of, and their lying lies in their claim that others besides Allah, the Exalted, deserve worship, or in their saying that those they took as protectors besides Allah are daughters of Allah, the Glorified above that by a great exaltation; or that the one taken is the son of Allah, the Exalted. So "one who is a liar" is an apparent noun placed in the position of a pronoun, meaning that Allah, the Exalted, does not guide them, that is, those who take protectors, branding them with lying and disbelief, and this is made a preparation for what follows. Some said: The sentence is a justification for the ruling.

Anas ibn Malik, al-Jahdari, al-Hasan, al-A'raj, and Ibn Ya'mar read "*kadhdhabun kaffarun*" (intensive forms). Zayd ibn Ali read "*kadhubun kafurun*." For these two readings they took "liar" here to mean one firmly established in lying, and likewise they took *kufr* (disbelief) here to mean ingratitude for blessings rather than disbelief in belief, according to Zayd's reading. The Imam (al-Razi) mentioned two possibilities regarding this.

[Page 237]

﴿Had God wished to take a son, He would have chosen whom He wills from among what He creates.﴾ This is a resumptive sentence (istinaf), brought to establish the truth and refute the claim that the angels are God's daughters and that 'Isa is His son. Exalted is God far above that, with a great exaltation. It demonstrates the impossibility of taking a son for Him, glorified be He, absolutely, so that the impossibility of what was said is included in it by primary inclusion. The meaning in summary: if God, glorified be He, wished to take a son, that wish would be impossible, because it would be directed at something impossible, namely taking a son. But it is not permissible for the Creator to have an impossible wish, because such a wish would give preference to some of the possible things over others.

The original sense of the statement is: "If He had taken a son, it would be impossible, because that would entail what contradicts divinity." He then shifted to "if He wished to take a son, it would be impossible for Him to will it," in order to be more emphatic and more forceful. Then this apodosis was omitted and replaced by "He would have chosen" (*li-astafā*), to alert the reader that the possible case is this and not the first. And if this were a kind of taking a son, it would be permissible for Him to have a son, and He, glorified be He, is exalted above that. Thus the implication (*talāzum*) is established, and the denial of the consequent and the affirmation of the antecedent are justified without difficulty.

It is also possible that the meaning is: "If God wished to take a son, it would be impossible and would not be valid." But this is with the intention of negating validity under every supposition, whether He wills it or not, in the manner of: "If he did not fear God, he would not disobey Him." In that case the second part is not negated, and there is no need to explain the implication. And when that is impossible, then what is possible is choosing (*iṣṭifā'*). God, glorified be He, has chosen from His creatures whomever He wills, such as the angels and 'Isa. Yet you should be aware that choosing (*iṣṭifā'*) is not taking (*ittikhādh*). The answer on this view is also omitted and replaced by something that conveys greater emphasis. The reason "*li-astafā*" was not made the apodosis of this is that the meaning would become: "If He wished to take a son, He would have chosen [someone]; and if He did not wish it, He would have chosen [someone] all the more so." In that case, establishing choosing would be the very thing the statement aims to show, just as praising Him by negating disobedience is the aim in the example of the rule, and that is not what is at issue here. On both interpretations, this belongs to the style of the verse:

*"There is no fault in them, except that their swords are notched from the clash of battalions."*

It is also permissible that the meaning of the verse is: "If God, exalted be He, wished to take a son, He would have made the created thing a son, since there is nothing existing besides Him except that it is created by Him. The consequent is impossible because of the complete difference between the created and the Creator, and sonship contradicts that difference. Therefore the antecedent is likewise impossible." And His words, exalted be He, "*He would have chosen whom He wills from among what He creates*," would be in the sense of: "He would have taken it as a son" by way of metaphor (*kināya*). What preceded is better, because of the emphasis it contains, which I have pointed out.

His words, exalted be He, ﴿Glorified is He﴾, confirm what was mentioned about the impossibility of taking a son for God, exalted be He, and reinforce it by showing His transcendence above it. That is, His transcendence is specific to Him, exalted be He. [The word] *subḥānahu* is a verbal noun from *sabaḥa*, meaning "he was far away," or it means "I glorify Him with a glorification fitting for Him," since it is a proper noun for glorification (*'alam al-tasbīḥ*), spoken on the tongues of the servants. Or it means "Glorify Him with a glorification fitting to His majesty, may His majesty be exalted."

His words, exalted be He, ﴿He is God, the One, the Subduer﴾, form a resumptive sentence confirming His transcendence above that as well. Taking a son requires division (*tabaʿḍ*) and the separation of one thing from another. Likewise it requires similarity between the son and the father. The essential, true oneness (*al-waḥda al-dhātiyya al-ḥaqīqiyya*), which is at the highest level of the oneness necessary for Him by decisive rational proofs, rejects division and separation with evident rejection, because these are properties of quantity (*kamm*). Negation of them has been taken into the concept of essential oneness. Therefore it rejects the mentioned taking, and likewise it rejects similarity. This holds whether similarity is explained according to the view of the early Mu'tazila such as al-Jubba'i and his son Abu Hashim, namely sharing in the most specific essential attributes, like the sharing of Zayd and 'Amr in rationality (*nāṭiqiyya*); or whether it is explained according to the view of the verifying scholars of the Maturidiyya, namely sharing in all essential attributes, like his sharing with him in animality (*ḥayawāniyya*) and rationality; or whether it is explained according to what is attributed to al-Ash'ari, namely equality between two things in every respect. Perhaps his intention is close to what passed from al-Maturidi. Otherwise, with equality in every respect, plurality is negated, and so similarity is negated, on the basis of what they established: that essential oneness, just as it requires the negation of quantitative parts, requires the negation of rational plurality, and that similarity requires plurality, and plurality requires the existence of the parts mentioned. So it is said. But in this there is lengthy discussion and much talk, and we will mention some of it, God willing, in the commentary on the Surah of Sincerity (al-Ikhlāṣ). It is better to limit ourselves to the incompatibility of essential oneness with division and separation, because these imply external composition (*tarkīb khārijī*). The philosophers and the theologians (*mutakallimūn*) are agreed on its impossibility in relation to God, exalted be He, and its proof is too clear to be mentioned. Likewise the attribute of Subduer (*qahhāriyya*) rejects taking a son. This was established in several ways. It was said: the reason it rejects that is that the attribute of Subduer requires self-sufficiency (*ghinā dhātī*), which is the highest level of sufficiency, and this requires freedom from matter (*tajarrud 'an al-māda*), while the begetting of a son from a thing requires matter. It was also said: the attribute of Subduer requires complete sufficiency, and this requires complete freedom, which is simplicity (*basāṭa*) in every respect. Then there would be no genus, differentia, matter, form, accidents, or parts, and so on, of what harms complete true simplicity. Taking a son, because of the separation and similarity it involves, harms that simplicity, so it harms sufficiency, and so it harms the attribute of Subduer. He, glorified be He, has indicated that sufficiency negates that He has a son, in His words, exalted be He: ﴿They say: God has taken a son. Glorified is He; He is the Self-Sufficient﴾. It was said: taking a son requires that something separate from Him, exalted be He, and that requires that He be affected and subdued, not an effecting subduer. Exalted is He above that with a great exaltation. Since He, may His majesty be exalted, is the Subduer, as the requirement of divinity demands, it is impossible for Him, glorified and exalted, to have a son. It was also said: the attribute of Subduer is incompatible with cessation (*zawāl*), because if the Subduer accepted it, He would be subdued, since that which removes is a subduer over it. For this reason it is said: "Glory be to Him who subdues the servants by death."

Among the greatest benefits of a son, in their view, is that he takes the place of the father after his cessation. So when there is no cessation, there is no need for a son. This, although it is an argument ad hominem (*ilzāmī*), is not free from discussion, as is not hidden.

Al-Zamakhshari connected His words, exalted be He, ﴿Glorified is He; He is God﴾ etc., with His words, glorified and exalted be He: ﴿And those who take protectors besides Him﴾ etc., on the ground that it confirms the negation that He has any protector (*walī*) and negates that He has a son. Perhaps the explanation of that is not hidden, so reflect.

[Page 238]

Al-Alusi's commentary (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 39, verse 5:

His saying, glorified is He: ﴿He created the heavens and the earth with truth﴾ is a confirmation of what was mentioned earlier of His oneness and dominion. It also contains what you will learn, God willing: that He created this observed world bound up with truth and rightness, comprising wisdoms (hikam) and benefits (masalih).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He wraps the night over the day and wraps the day over the night﴾ explains the manner of His governance over what was mentioned after the explanation of creation. The occurrence of night and day is contingent upon the movement of celestial bodies. Al-takwir (wrapping) in its basic sense is winding and coiling, as in one who winds a turban (kara al-'imamah) on his head and wraps it. The meaning, according to what is related from Qatadah, is that each of them covers the other. It is said that the meaning is that one of them departs and the other covers its place, i.e., clothes it in its place, so that what was white and bright becomes black and dark, and vice versa. Thus the literally covered thing is the place. It is also permissible that what is covered is the night and the day in a figurative sense (al-isti'arah, metaphor), with the place being a container. The intended point is that, since one of them is covering the other, it resembles a garment wrapped around its wearer in concealing him, enveloping him and enshrouding him with it.

Its verification is that, since one of them encompasses everything that the other encompasses, with nothing additional beyond visibility and concealment, its encompassing over what the other encompasses is made an encompassing over it, a figurative (majaz) sense of enveloping, and it is expressed by covering (ghashayan) and wrapping (takwir) because of the aforementioned resemblance.

It is also permitted that the intended meaning is that each of the night and the day conceals the other when it comes upon it, so that in its concealing of the other it is likened to a visible thing that is wrapped around what it has hidden from the gaze of eyes. The first view is preferred because it includes, together with the consideration of concealment, the consideration of coiling and enveloping the extremities. Then, because this is obvious, it is a commonly available comparison.

It is also possible that the meaning is that this one is wound over that one in successive turning, so that this is likened to the successive coiling of the turban's layers one upon another. It has been said: this is the preferred view, because it takes into account what was taken into account in the first, together with regard to the recurrent word "takwir" in it, for it is a winding after a winding. The first also has this, except that the layers of a turban are overlapping, whereas in our case they are alternating. This is not objectionable, for every single winding is literally called a takwir.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas that the meaning is that one of them is carried over the other, and this carrying was interpreted as joining and increase: the night increases over the day and joins it to itself by making some parts of the night into day, so the day lengthens and the night shortens; and the day increases over the night and joins it to itself by His, glorified is He, making some parts of the day into night, so the night lengthens and the day shortens.

To this view al-Raghib (al-Isfahani) went, and it is a clear meaning. On it the verse is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night﴾, according to one opinion. Some of the learned have mentioned that, on the first meaning, there is in it something of His saying: ﴿He made the night and the day alternating (khilfah) for whoever wishes to take heed﴾; on the second meaning there is in it something of His saying: ﴿By the night when it covers﴾ ﴿and by the day when it displays itself﴾; and on the third there is in it something of His saying, glorified is He: ﴿He covers the night over the day, pursuing it swiftly﴾. And it may be that in it there is the metaphor (isti'arah) of the subordinate (tab'iyyah) type, the implicit (makniyyah) type, the imaginative (takhyiliyyah) type, and the representational (tamthiliyyah) type, and the representational is more worthy of consideration. Whatever the case, the form of the present tense (al-mudari') is for indicating renewal (tajaddud).

﴿And He subjected the sun and the moon﴾, making them submissive to His command, mighty and majestic is He. ﴿Each runs for a specified term﴾ explains the manner of their subjection, i.e., each of them runs to the end of its cycle or the limit of its motion. The full discussion of this has already passed. In it is evidence that the sun is in motion. Some disbelievers claimed that it is stationary and that it is the center of the universe. I heard in these days that there appeared among the Europeans, about two years ago, one who claims that it moves around another center, just as the earth moves around itself according to their claim. Some earlier thinkers also claimed things, and they have in astronomy (al-hay'ah) statements other than this, and in them is the worthless and the valuable. However, their denial of the heavens, which the revealed laws speak of, entirely is among the most astonishing wonders, and their feeble speculations lead them to what is even more astonishing than that in the view of sound minds. We ask God, exalted is He, for safety and success. I have a resolve to compose a book in which I will explain, God willing, what is closest to truth among the old and new astronomical systems, moving on the axis of fairness and refraining from the paths of injustice. God, exalted is He, is the one who grants success for that.

﴿Unquestionably He is the Mighty﴾, who is able to punish the persistent, ﴿the Forgiving﴾, toward the sins of the repentant. Or, the Overpowering who is able to hasten punishment upon them, and He, glorified is He, forbears toward them and delays them until a specified term. Then the forbearance toward them is called by the name, and He has left hastening the punishment by forgiveness, which is leaving off punishment, by way of metaphor (isti'arah) because of the relation between them in leaving off. It is permitted that this is of the type of figurative speech (majaz mursal), but the first is more eloquent and better. These two aspects regarding ﴿the Mighty, the Forgiving﴾ were mentioned by al-Zamakhshari. Some thought that what motivated the first was preserving the Mu'tazili school (madhhab al-I'tizal), since it restricted forgiveness to the sins of the repentant, so he left it and said: the Mighty is the one able to do every possible thing, dominant over everything; the Forgiving is the one who did not hasten punishment and the removal of what there is in these crafts of mercy and general benefit. There is no obligation upon us to interpret as he interpreted, and we can say that His forgiveness, exalted is He, is not restricted to the repentant, but He may forgive others too, mighty is His majesty. However, the restriction is more fitting for what preceded, in the most complete fitting. In al-Kashf it is stated that the first of those two aspects fits His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He created the heavens and the earth with truth﴾ in two respects. One of them is what it contains of indication of perfect power and perfect mercy, which requires the punishment of the persistent and the forgiveness of the sins of the repentant. The second is that His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He created the heavens﴾ etc. is brought for two matters: the confirmation of the oneness and dominion mentioned before, as a negation of offspring, indeed as a severing of polytheism from its root, and the ascent to what He had earlier laid down of worship and sincerity lest it depart from the mind. So it was said: ﴿with truth﴾, as was said there: ﴿We have sent down to you the Book with truth﴾. And it was incorporated into it that the sending down of the Book, just as it indicates His entitlement to worship, so likewise the creation of the heavens and the earth is with truth and wisdom, of which is the recompense for what has preceded. So the appended concluding phrase, ﴿the Mighty, the Forgiving﴾, is for encouraging the seeking of forgiveness through worship and sincerity, and warning against the opposite, whether it opposes the foundation of religion, like disbelief, or opposes sincerity in it, like all other sins, in the most complete fitness. He singled out opposition to religion for explicit mention in His saying: ﴿And those who take (others) as allies﴾, etc., as a warning about their condition, because it breaches the protection of salvation, so it deserved warning the most. He hinted at this second by the aforementioned concluding phrase, to complete the intended meaning. The axis of this noble surah rests on the command to worship and sincerity and the warning against disbelief and sins. The second of those two aspects fits the topic of polytheism, and the concluding phrase with it, to emphasize the enormity of what they attributed to Him. When He mentioned the sending down of the Book and followed it with the attributes requiring worship and sincerity, He appended to it His saying, glorified is He:

[p. 240]

﴿Unquestionably, to God belongs the pure religion﴾, according to what its aspect has been verified, and we ourselves have transmitted it from him earlier. Then, when after it was mentioned the magnitude of what they attributed to Him, glorified is He, of polytheism and offspring, and what indicates His transcendence in divinity, it was fitting to append to it His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Unquestionably He is the Mighty, the Forgiving﴾, for the aforementioned emphasis. Al-Allamah al-Tibi preferred this, and it is known from what we have mentioned why the first is preponderant. (End of quote.) The second of the two aspects of relevance is, according to the first view, the better of the two. The verse, according to what some have mentioned, may be connected with what precedes it of creation, wrapping, and subjection.

And His saying, ﴿He created you from a single soul﴾, etc., is another proof of [His] oneness and [His] dominion.

The conjunction [of this clause] to ﴿He created the heavens﴾ is omitted, to signal that it is independent in its indication, and because it relates to the lower world. It also begins with the creation of man, since he is nearer and more wondrous compared with others, in view of what he has of intellect, his acceptance of the divine trust, and other things. Hence it was said:

*You think you are a small body, yet within you the greater world is folded.*

By "the soul" is meant Adam, peace be upon him. His saying, ﴿then He made from it its mate﴾, means Eve, for she was created from the lowest of the left rib of his, peace be upon him, that is, the lowest of the ribs. This may mean she was created from part of it, or that she was created from all of it, and God Most High created for Adam a replacement for it. [The phrase "then He made from it its mate"] is coordinated with an omitted element which is a second attribute of "soul", meaning: from a single soul which He created, then He made from it its mate. Or it is coordinated with "single" (wāḥidah), because it is originally a derived noun (ism mushtaqq), so it is permissible to coordinate a verb with it, as in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿the Splitter of the dawn, and He made the night for rest﴾. The verb is considered past, because the active participle may refer to the past when it does not govern, meaning: from a soul that was unified, then He made from it its mate. This is preferred because it avoids the supposition (taqdīr) which contradicts the basic principle. Or [the phrase is coordinated] with ﴿created you﴾, because there is a difference between the two in indication: although both are signs indicating the sublime attributes mentioned, the creation of Eve from the rib is greater and more provocative of wonder. For this reason He used the word "making" (ja'l) rather than "creating" (khalq). Thus "then" (thumma) indicates a graded sequence (tarākhī rutbī), and it is permissible that the second be of higher rank than the first, or the reverse.

It was also said that God Most High brought out the offspring of Adam, peace be upon him, from his back like tiny particles (dharr), then He created Eve from him. So the meaning of "creating them from him" is bringing them out from his back like particles. Then the coordination is with "created you", and "then" is on its apparent sense. This, however, is not accepted unless it is established as a report traced to the Prophet (marfū'), or as having the same status.

The verse contains three signs: the creation of Adam, peace be upon him, without father or mother; the creation of Eve from his rib; and the creation of his descendants, whose number none can count except God, Mighty and Majestic.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And He sent down for you of the cattle eight pairs﴾, is an argument from another kind of the lower world. "Sending down" (inzāl) is a metaphor for decree and allotment, for when God Most High decrees and apportions, He records that in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawḥ al-Maḥfūẓ), and the angels charged with making it manifest descend with it. Describing it with "descent", although it is a common and familiar meaning like a literal one, the connection between "sending down" and "decreeing" is the appearance after concealment. So in the statement there is a sequential metaphor (isti'ārah tab'iyyah). It has also been permitted that there is a metonymic metaphor (majāz mursal) in it. It is also possible that the figurative usage lies in attributing "sending down" to the cattle, and what is literally sent down is the causes of their life, such as rains. The basis for this is the relation between them. It was also said that by "pairs" is meant the causes of their sustenance, or that "sending down" is made a metaphor for bringing that about through heavenly causes. This, as you see, is [weak]. It was also said that the statement is on its apparent sense, and God Most High created the cattle in Paradise, then sent them down from it. I do not see any soundness in this report.

The cattle are camels, cows, sheep and goats, and they are eight pairs because each of them is male and female. The placing of the two adverbial phrases before the direct object is, as has been mentioned many times, for giving attention to what is placed first and creating anticipation for what is delayed.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿He creates you in the wombs of your mothers﴾, explains how those mentioned among humans and cattle are created, to display what there is in it of the wonders of power. In it there are two instances of *taghlīb* (predominance of one category in grammatical expression): the predominance of the rational over the non-rational, and the predominance of address (khiṭāb) over absence (ghaybah). So it has been said. But the more evident view is that the address is specific, and the form of the present tense indicates gradualness and renewal.

[Page 241]

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿a creation after a creation﴾, is a verbal noun (maṣdar) emphasizing the connection of "after" (min ba'd) with the verb. Otherwise it would be non-emphatic, meaning: He creates you therein as a creation gradually developing into a sound living being, after bones clothed with flesh, after bones bare, after a lump not formed, after a clot, after a drop. So His saying, "a creation after a creation", is merely for repetition, as one says "once after once", not that it is restricted to two creations.

ʿĪsā and Ṭalḥah read ﴿yakhluqukkum﴾ (with the *qāf* assimilated into the *kāf*, i.e., "yakhluqkkum") by the assimilation of the *qāf* into the *kāf*.

﴿In three darknesses﴾: the darkness of the belly, the womb and the amniotic membrane (mashīmah). It has been said: the darkness of the loin, the belly and the womb. The prepositional phrase is connected to "He creates you". Al-Shihāb permitted its connection to "a creation" on the basis that it is non-emphatic. It may also be in apposition to His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿in the wombs of your mothers, that is God, your Lord﴾. The demonstrative refers to Him, Exalted is He, by way of His actions mentioned, in a manner that indicates the remoteness of His station in greatness and majesty. The demonstrative is the subject, and the divine name is its predicate, and "your Lord" is a predicate after a predicate; or the divine name is an attribute or an apposition, and "your Lord" is the predicate. That is: that Exalted One whose acts have been enumerated is God, who nurtures you through the stages mentioned and what follows them, and your Owner, who deserves that worship be specific to Him, Exalted is He. ﴿To Him belongs the dominion﴾ absolutely, in this world and the Hereafter; no other than God has any partnership in that in any way. This sentence is another predicate.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿There is no god but He﴾, is a sentence derived from what precedes it, and it is not explicitly joined with the derivative *fā'* (fā' tafrī'iyyah), relying on the listener's understanding. In *Irshād al-'Aql al-Salīm* it is said that it is another predicate. The *fā'* in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿then how are you turned away?﴾, is for making what follows it a consequence of what has been mentioned.

From His affairs, Mighty and Majestic, that is: how then are you turned away from His worship, Exalted is He, despite the abundance of its requirements and motives, and the complete absence of anything turning you away from it, towards worshipping other than Him, Glorified is He, without any motive toward it, and despite the multitude of things turning you away from it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 39, verse 7 (part 1 of 2):

﴿If you disbelieve﴾ in Him, the Exalted, despite witnessing what was mentioned of the requirements of faith and gratitude, ﴿then indeed God is free of need of you﴾. That is, He, the Mighty and Majestic, has informed you that He is free of need of your faith, and your gratitude is not something whose absence affects Him. ﴿And He does not approve disbelief for His servants﴾, because of the harm it causes them. ﴿And if you are grateful, He approves it for you﴾, that is, gratitude, ﴿for you﴾, because of the benefit it brings you. Whoever holds that moral goodness and badness are known by reason (al-husn wal-qubh al-'aqliyyan, the view that good and evil are rationally discernible) says: non-approval of disbelief is due to its rational ugliness, and approval of gratitude is due to its rational goodness. Approval (al-rida) means either love (al-mahabba) or will (al-irada) together with the absence of objection. Its opposite is anger (al-sukhut), as in the commentary on al-Musayara. So the word "His servants" is on its apparent generality. Some have interpreted it as will without qualification, and its opposite is aversion (al-kurh). These scholars say: He may approve of disbelief, that is, He wills it for some people, such as the disbelievers. Al-Sakhawi transmitted this from al-Nawawi in his book al-Usul wal-Dawabit. Ibn al-Humam transmitted it from al-Ash'ari, and Imam al-Haramayn (al-Juwayni) likewise; so said al-Khafaji in his glosses on the tafsir of al-Baydawi. What I saw in al-Dawabit, which is a very small volume, reads as follows: "The issue: the doctrine of the people of truth (Ahl al-Haqq) is belief in divine decree (al-qadar) and affirmation of it, and that all existing things, good and evil, are by God's decree and predestination, and He wills all of them, yet He dislikes sins, although He, glory be to Him, wills them for a wisdom He knows, exalted is He. Is it said that He, the Exalted, approves of sins and loves them? On this there are two positions among our theologians (al-mutakallimun), related by Imam al-Haramayn and others. Imam al-Haramayn said in al-Irshad: Among the matters on which the people of truth differ is the unqualified use of love and approval. Some of our companions said: it must not be said without qualification that God loves sins and approves of them, because of His saying: ﴿and He does not approve disbelief for His servants﴾. But those among our imams who investigated did not heed the alarm raised by the Mu'tazilah, rather they said: God wills disbelief, loves it and approves of it, and will, love and approval are one and the same meaning. He said: the intended 'servants' in the verse are those granted success in faith, and they are attributed to God as an honour to them, each in His saying: ﴿from which the servants of God drink﴾, that is, their elite, not all of them." End of quotation. So do not overlook the difference between this and what al-Khafaji mentioned. It was also related from Ibn 'Abbas in al-Bahr that "servants" is restricted (to the believers).

It has been said: even with this, it is permissible to take "servants" in its generality, and the meaning becomes: He does not approve disbelief for all His servants, but He approves it and wills it for some of them, like His saying: ﴿No vision perceives Him﴾ according to one opinion. The great scholar of his age, the author of al-Kashf (al-Zamakhshari), has a precious investigation on this point which I have not seen from any other of the eminent scholars. It is that approval is the opposite of anger, and it may be used with ﻋﻦ (ʿan) and with ﺑ (bi), and it may be transitive by itself. So when you say: "I am pleased with so-and-so" (raditu ʿan fulan), it applies to the essence, not to the meaning. But it is in view of a meaning proceeding from him that requires approval. Its opposite is: "I was angered with him" (sakhattu ʿalayhi). There are two differences between them. When you say, "I am pleased with so-and-so for his kindness" (raditu ʿan fulan bi-ihsanihi), the ﺑ does not become definitely causal; it may be a complement (silah), like its use in "I am content with God's decree" (radītu bi-qada'i Allah). When you say, "I was angered with him for his offence" (sakhattu ʿalayhi bi-isa'atihi), causality is definite, so the original form here is to mention the complement; but omission is frequent in usage in contrast with that case, where there is no omission. When it is said, "I am pleased with him" (radītu bihi), this must apply to the meaning, unless it applies to the essence as a preparation for the meaning, to be more forceful. You say: "I am content with God's decree" and "I am content with God, the Lord and Judge." Close to this is: "I heard the speech of so-and-so" and "I heard him speaking." When it is transitive by itself, it may apply to the essence, as in your saying, "I approve of Zayd," though if it is according to the meaning, it is a sign that all of him is approved in that quality, and there is exaggeration in it. It may also apply to the meaning, as in "I approve of the governorship of so-and-so." The first is more common in usage, and it is like the saying "I praised Zayd" and "I praised his knowledge." As for when it is used with the ﻝ (li), it is transitive by itself, as in "I approve this for you," whose meaning will come shortly, God willing. Once this is established, it becomes clear to you that approval originally has the meaning as its object, and it may have the essence as object by way of its connection to the meaning, or by way of preparation. These are three divisions, verified with their examples. In reality it is an inner state that follows the attainment of something agreeable, along with delight in it and contentment. It is therefore, by necessity, other than will, because will precedes the act, while this follows it. This meaning is so clear in the case not used with ﻝ that it is hidden from no one with two eyes. As for the case with ﻝ, the matter becomes confused, because when you say, "I approve of the trade for you" (radītu laka al-tijarah), the one approving of the trade is your addressee, and you have only shown him that the trade is something that ought to be approved. The meaning is not "I approve of your trade," but rather that you are praising the trade for him. So the agreement here is between the object on which the verb acts and what the ﻝ is attached to. Then he may approve of what you approve for him when he recognises the reason for agreement, and he may not approve. There is figurative usage here, either by making approval a metaphor for praise, since everything approved is praiseworthy, or because you have made its being approved for him equivalent to its being approved by you. Know then that approval with respect to God, exalted is His state, is impossible, because no quality arises in Him immediately after any event; so it is metaphorical, just as anger is similarly so. Either it is among the names of attributes if it is interpreted as His will to reward them as one who is pleased with those under his authority is pleased, or it is among the names of acts if praise is intended. And the like of His saying: ﴿God is pleased with them and they with Him﴾ is either by way of reciprocal correspondence (al-mushakalah), or by way of the metaphor mentioned. And the like of His saying: ﴿and I have approved Islam as a religion for you﴾ is definitely of that type in relation to one who can truly be characterised by approval as well. Thus His saying: ﴿and He does not approve disbelief for His servants﴾ is a statement coming in its own manner without any interpretation indicating that He, whose majesty is exalted, does not consider disbelief praiseworthy for His servants as He considers Islam praiseworthy for them and approves of it. As for whether He does not will disbelief to exist, this is not of this type at all, nor is it a requirement of this construction. The leap to restricting "servants" comes from narrowness of outlook. And the saying of the verifying scholars, may God be pleased with them: "Acts of obedience are by God's approval, and sins are not so," is not due to this verse, but because approval in its original sense is impossible for Him, while He has informed us that He approved of the believers for their obedience in many places in His noble Book.

Al-Zamakhshari, may God treat him with His justice, interpreted approval in such contexts as choice (al-ikhtiyar), and choice is inseparable from will. You know its falsehood from what has been verified here. Furthermore, we say: when He, glory be to Him, guided to the truth and warned against falsehood, completing mercy upon all His servants, both groups, by His saying ﴿If you disbelieve﴾ up to His saying, glory be to Him, ﴿He approves it for you﴾, as a notice of His essential self-sufficiency, and that His command to good is not for His benefit from it, nor His prohibition of evil for harm to Him from it; then the shift from the apparent address to His saying ﴿and He does not approve disbelief for His servants﴾ indicates that their servanthood and His lordship, exalted is His majesty, require that He not approve this for them. In it is also that when they are characterised by disbelief, it is as if they have left the rank of servanthood to God, and they remain in perpetual humiliation. Then it is said ﴿He approves it for you﴾ to notify of greater particularity. This is the secret arrangement (al-nazm al-sirri) whose subtleties the human intellect is unable to fully grasp in some respects, and God knows best. End of quotation. It is a weighty statement, worthy of acceptance. However, it may be said that it does not accord with the position of the Salaf, since they do not interpret approval with respect to God, and that being an expression of an inner state with all that was mentioned in its explanation applies only to us; and since His essence, exalted is He, is distinct from all other essences, so His attributes are likewise; therefore the reality of approval with respect to Him is distinct from its reality in us. How far is dust from the Lord of lords! The discussion of this point has been given earlier in a manner that quenches thirst and cures illness. So we say: non-interpretation does not harm in what we are concerned with. Approval, whether interpreted or not, is other than will, by the argument of precedence and succession mentioned earlier. Among those who explicitly stated this is Ibn 'Atiyyah, who said: Consider will, for its reality lies only in what has not yet occurred, while the reality of approval lies only in what has occurred. Consider this in the verses of the Qur'an and you will find it so; though the Arabs may in their poetry use this in place of that by way of figurative speech.

Ibn al-Munir also went to the distinction between them as mentioned here, except that he interpreted approval, and mentioned that it is not possible to take it in the verse to mean will. He censured al-Zamakhshari for that, in return for what al-Zamakhshari said against some of the Ahl al-Sunnah who opposed the Mu'tazilah in their claim that approval and will are identical, and that He, the Exalted, may will what the servant does not do, and the servant may do what He, the Mighty and Majestic, does not will. He said: Suppose the one who persists in this belief has a rust on his heart or a flaw in his scale of reason; does he not claim, or is it not claimed for him, that he is the expert in the crossings of expressions? How then has he strayed from the right path of excellence into the mute desert, and lent his ear deaf to the caller of skill? Unless it is that desire, when it takes hold, makes falsehood appear as truth and covers the plain expression, so away, away! Is it not the requirement of Arabic, let alone the rational laws, that the conditioned is subordinate to the condition, so that the existence of the conditioned before the condition is not conceivable by reason, nor is its past or future relative to the condition conceivable linguistically or by transmission? It is established by the agreement of both groups, the People of the Sunnah and the People of innovation, that God's will for the thankfulness of servants, for example, precedes their thankfulness. Then how is it acceptable to interpret approval as will, when in the verse it is made a conditional and a consequence, and the occurrence of gratitude is made a condition and a reward? What follows rationally is that the intended (the gratitude) precedes the will, and that is approval; and linguistically, the conditioned precedes the condition. So when the invalidity of interpreting approval as will is established, both rationally and by transmission, the correct sense of it is definite, namely recompense for gratitude with what is customary to recompense the one approved of, namely reward and honour. So the meaning of the verse, and God knows best, is: "And if you are grateful, He will reward you for your gratitude with the reward of one approved of." There is no doubt that the reward is future relative to the gratitude, so the condition and consequence run according to their linguistic requirement, and the matter is consistent with the requirements of the rational proofs of the invalidity of the intended preceding the will, rationally. The same is said of His saying: ﴿and He does not approve disbelief for His servants﴾, meaning: He does not reward the disbeliever with the reward of one approved of, but with the reward of one angered against, namely punishment and chastisement. End.

[p. 242] [p. 243] [p. 244]

It may be said: since His saying, ﴿Indeed, God is free of need of you﴾, is an apodosis (jaza') with respect to the report (ikhbar), as was pointed out earlier, then His saying ﴿and He is pleased with it for you﴾ should likewise be an apodosis with respect to that same consideration. Thus it would not follow that the good pleasure itself is postponed.

We reply: this kind of consideration is common in general in the nominal sentence (al-jumla al-ismiyya, a sentence beginning with a noun) whose content is established before the condition (shart), such as His saying: ﴿And if He touches you with good, then He is over all things competent﴾. It also occurs with the past tense verb when it is an apodosis, such as His saying: ﴿If he steals, then a brother of his stole before﴾. But with the present tense verb the matter is not so, and sound taste rejects this consideration in it. Moreover, what need is there for this here? I see it as nothing but support for falsehood, and we seek refuge in God, exalted is He.

Then it is known from the totality of what we have presented that the claim of those who say there is no necessary connection between will (irada) and good pleasure (ridā) is correct, just as good pleasure is not an expression for the reality of will. However, Ibn Taymiyya and his student Ibn al-Qayyim divided will into two kinds: the creational (takwini) and the legislative (shar'i). They mention that sins, such as disbelief and others, occur by the creational will of God, exalted is He, not by His legislative will. On this basis, good pleasure is never separated from the legislative will, so everything willed by God, exalted is He, by the legislative will is something with which He is pleased. This division I cannot conceive of, unless the legislative will is the will by which the willed thing is approved. So reflect on this.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi' in one transmission, Abu 'Amr, and al-Kisa'i read ﴿yarḍahu﴾ with ishbā' ḍamma al-hā' (prolonging the vowel of the hā'). The rule concerning prolonging the hā' or not is this: if the letter before it is silent (sākin), it is not prolonged, as in ʿalayhi and ilayhi; if it is vowelled (mutaharrik), it is prolonged, as in bihi and ghulāmihi. Here, the letter before it is silent by estimation, namely the elided alif of the jussive (al-jāzim). If that alif is considered present in terms of ruling, the hā' is not prolonged, as in the reading of Ibn 'Amir and Hafs. If the consideration of it is set aside, the hā' is prolonged, as in the reading of the one you have heard about. This is the eloquent usage, though it may also be prolonged or shortened (ikhtilas) in other cases. Prolonging it may also be good despite the absence of the condition, for a particular reason.

Abu Bakr read ﴿yarḍahū﴾ with a silent hā' (yarḍahْ). Abu Hatim rejected it and said: it is an error that is not permissible. But it is said that it is a dialect of the Banu Kilab and Banu 'Uqayl, who treat the connected speech (al-waṣl) as if it were pausal (al-waqf).

﴿And no bearer of burdens bears the burden of another﴾: this is an explanation that the disbelief of the disbeliever does not spread to others. The discussion of this sentence has already passed, and likewise His saying: ﴿Then to your Lord is your return, and He will inform you of what you used to do. Indeed, He is Knower of what is within the breasts﴾. So reflect.

﴿When harm touches man﴾, from illness or other adversities, ﴿he calls upon his Lord, turning to Him in repentance﴾, returning from those he used to call upon besides Allah, ﹣ Mighty and Majestic is He ﹣ in times of ease, because he knows they have no power to remove his harm. This is a description of the species through the condition of some of its individuals, like His saying, ﴿Indeed, man is greatly unjust and ungrateful﴾. Abu Hayyan (Abu Hayyan al-Andalusi) inferred that what is meant by "man" is the category of the disbeliever. It was said that it refers to a specific person, such as Utbah ibn Rabi'ah. ﴿Then when He bestows upon him a favor from Himself﴾, meaning He gives him a great blessing from His bounty. The word "khawwala" (to bestow, to entrust) is from "khawal" with two fathas, which means to take care of a thing, that is, to return to it again and again. It is applied to giving, because the generous giver takes care of the one who is raised under his kindness, and his bounty grows through repeated gifts. Some have said that the meaning of "khawwalahu" originally is "he gave him khawal" with two fathas, meaning servants and attendants, or he gave him what needs to be cared for and attended to. It was then generalized to any kind of giving. Al-Zamakhshari allowed that it may derive from "khala yakhulu khawlan" with a sukun on the waw, meaning to boast. This was objected to on the grounds that al-Sihah (of al-Jawhari) explicitly states that "khala" in the sense of "to boast" is a ya'i root, and that "al-khuyala'" in the sense of arrogance clearly indicates this. Furthermore, "khawwala" is transitive to two objects, and deriving it from that does not require that it be transitive to the second object.

It was answered regarding the first point that al-Zamakhshari is among the imams of transmission, and this was established for him, and its root is from "al-khal" which is the mark. The waw was transposed and the ya', then it is said: especially beauty and goodness are a "khal" of that. From it comes "al-khayal" (imagination). As for "al-ikhtiyal" in the sense of arrogance, it is derived from "al-khayal," because he imagined himself above his true rank, or he made for himself a mark of goodness, just as it is said, "a man was made to be impressed (u'jiba)." It has become clear that the derivation suits both meanings. The existence of the ya' is not denied, as evidenced by "al-khuyala'," but there is no obstacle to the existence of the ya' as well. "Al-ikhtiyal" is not derived from "al-khuyala'"; rather "al-khuyala'" is its noun form. Therefore it cannot serve as an obstacle, but it can serve as a proof for the presence of the ya'.

As for the second point, it is not meant that "khawwala" as a doubled form of "khala" in the sense of boasting, so that its transitivity to a second object would be problematic. Rather, it is established in the language for the meaning of "to give," and what was mentioned is an explanation of the source of its derivation. The original meaning considered in its coinage is something similar, and there are many such cases. So the root of "khawwalahu" is "he made him boast about what He bestowed upon him," and then the consideration of that was dropped, and it came to mean simply "he gave him" without qualification.

﴿He forgets what he used to call upon Him for﴾, meaning he forgets the harm which he used to ask Allah to remove and relieve. ﴿Before﴾ the bestowal, so "ma" refers to the harm. "Da'a" is from "al-da'wah" and it is transitive with "ila" (to). It is said: "The muezzin called (da'a) the people to prayer," and "So-and-so called (da'a) the people to his feast." "Al-da'wah" is used metaphorically for "al-du'a'" (supplication). The meaning, taking the omitted noun into account as indicated, is "he forgets what he used to call upon Him for." It is also permissible that "ma" be understood in the sense of "man" (who), to indicate the description and exaltation, referring to Him, Exalted is He, as in His saying, ﴿And He who created the male and the female﴾, and His saying, ﴿Nor are you worshipers of what I worship﴾. The "du'a'" remains in its literal sense, and its transitivity with "ila" is due to implying the meaning of "inabah" (turning in repentance) or "tadarru'" (humble supplication) and "ibtihal" (earnest pleading). The meaning is: he forgot his Lord, whom he used to call upon turning to Him or humbly pleading to Him. This is an acceptable view. As for what has been said, that it is far-fetched, since one does not say "da'a ilayhi" in the sense of "da'ahu" (called Him), and there is no need to make "ma" mean "man," it is rejected because of the excellent fit of the implication and the use of "ma" in a context of exaltation. In al-Irshad, it is stated that in this way there is a signal that his forgetfulness reached the point where he does not know what his object of supplication is, let alone knowing who it is. It was also said that "ma" is verbal (masdariyyah), meaning "he forgot that he was calling," and it was said that it is negative, and the sentence is complete at His saying, ﴿He forgot﴾, meaning he forgot what harm he was in. Then it negates that this disbeliever's supplication was sincerely for Allah, Exalted is He, before that, meaning before the harm. What is there is not hidden.

﴿And he sets up rivals to Allah﴾, partners in worship. The apparent usage of "andad" is that it applies to partners in general. In al-Bahr: "andad" means likes that oppose and contend with one another. Qatadah said: that is, men whom he obeys in disobedience. Others said: idols. ﴿So that he may lead astray﴾ people by that ﴿from His way﴾, Exalted is He, which is monotheism.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and 'Isa read "liyadilla" with a fatha on the ya', meaning "so that he may increase in misguidance," or "so that he may persist in it." Otherwise, the origin of misguidance is not later than the aforementioned setting up of rivals. The lam here is the lam of consequence (lam al-'aqibah), as in His saying, ﴿Then the family of Pharaoh picked him up, so that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾. Nevertheless, this is closer to the literal reality, because the one who sets up rivals here intends by his act the real act of misleading and being misled, even if he does not know in his ignorance that they are misleading and being misled. As for the family of Pharaoh, they did not intend enmity at all by picking him up.

﴿Say﴾, as a threat to that one who sets up rivals, and as a clarification of his condition and final outcome: ﴿Enjoy your disbelief for a little while﴾, meaning a brief enjoyment or a short time. ﴿Indeed, you are among the companions of the Fire﴾, meaning those who abide in it and are punished therein forever. This is a reason for the briefness of the enjoyment, and it contains, in what is not hidden, a despair of salvation and a censure of disbelief, as if it were said: since you have refused what you were commanded of faith and obedience, it is your right to be commanded to abandon it, so that you may taste its punishment.

[Page 246]

﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night﴾, etc., is part of the speech commanded to be said, according to one view. The particle (*amm*, "or") is either connected (*muttasila*), with its counterpart omitted because the context clearly indicates it, as if it were said to him, as emphasis for the threat and in mockery of him: "Are you better in condition and outcome, or is one who is steadfast in the duties of obedience and constant in the functions of worship during the hours of the night, when worship is closer to acceptance and further from ostentation, in both states of ease and hardship, not only at the touch of harm, like your practice, while he is ﴿prostrating and standing﴾?" Al-Akhfash (*al-Akhfash*) held that the first omitted counterpart is as stated, and many agreed with him. There is no harm in this when the meaning is clear. But Abu Hayyan said that such a construction requires a hearing from the Arabs. The accusative of ﴿prostrating and standing﴾ is circumstantial (*hal*), as indicated, meaning combining the two praiseworthy attributes. The one whose circumstance is described is the hidden pronoun in ﴿devoutly obedient﴾.

It has been permitted that the circumstantial clause refers to the pronoun in ﴿fearing﴾ that comes later, placed before it, but there is no need for this. Al-Dahhak read "sājidun wa-qā'imun" with the nominative on each, as a predicate after a predicate. Abu Hayyan permitted that it be a qualifier (*na't*) of ﴿devoutly obedient﴾, but this is not so. The conjunction (*wāw*), as indicated, is for combining the two attributes. The conjunction was left out before ﴿devoutly obedient﴾. It is said: because *qunūt* is general worship, it is not different from prostration and standing, so they were not joined to it, unlike prostration and standing, which are two different attributes, so one was joined to the other. The mention of prostration before standing is because it is more included in the meaning of worship. Most scholars went to the view that it is more excellent than standing, due to the hadith: "The closest a servant is to his Lord is when he is prostrating." And His saying, exalted is He, ﴿fearing the Hereafter﴾ is another circumstance, by overlap or synonymy, or a resumptive clause (*isti'nāf*) that came as an answer to what arose from the description of his state, as if it were said: "What is the matter with him that he does that?" So it was said: "He fears the Hereafter," meaning the punishment of the Hereafter, as Ibn Jubayr read.

﴿And hopes for the mercy of his Lord﴾, so he is saved by that from what he fears, and attains what he hopes for, as is indicated by the mention of the title of Lordship, which suggests the bringing to perfection, together with its attribution to the pronoun of the one who hopes. It does not mean that he fears only the harm of this world and hopes only for its good. The particle may be disjunctive (*munqati'a*), and the reversal in it is for transition (*idrāb*) from rebuke by imposing an answer that compels acknowledgment of the clear difference between them, as if it were said: "Rather, is one who is devoutly obedient, etc.?" Al-Zamakhshari and others estimated: "Like you, O disbeliever." Al-Nahhas said: it has the meaning of *bal* ("rather"), and *man* has the meaning of *alladhī* ("the one who"), and the estimate is: "Rather, the one who is devoutly obedient, etc., is more excellent than what is before him." Abu Hayyan in al-Bahr criticized this, saying that there is no excellence for the one before him so that this would be made more excellent. Rather, the predicate is estimated: "from the people of Paradise," because its opposite indicates it, I mean ﴿Indeed you are from the people of the Fire﴾. It is not far-fetched to estimate: "more excellent than you," and this would be by way of mockery.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Hamzah, al-A'mash, Isa, Shayba, and al-Hasan in one narration read "amman" with the *mīm* lightened. Al-Akhfash and Abu Hatim considered it weak, but no attention is paid to that. It is explained by the entry of the interrogative particle of affirmation (*hamzat al-istifhām al-taqrīrī*) upon *man*, and the counterpart is omitted, i.e., "the one who is devoutly obedient, etc., is better, or you, O disbeliever?" Similar to it in omitting the counterpart is the poet's saying:

*Daʿānī ilayhā al-qalbu innī li-amrihi / samīʿun fa-mā adrī arushdun ṭilābuhā*

[My heart called me to her, and I hear its command, / but I do not know whether her pursuit is right guidance.]

He intended: "or is it error?" Al-Farra' said: the *hamzah* is for calling, as if it were said: "O one who is devoutly obedient." And His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Say﴾ was made an address to him. Abu Ali al-Farisi weakened this view, and it is so. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Say﴾ means: say to him also, as an explanation of the truth and a clear statement of it, and an alert to the nobility of knowledge and action: ﴿Are those who know equal to those who do not know?﴾ So that they act according to the requirement of their knowledge, and are devoutly obedient in the night, prostrating and bowing, fearing the Hereafter and hoping for the mercy of their Lord, ﴿and those who do not know﴾, so they act according to the requirement of their ignorance and error, like your practice, O disbeliever, who sets up rivals to God, exalted is He. The interrogation is to alert that the state of the first ones at the highest ascents of goodness, and the state of the last ones at the furthest levels of evil, is so evident that it is hardly hidden from anyone, whether fair or obstinate. And it is known from what we have mentioned

[Page 247]

that the intended meaning of "those who know" is the practising scholars of religion. Some eminent scholars stated this intention under both the connected and disjunctive estimates. The discourse is an explicit denial of equality between the devoutly obedient and others, contained in the two interrogative particles, I mean the *hamzah* and *am*, on the connected reading, or by way of comparison on the disjunctive reading. And on the reading with the lightened *mīm* as well, he said: this expression was only used to indicate that this is the requirement of knowledge, and that knowledge which does not result in action is not knowledge in the sight of God, exalted is He.
