Whether it is taken as placing an apparent noun in place of a pronoun for the indicated meaning above, or as a resumed rebuking question, clarifying the first from the aspect of explicit statement, and from the aspect that they were described with another attribute that requires their being characterized by those qualities, and their distinction from the class of those who are not so characterized. This is more eloquent and more apparent in wording than His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Say﴾. It was permitted that the speech be presented by way of comparison, so that it establishes the denial of equality, not an explicit statement of the requirement of the first. That is, just as there is no equality between the one who knows and others in your sight without doubt, so likewise you should not doubt the denial of equality between the mentioned devoutly obedient one and others. That it is for explicit denial of equality, and taking ﴿those who know﴾ to mean the practising scholars of religion, as you have heard, is not what should be chosen over it, in order to increase the benefit. As for one who doubts this clear matter, it is not far from him to doubt this clear matter as well, by its answer: abstaining from ignorance is rooted in natures, unlike the first. The words of many indicate that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Is one who﴾ etc., is not within the scope of the speech, and the meaning upon it is as in the first, with a slight change that is not hidden.

It is reported from Ibn Umar, may God be pleased with them both, that he recited ﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient﴾ to the end of the verse, and said: it was revealed concerning Uthman ibn Affan. Ibn Sa'd in his Tabaqat, Ibn Mardawayh, and Ibn Asakir reported from Ibn Abbas that it was revealed concerning Ammar ibn Yasir. Juwaybir reported from him that it was revealed concerning Ammar, Ibn Mas'ud, and Salim, the freedman of Abu Hudhayfah. From Ikrimah: limited to Ammar. From Muqatil: by "one who is devoutly obedient" is meant Ammar, Suhayb, Ibn Mas'ud, and Abu Dharr. In a narration of al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas: and Abu Bakr and Umar. Yahya ibn Salam said: the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace. The apparent meaning is that it refers to whoever is characterized by this without specification. Its being revealed concerning those you know does not prevent this. In it is evidence for the excellence of fear and hope.

Al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, and Ibn Majah reported from Anas, who said: "The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, entered upon a man who was in his death throes, and he said: 'How do you find yourself?' He said: 'I hope and I fear.' Upon him be prayers and peace: 'Fear and hope do not gather in the heart of a servant in such a situation except that He gives him what he hopes for, and secures him from what he fears.'"

In it is also a refutation of those who blame worship out of fear of the Fire and hope for Paradise, and this is Imam al-Razi, as al-Jalal al-Suyuti said. Indeed, worship for that alone is blameworthy. Some even said that whoever says "If there were no Paradise and Fire, I would not worship God, exalted is He" is a disbeliever, in the sense of denying intrinsic deserving. In it is also evidence for the excellence of night prayer, and that it is more excellent than daytime prayer. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Are they equal﴾ etc., indicates the excellence of knowledge, the elevation of its rank, and that ignorance is the opposite. Some used it to show that the ignorant man is not equal to the learned woman, just as he is not equal to the daughter of a learned man. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Only those of understanding are reminded﴾ is an independent statement, not included, according to all, in the speech commanded, but coming from Him, exalted is He, after the command with what contained the awe-inspiring warnings restraining from disbelief and sins, to explain that they have no effect on the hearts of the disbelievers because their minds are disordered, as in the saying:

*ʿūjū fa-ḥayyū li-nuʿmā dimnata al-dār / mādhā tuḥayyūna min nuʾyin wa-aḥjār*

[Halt, and greet the ruins of the abode of Nu'ma, / why do you greet a mound of earth and stones?]

It is also like a preparation for addressing the believers individually afterwards, and turning away from others. That is: only those of pure intellects, free of defects, are admonished by these clear proofs. As for these, they are far removed from that. It is also read as *yadhdhakkaru* with assimilation (*idghām*).

﴿Say: O My servants who have believed, fear your Lord.﴾ The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was commanded to admonish the believers and to urge them toward taqwa (God-consciousness) and obedience, following the restriction of the admonition to people of understanding (ulu al-albab). This implies that they are the ones addressed, meaning: say to them this very statement of mine. It also honours them by attributing them to the Divine Name (the pronoun of majesty), and it adds emphasis to the importance of what is commanded, for conveying the very command of Allah, exalted is He, is more effective in making obedience to it obligatory.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For those who do good in this world there is a good [reward]﴾ and so on, is a justification of the command, or of the obligation to obey it. The prepositional phrase (al-jar wa al-majrur) is related to a deleted element, which is the predicate placed first (khabar muqaddam). His saying, glorified is He: ﴿in this world﴾ is related to "do good" (ahsanu). The demonstrative (ism al-ishara) is used for bringing the matter to mind (li al-ihdar). His saying, blessed and exalted is He: ﴿a good [reward]﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and its tanwin is for magnification, meaning: for those who do good in the world there is a good [reward] in the Hereafter, what a good reward! By it is meant Paradise.

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And Allah's earth is spacious﴾ is a parenthetical clause (jumla mu'tarida), intended to remove what might be imagined from the excuse of negligence due to not being able to settle in one's homeland, so as to observe the commands and prohibitions as they should be observed. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Only those who are patient will be given their reward without reckoning﴾ is a continuation of the parenthetical clause. It is as if it were said: fear your Lord, for those who do good in this world have Paradise in the next, and there is no excuse for those who fall short in doing good due to not being able to settle in their lands, for the earth of Allah, exalted is He, is spacious and His lands are many; so let them migrate if they cannot settle in them, and let them emigrate to their Lord to attain His good pleasure, for in return for that they have what Paradise falls short of and for which every trial becomes sweet.

And it is as if, when He, glorified is He, removed their pretext by stating that in Allah's earth there is ample room, the thought came into their minds: will we be, and will those who are able to do good in their own town, carefree and at ease, equal? So they were answered: ﴿Only those who are patient﴾, namely those who endured emigration and the separation from what they love, and who followed the examples of the Prophets and the righteous, ﴿will be given their reward without reckoning﴾. Its original form was: "Indeed you will be given your rewards without reckoning," in the second person (al-khitab), but this was changed to the third person (al-munazzal) to draw attention to the fact that what necessitates this is their patience. Thus it conveys that you will be given your rewards for your patience, just as the reward of those before you was given for their patience. This is to be understood in its generality, encompassing patience upon every trial, though it is not restricted to patience in emigration; rather it was mentioned in the verse for that reason, and to include those who are patient through the pain of emigration with primary inclusion.

The prepositional phrase is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), either from the reward, meaning: they will be given their reward being without reckoning, and this is by being poured out for them in handfuls and poured upon them in abundance; or from "those who are patient," meaning: they will be given that while being without reckoning for it. The intended meaning in both cases is exaggeration in abundance, and this is what is meant by the saying of Ibn 'Abbas: "No reckoner can reach it or know it." It is also permissible to make the circumstantial clause from "those who are patient" refer to those who are not reckoned at all. What is more evident is what conveys exaggeration in the abundance of the reward. The meaning of restriction (qasr) is: those who are patient will not be given their reward except without reckoning; the prepositional phrase is made a circumstantial clause of the accusative or nominative element, because the restriction falls on the final part, and in this there is all the attention to the matter of the reward that there is. As for its being specific to the patient rather than others, it follows from the attaching of the judgment to a derived noun (al-mushtaqq).

This is what is said. It is also reported from al-Suddi that His saying: ﴿in this world﴾ is related in meaning to "a good [reward]." Accordingly, it was said that it is then a circumstantial clause from ﴿a good [reward]﴾, but this was refuted on the basis that the latter is a subject (mubtada'), and a circumstantial clause from it is not permitted according to the correct view. If it is said that it is taken as the agent of the adverbial (fa'il al-zarf), it is answered that this is only possible according to the school of al-Akhfash, which is weak.

It was also said that it is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun concealed in the predicate, which refers back to ﴿a good [reward]﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is an explanation (bayan) of ﴿a good [reward]﴾, and the estimated sense is: it is in the world, and by it is meant health and well-being, meaning: for those who do good there is health and well-being in this world. In al-Kashf he said: he preferred that it be an explanation, although it may also be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun referring back to ﴿a good [reward]﴾ in the predicate, because the meaning on the explanation reading is not that of restriction by a circumstantial clause; this is because the meaning on this view is that for those who do good there is a small reward in this world, which is health and well-being, while the full recompense of their rewards is in the Hereafter. Had it been restricted by a circumstantial clause, it would not fit, as is not hidden. The right placement of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah's earth is spacious﴾ on this view is that it be a parenthetical clause, removing what may stir in some souls of contrary opinion about that reward through the difference of air, soil and other things that lead to ailments in the body. So it is said: Allah's earth is spacious, so no one lacks a place suited to his condition; let him therefore move from it to another if it does not suit him. Then there is in this an indication that whoever has made the earth, with its length and breadth, into adjoining plots for the completion of their revival and their comfort, his blessings must be met with gratitude, so that they may be counted among those who do good.

Then it was said: ﴿Only those who are patient﴾, meaning: the full payment of the reward to these doers of good happens only in the Hereafter, and what they attained in this world is the swift portion of their share. As for the reward given in full without reckoning, that is for the patient. And whoever We have deprived of that swift [reward] is for purification and drawing near. In this there is consolation for the people of trials, and encouragement for the worshippers to bear the hardships of acts of worship, and an incitement to persist in acts of obedience. Then he said: this too is a good and subtle view, but the preferred view is the first, for several reasons:

The first: that the parenthetical clause removing the pretext for negligence is more evident, because that is the intended purpose of the context, as appears from His saying: ﴿Fear your Lord﴾.

The second: that it corresponds to what came in revelation, such as: ﴿Was not Allah's earth spacious, so that you might migrate therein?﴾ and ﴿Indeed My earth is spacious, so worship Me alone﴾.

The third: that the attachment of the adverbial to the earlier mentioned element is the default, unless some diverting factor occurs.

The fourth: that on that estimate it is not consistent nor predominant, for the good [reward] in that sense is more complete in the case of opponents, and the claim that it is a respite for them and not a good [reward] is not apparent, since He, glorified is He, said: ﴿But when good came to them, they said: "This is ours."﴾ End quote. By my life, what he preferred by preference is indeed correct, while what he found good and subtle is neither good nor subtle. What al-Tabarsi related from al-Suddi is the interpretation of the good [reward] in this world as good repute, a fine remembrance, health and safety. Some of them interpreted it as the guardianship (wilaya) of Allah, exalted is He, and on that basis the opponents have no share of it. There are other views on the verse. From 'Ata': "Allah's earth is Medina." Abu Hayyan said: on this view, "did good" means "emigrated," and "a good [reward]" means rest from enemies. Some people said: Allah's earth is Paradise, and Ibn 'Atiyya criticised this as an arbitrary claim with no proof.

Abu Muslim said: there is nothing to prevent that, for He, exalted is He, commanded the believers to taqwa, then made clear, glorified is He, that whoever fears Him will have a good [reward] in the Hereafter, which is abiding in Paradise. Then He, majestic is His state, made clear that Allah's earth is spacious, by His saying: ﴿And We have made the earth an inheritance; we dwell in Paradise wherever we will﴾ and His saying: ﴿And a Paradise whose breadth is the heavens and the earth, prepared for the God-fearing﴾. The preference lies with what you heard first, and in it is chosen the inclusion of the good [reward] of the worldly and the otherworldly goods. By doing good is meant performing good deeds, both of the heart and of the body.

The Prophet (ﷺ) said in explaining it, in the hadith of Jibril (peace be upon him): "That you worship Allah as though you see Him; and if you do not see Him, then indeed He sees you."

It is reported in some traditions that the verse was revealed concerning Ja'far ibn Abi Talib and his companions when they resolved to emigrate to the land of Abyssinia. In it there is, of the evidence for the virtue of the patient, what there is.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 39, verse 11:

﴿Say: Indeed, I have been commanded to worship Allah, making the religion sincerely His﴾. That is, free from everything that corrupts it, such as associating partners with Him (shirk), showing off (riya'), and other things besides that. He (ﷺ) was commanded to explain what he himself had been commanded of sincerity (ikhlas) in the worship of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, which is an expression of what the believers were commanded regarding piety (taqwa), as an emphasis in urging them to carry out what they were charged with, and as a preparation for what follows, namely what the polytheists were addressed with.

The non-mention of the one who issues the command is because it is definitely Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. It has been said that it is to indicate that this command is something that ought to be obeyed, whether it proceeds from Him, exalted is He, or proceeds from other than Him, glorified is He.

[Page 250]

﴿And I have been commanded to be the first of the Muslims.﴾ That is: and I have been commanded to this for the purpose of being the foremost of the Muslims in this world and the Hereafter. This is because attaining the prize of precedence in religion comes through sincerity in it, and his sincerity, upon him be blessings and peace, is more complete than the sincerity of every sincere person. Thus, by "firstness" is meant firstness in nobility and rank. The conjunction (ʿaṭf) serves to differentiate the second term from the first by restricting it with a cause (ʿillah). It also indicates that the act of worship mentioned, just as it requires the command to it for its own sake, also requires it for what follows from it of precedence in religion. The Basrans (al-Baṣriyyūn, the grammarians of Basra) held that the object of the command is omitted and that the lām is causal (taʿlīliyyah) in this verse and similar ones. Others held that it is superfluous (zāʾidah), and they cited as evidence its omission in the words of the Exalted: ﴿And I have been commanded to be among the Muslims﴾, and ﴿And I have been commanded to be among the believers﴾, and ﴿I have been commanded to be the first of those who submit﴾. All of these allow for the lām to be understood, so do not overlook this. It is not added except with inna, either explicitly or by implication, not with a plain noun. This is because the original form of the direct object is that it be a plain noun, so the lām is added as a substitute for the departure from the original form to what takes its place, just as the sīn in istaṭāʿa is added as a substitute for the departure from the original form, which is aṭwaʿa. Although this addition is anomalous by analogy, since it has become frequent in usage, its use is permitted in the Qur'an and in eloquent speech. The same applies to its addition with the verb of will (irādah), as in: aradtu li-an afʿala ("I wanted to do"). Al-Zamakhsharī (al-Zamakhsharī) made the reason for its addition with that verb that, since the verb contains the meaning of will, the lām is added as an emphasis for it. He also gave a reason for its addition with the imperative verb as well, especially since in their view demand (ṭalab) and will (irādah) are of one category. As for the meaning, there are several views: (1) "that I be the first to submit in my time and among my people," that is, submission in accordance with the command; (2) "that I be the first of those whom I call to Islam to submit"; (3) "that I be the first to call himself to what he calls others to, so that I may be a model followed in my words and deeds together, and my character not be that of the kings who command what they do not do"; and (4) "that I do the deeds by which I deserve firstness and nobility, from the deeds of the foremost, as an indication of the cause, which are the deeds by which nobility is deserved as an effect, namely firstness, and the nobility mentioned in the sublime composition." Al-Zamakhsharī mentioned this. In al-Kashf (al-Kashf, by al-Ṭībī): "The preferred of the four views is the second, for it is the frequently repeated and common one in the Noble Qur'an, and it includes the remaining meanings: the agreement of word and deed, and the necessity of firstness of nobility from firstness of founding, although it does not state that he is commanded to be more noble and more foremost. So understand."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 39, verse 13:

﴿Say: Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord,﴾ by abandoning sincerity (ikhlas) and inclining toward the polytheism (shirk) that you hold to. It has also been permitted that the wording be general, meaning: I fear, if I disobey Him in any of the sins, ﴿the punishment of a tremendous day.﴾ That day is the Day of Resurrection. Its description as "tremendous" is due to the magnitude of the calamities (dawahi) and terrors (ahwal) in it. This is a metaphor (majaz) in the temporal adverb (zarf), or in the predication (isnad), and the latter is more eloquent. For this reason the punishment was not described by that quality, and the purpose of saying this to them is to threaten them, and to hint to them that he, peace and blessings be upon him, despite his greatness, if he were to disobey God Most High, would not be safe from the punishment, so how about them?

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 39, verse 14:

﴿Say: It is Allah I worship﴾, not other than Him, glorified is He, neither independently nor as a partner, ﴿sincerely devoting my religion to Him﴾. This is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the subject of ﴿I worship﴾. It has been said that it is emphatic (mu'akkidah), since the fronting of the object (taqdim al-maf'ul) has already conveyed restriction (hasr), and this indicates his sincerity free from both apparent and hidden shirk. It has also been said that it is informative (mu'assisah). The sincere devotion of religion to Him, exalted is He, has been explained as worshipping Him, glorified is He, for His own sake without seeking anything, like the saying of Rabi'ah: "Glory be to You, I did not worship You out of fear of Your punishment nor out of hope for Your reward." Or it may be explained as freeing it from shirk in both its forms, and that there be with it nothing else that would taint it, as has been indicated just above. The difference between this and His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿Say: Indeed I have been commanded﴾ etc., is that the latter is a command to declare that he, upon him be blessings and peace, has been commanded to worship Him, exalted is He, sincerely devoting the religion to Him, whereas this is a command to report his compliance with the command in the most emphatic and forceful manner, to show his firmness in the religion (ﷺ), and to cut off their empty hopes, since the disbelievers of Quraysh invited him (ﷺ) to their religion, and this was revealed for that reason, and as a preparation for threatening them with the saying of the Mighty and Majestic:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 39, verse 15:

Page 251

﴿So worship what you will﴾ other than Him, [Exalted and Majestic is He], "[and it is] ﴿from besides Him﴾." In this is an indication of the intensity of His anger toward them that is not hidden: it is as though, since they did not desist from what they were forbidden, they were commanded to do it so that punishment would descend upon them. ﴿Say: Indeed, the losers﴾, i.e., those who are complete in loss, which is the squandering of what is theirs and the destruction of what is indispensable, since they combine the greatest kinds of loss, ﴿who have lost themselves and their families﴾ by their choosing disbelief for both of them. So the "families" here means their followers whom they led astray; that is, they squandered their own selves, squandered their families, and destroyed both. ﴿On the Day of Resurrection﴾, when they enter the Fire, where they expose both of them to everlasting punishment and cast them into a destruction beyond which there is no destruction. Had the Day of Resurrection been retained in its literal sense, so that their state would become manifest on it and the beginning of their loss would be realized, it would be correct according to what has been said. It has also been said: the "families" means followers in general, and their losing them is because, if they were among the people of the Fire, they too have lost, just as they lost themselves; and if they were among the people of Paradise, they have departed from them in a departure with no return thereafter. It has been objected that the thing feared is the departure of one who, if he returned, would benefit the loser, and that is not conceivable in the latter case. It has also been said: the "families" means what Allah, Exalted is He, has prepared for those among the elite who enter Paradise; that is, "and they lost their families who would have been theirs in Paradise had they believed." Abd al-Razzaq and Abd ibn Humayd related from Qatadah, who said: "There is no one for whom Allah, Exalted is He, has not prepared a family in Paradise, if he obeys Him." And he related something similar from Mujahid, and it is also narrated from Maymun ibn Mihran, and all of them mentioned this in regard to the verse. Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Abbas that he also said regarding it: "They lost their families from among the people of Paradise, whom they had been prepared for had they acted in obedience to Allah, Exalted is He, so they were cheated of them." This is also what the statement of al-Hasan seems to require, for it is related from him that he interpreted "the families" as the Houris (al-hur al-'in). It is not hidden that carrying the verse upon this meaning is not free from remoteness.

Whatever the case, the intent is not merely to define the complete in loss by what has been mentioned, but to state that they are the ones addressed by what preceded, either by making the relative clause (al-mawsul) a reference to them, or by making it a reference to what they are included in by initial inclusion. As for what is in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Unquestionably, that is the manifest loss﴾, it is a resumption of the sentence, its opening with the particle of alertness (ala), and the indication with "that" (dhalika) to the great remoteness of the rank of the thing pointed to in evil, and that because of its greatness it is like something perceptible; the inserting of the pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl); the definiteness of "loss" (al-khusran); bringing it in the form fu'lan, which is more emphatic than fu'l; and describing it as "manifest" (al-mubin), which indicates the perfection it possesses, its heinousness, and that there is no kind of loss beyond it, which is not hidden.

Al-Alusi's commentary (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 39, verse 16:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿For them there will be canopies of fire from above them﴾ to the end of the verse, is a kind of explanation of their loss, after its terror was described in a vague manner, with lam (for them) being the predicate of "canopies" (ẓulal). "From above them" is related to a omitted element and is a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) from its pronoun in the preceding adverbial phrase, not from the canopies themselves, because a circumstantial phrase from the subject (mubtada') is weak. Making it (the pronoun) the agent of the adverbial phrase in that case follows the view of al-Akhfash, and it is weak. And ﴿of fire﴾ is an attribute of "canopies" (ẓulal).

The speech runs in the manner of mockery toward them, and for this reason it was said to them. He expressed what was above them of the fire by "canopies" (ẓulal), meaning: for them, from above them, are many canopies, piled one upon another, consisting of fire. ﴿And from beneath them canopies﴾ also consisting of fire, and what is meant is many layers of it. Calling them canopies (ẓulal) is by way of mushakala (matching of terms). It has been said: they are canopies for those beneath them in another layer of the layers of the Fire. This does not hold generally for the people of the last layer among these losers, unless it is said that they are for the devils and others like them who are not mentioned here. It has also been said that what is beneath them blazes, and something rises from it until it becomes a canopy, so it was called a canopy in consideration of what it eventually became. But this is not the right view. What is meant is that the Fire encompasses them. ﴿That﴾ dreadful punishment ﴿is what Allah causes His servants to fear﴾: He, glorified be He, reminds them of it through the verses of warning so that they may fear, ﴿so fear Me, O My servants﴾

صفحة 252

and so that they avoid what would bring them into it. Some scholars restricted "servants" to the believers, because they are the ones who benefit from the warning, while others gave it a general sense.

Likewise in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O My servants, so fear Me﴾ — do not expose yourselves to what would incur My wrath. The meaning of the command differs according to the two interpretations, as is not hidden. This is an admonition from Allah, majestic is His majesty, and His bounty is all-encompassing, containing the utmost gentleness and mercy. It was also read "Yā ʿibādī" with a yā' (ya).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 39, verses 17–18:

﴿And those who avoid the Taghut (false deities)﴾ etc. Ibn Zayd said: It was revealed concerning three men who used to say in the pre-Islamic period, "There is no god but Allah": Zayd ibn Amr ibn Nufayl, Salman, and Abu Dharr. Ibn Ishaq said: It refers to Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Sa'id ibn Zayd, and al-Zubayr. This was because when Abu Bakr embraced Islam, they heard of it and came to him and said, "Have you become a Muslim?" He said, "Yes," and he reminded them of Allah the Exalted. So they all believed, and it was revealed concerning them. It is definitive (muhkamah) and applies to people until the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Taghut (the false deity) is on the pattern fa'lut, from al-tughyan (transgression), as they said la-fa'ul (a pattern used for certain words), as it was said with the lam placed before the ayn, as in ṣā'iqah and ṣāqi'ah. The derivation shows this, and that ṭawagha and ṭayagha are both unused as roots.

Its original form is ṭaghayut or ṭaghawut, from either the yā' or the wāw, because ṭaghā (yaṭghā) and ṭaghā (yaṭghū) are both attested in Arabic. Al-Jawhari transmitted this and transmitted that al-ṭughyan and al-ṭaghawan have the same meaning. Al-Raghib likewise. Its plural, al-ṭawāghīt, indicates that the plural was formed on the wāw. Their saying "from al-ṭughyan" does not mean specifically the yā', but rather the meaning. According to what is in al-Ṣiḥāḥ, it is: the soothsayer, the devil, and every head of misguidance. Al-Raghib said: It is an expression for every transgressor and every object of worship besides Allah the Exalted. It is also applied to the sorcerer, the soothsayer, the rebellious jinn, and whatever turns one away from good. It is used for both the singular and the plural.

Al-Zamakhshari said concerning this surah: It is not applied to anything other than Satan. He mentioned that there are intensifications in its form, for the pattern fa'lut is for emphasis, which is why they said al-raḥamut (the vast mercy). There is also intensification in naming it by the verbal noun, and in the transposition (qalb), for it indicates exclusivity, as in al-jāh (status). He applied it in al-Nisā' to Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and said: He was called ṭāghūt because of his excessive transgression and enmity toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or by way of likeness to Satan. Perhaps he meant: it is not applied in the literal sense to anything other than Satan, and he seems to have made Ka'b, in the first of the two senses, one of the devils of mankind. In al-Kashf: It seems that when he saw it as a verbal noun originally, transferred to a concrete object and frequently used for Satan, he ruled that it is literally applied to him after the transfer, and figuratively to the rest, because the connection is evident, either as a metaphor or by consideration of the harmony of meaning. What is most likely in the mind is that al-ṭāghūt was originally a verbal noun transferred to one who reaches the utmost extent of transgression and exceeding of bounds. Its use for an individual of this general concept, whether Satan or other, is literal, and is figurative according to what they have established regarding the use of a general term for one of its individuals, like the use of "human" for Zayd. Its prevalence for Satan is only because he is the head of the transgressors.

Mujahid interpreted it here as Satan. It is permissible to interpret it as devils, in the plural, according to what you have heard from al-Raghib. This is supported by the reading of al-Hasan: "those who avoid the ṭawāghīt."

﴿That they should worship them﴾ is a badal ishtimal (inclusive apposition) of al-Taghut. Worship of other than Allah the Exalted is worship of Satan, since he is the one who commands it and makes it attractive. If al-Taghut is interpreted as idols, the matter is obvious.

﴿And turn penitently to Allah﴾ means they turned to Him, the Glorified, turning away from all else with complete devotion. ﴿For them is good news﴾ of reward from Allah the Exalted, conveyed through the tongues of the Messengers, peace be upon them, or the angels, at the time of death, when they are gathered, and after that.

﴿So give good news to My servants﴾ ﴿who listen to the word and follow the best of it﴾. This is praise of them, that they are critics in religion, distinguishing between the good and the better, and the excellent and the more excellent. When two matters present themselves, one obligatory and one recommended, they choose the obligatory. Likewise the permissible and the recommended.

[Page 253]

It was said: They listen to the commands of Allah the Exalted and follow the best of them, such as retaliation (qiṣāṣ) and pardon, vindication, overlooking, and disclosure or concealment, due to His saying, the Exalted: ﴿That you pardon is nearer to piety﴾ and ﴿If you conceal them and give them to the poor, it is better for you﴾. The difference between the two interpretations is that this one is more specific, because it is restricted to commands in which there is choice between the preferable and the more preferable, such as pardon and retaliation for example. It is as if it were said: they follow the better of the two statements transmitted concerning a particular matter. In the first, they follow the better of the two statements absolutely, like obligation in relation to recommendation, for example.

It is reported from al-Zajjaj: they listen to the Qur'an and other things, and then follow the Qur'an. It was said: they listen to speech from whoever it comes, and follow the one most worthy of acceptance, and the one who guides them most to the truth. It follows from their being described this way that they distinguish the ugly from the good and avoid the ugly. By "these servants" is meant those who avoided and turned penitently, and no others, so that the arrangement is not disrupted. The saying of the Exalted, ﴿So give good news﴾, is connected to His saying, the Glorified: ﴿For them is good news﴾. The apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun in order to honor them by attributing them to Him, and to repeat the explanation of their deservingness, and to indicate that they are critics, eager to prefer obedience and to seek greater nearness to Allah the Exalted. In this there is confirmation of turning penitently and a fine completion.

It was said: The pause is at "My servants," so that "those who" is the subject, whose predicate is the clause of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah has guided﴾, that is, to His religion. The sentence is a resumption, repeating the description of those about whom the discourse was resumed. What came before is preferable, because of the benefits mentioned previously, from placing the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun and completion, since that is not complete without the description. Also, the impetus for the question answered by the clause after His saying, the Exalted, ﴿So they follow the best of it﴾, is stronger, and that is the basis for the goodness of resumption. ﴿And those are the people of understanding﴾, that is, they are the possessors of sound intellects, free from the interference of illusion and the contention of desire, deserving of guidance and no others. In the verse there is an indication of the lowliness of pure imitation (taqlid), which is why it was said:

"Gird yourself and be striving in the affairs of religion,
and do not be like a donkey that is tied and so follows."

It has also been cited as evidence that guidance is attained through the act of Allah the Exalted and the soul's acceptance of it, as the Ash'aris maintain.

al-Alusi's commentary (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 39, verse 19:

Allah's words, ﴿Is then the one against whom the word of punishment is due [able to be rescued]? Would you then save one who is in the Fire?﴾, are an explanation, in summary form (ijmal, a general statement that is later detailed), of the opposites of those previously mentioned. They also record upon them the deprivation of guidance, and they are the worshippers of the Taghut (the false deities and tyrants) and those who follow its footsteps, as the expression "those against whom the word of punishment is due" alludes to. The "word" here refers to Allah's words: ﴿I will surely fill Hell with you and with whoever follows you among them, all together.﴾ It is said that the verse was revealed concerning Abu Jahl and his like. The hamza (interrogative particle, ء) is for denial (inkar), and the fa' (ف) is for coordination (ʿatf) with an implied element. Man (مَن) is conditional (shartiyya) according to the view of al-Hufi and others, and the answer to the condition is "fa-anta tunqidh" (فأنت تنقذ), etc. The hamza before it is for lengthening the speech, like the saying of the poet:

"The party of Yemen certainly knows that when I say, 'As to what follows...' I am its orator."

This is because the entry of the hamza into the answer or the condition is sufficient. You say: a-in akramaka tukrimhu (أإن أكرمك تكرمه)? just as you say: in akramaka atukrimuhu (إن أكرمك أتكرمه)? And you do not repeat it in both, except for emphasis, because the two sentences, meaning the condition and the response after the particle enters, are each single (mufradan, i.e. each functions as one unit). Interrogation (istifham) is directed at the contents of sentences when what is sought is assent (tasdiq). The denial conveyed by the hamza relates to the content of both the conjoined and the conjoined-to. However, what is intended in the conjoined clause is the denial of the requital. The estimated sense is: "Are you the owner of the affair of people, able to dispose of it? So is the one against whom the word of punishment is due, would you then rescue him?" meaning: you are not the owner of the affair of people, nor can you rescue, rather the owner and the one able to rescue is Allah, mighty and majestic. The expression "fa-anta tunqidhuhu" was departed from to what is in the noble arrangement, for greater emphasis of the denial and of the improbability, together with what it contains of an allusion to the fact that their deserving of punishment, while they are in this world, which the condition indicates, was made equivalent to their entry into the Fire. It also represents the state of him, upon him be blessings and peace, in his great effort to achieve their guidance and his striving in calling them to faith, by the state of one who wants to rescue those in the Fire from it.

In the Khafajiyya marginal notes (al-Hawashi al-Khafajiyya), quoting al-Sa'd: in this verse there is a metaphor that only the knights of rhetoric (eloquence) recognize, namely the implicit allegorical metaphor (al-istiʿara al-tamthiliyya al-makniyya), because he has treated what is indicated by Allah's words "Afaman" (أفمن) etc., namely their deserving of punishment while in this world, as the status of their entering the Fire in the Hereafter, so that it follows from that, treating his, upon him be blessings and peace, exertion in calling them to faith as the status of rescuing them from the Fire, which is among the requirements of entering the Fire. Then he said: and you have known from his method that the indicator (qarina) of the implicit metaphor may be factual (tahqiqiyya), as in "breaking the covenant." End quote. So reflect.

It has been said: the Fire is a metaphor for misguidance, by way of naming the effect with the name of the cause (ism al-musabbab ʿala al-sabab). "Rescue" then replaces "guidance" as a further development (tarshih) of the metaphor. Or it is a metaphor for calling to faith and obedience. But this is not the case. It is also permitted that the requital is omitted (mahdhuf), and the clause "fa-anta tunqidh" etc. is a new sentence (mustaʾnafa) establishing the first clause. The estimate is: "Is then the one against whom the word of punishment is due, so you would deliver him? Would you then rescue those in the Fire?"

There is no difference between the two views in that the fa' in the first is for coordination with an omitted element, nor in that the meaning is on the basis of treating the deserving of punishment, while they are in this world, as the status of their entering the Fire, and representing his, upon him be blessings and peace, exertion in achieving their guidance by the state of one who wants to rescue those in the Fire from it. Yes, on the first view the speech is one clause, and on the second it is two clauses. Abu Hayyan held that "man" (مَن) is a relative pronoun (mawsula) functioning as subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is omitted. It is reported that some estimate it as: "he grieves over him," some estimate it as: "he escapes from him," and some estimate it as: "you deliver him." It is not hidden that the last estimate is preferable. It is also mentioned that the grammarians hold that the fa' in this type of construction is for coordination, and its place is before the hamza, but the hamza was placed first because it has the front position of the sentence. He said: the view that each of them is in its place is a view that al-Zamakhshari alone held, as far as we know. In al-Mughni (Mughni al-Labib): preference is given to the view that the hamza is moved forward from its original place. On this view, the conjoined-to is estimated as: "You are not the owner of their affair," or "What Allah, exalted is He, has informed of is certainly going to happen," or "Every disbeliever deserves punishment," or something similar to these that fits the intended meaning.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 39, verse 20:

﴿But those who have feared their Lord, for them are chambers, above them are chambers built [high]﴾ — a istidrak (a contrasting particle, "but/however") between two things that resemble opposites and contraries, namely the believers and the disbelievers, and their conditions. What is meant by "those who have feared" (alladhina ittaqaw) is those described by the virtuous qualities that were enumerated. Ghuraf is the plural of ghurfah, which is an upper chamber (ʿaliyyah), that is, for them are many lofty upper chambers, some above others. ﴿Built﴾ — it was said: this is like a preparation for His words, exalted is He, "beneath which rivers flow," meaning: beneath those upper and lower chambers. ﴿Rivers﴾ — that is, they are built in a manner that allows rivers to flow beneath them, and this is unlike the upper chambers of this world. The description thereby indicates that they were levelled like a building upon the ground and made into one single surface, so that rivers can flow over it. Moreover, since the waters of Paradise descend from the bottom of the Throne, as is mentioned in the hadith, they are higher than the chambers, so there is no wonder in the water flowing over them above and below. Yet there must be an arrangement that allows the flow, and the aforementioned description serves to convey this.

Some of the eminent scholars said: "The apparent meaning is that this description is an affirmation of the reality, and a clarification that the chambers are not like shades, as would be the case if the metaphorical meaning were intended by way of a sarcastic metaphor (isti'arah tahakkumiyyah)." And some of our virtuous contemporary brothers said: "The benefit of describing them with what has been mentioned is to point to the exalted rank of the chambers, since it signifies that Allah, exalted is He, is their builder; and what could one say about a building that Allah, Majestic and Exalted, has built?"

And I say, and Allah knows best: the chambers were described thus to indicate that they are prepared and readied for them, their affair having been completed, as is the apparent sense of the description, not that they will be built for them on the Day of Resurrection. In this there is what there is of magnifying the rank of the God-fearing. And the verse, on this reading, is a refutation of the Mu'tazilah. It seems that al-Zamakhshari, for this reason, did not dwell on this aspect and confined himself to what we related first, although what we have said is closer to the truth, so let it be memorised.

﴿The promise of Allah﴾ — a verbal noun (masdar) emphasising the content of the sentence before it, for it is a promise, and what a promise! ﴿Allah does not fail in His promise﴾ — because failing to keep it would involve a deficiency that is impossible for Him, exalted and majestic is He.

[Page 256]

This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf). It may serve to illustrate the worldly life in its swift passing and its nearness to ruin, through the states of the crop just described, as a warning against being deceived by its splendor. Or it may serve as evidence for the realization of the promised rivers flowing beneath the lofty chambers, by what is observed of the sending down of water from the sky and what follows from it of the effects of His power, glorified is He, and the rulings of His wisdom and mercy. By "water" is meant rain, and by "sky" the direction of above. It has been said that it refers to the celestial bodies. The sending down of rain from them is understood as being through causes arising from them: the rising of vapors and the formation of clouds through the pull of the sun, the variation of its positions, and similar causes that God Most High knows. As for the sending down of rain from the very body of the sky itself, known as such, it often happens that a cloud rises and rains heavily, while there is someone on the summit of a mountain who has no cloud near him and no rain. To hold that the rain in that case descends from the body of the sky also, onto the cloud, but is not seen by one who is above the cloud, whereas his condition standing atop the mountain is not hidden, is a far-fetched claim.

It has also been said that by "water" is meant every water in the earth, and that by the sending down mentioned is meant the sending down at the beginning of creation. This is because, when He, mighty and majestic, created the earth, He created it empty of water, so He sent down water from a sea beneath the Throne. ﴿فَسَلَكَهُ﴾ means "and He made it flow" (fa-salakahu), i.e. caused it to enter, ﴿يَنابِيعَ فِي الْأَرْضِ﴾ meaning "springs in the earth", that is, in springs, namely fountains and channels existing in the earth like veins in bodies. On the first view, the apparent meaning of the verse requires that the water of springs and channels is from rain water; on the second view, it is not from it.

It is widely reported from the philosophers that the water of springs, and what runs in their manner from vapors, is as follows. They said: when vapor is confined in the earth, it inclines toward one direction and cools there, so it turns into waters mixed with vaporous particles. When it increases to the point where the earth cannot contain it, it causes the earth to split, and the springs gush forth from it. Abu al-Barakat al-Baghdadi refuted this, saying in al-Mu'tabar: The cause of springs and what runs in their manner is what flows from snows and rain waters, because we find them increasing with the increase of these and decreasing with their decrease. The transformation of airs and vapors confined in the earth has no role in that, for the interior of the earth in summer is colder than in winter. So if the cause of these were that transformation, springs, channels, and well waters would have to be greater in summer and less in winter, whereas the matter is the opposite of that, as experience shows. Al-Maybudi said: The truth is that the cause mentioned by the author of al-Mu'tabar is undoubtedly valid, but it does not preclude the consideration of the cause that was reported. His argument in denial only shows that it is not permissible for that to be the complete cause, not that it is impermissible for it to be a cause in general. End of quotation.

In Sharh al-Mawaqif: they differed as to whether waters are generated from scattered watery particles in the depth of the earth when they gather, or from vaporous air which turns into water. The second, though possible, is less preferable than the first, because the waters of springs, channels, and wells increase with the increase of snows and rains. In my view, the better course is to take "water" in the verse as rain and the like, including snow. The verse indicates that God Most High makes that water flow into springs in the earth, but it does not indicate that what is in the springs is nothing but that water. Thus it is possible that part of what is in them is the water sent down from the sky, and part of it newly arisen from vaporous air turned into water by causes that God, mighty and majestic, knows. The sending down was taken to mean the sending down at the beginning of creation, as you have heard, although I have not come upon a sound report that supports it, and the apparent meaning of the verse strongly opposes it. This is because the address in ﴿أَلَمْ تَرَ﴾ ("Did you not see") is general, and generality cannot be realized in seeing that. It seems necessary to make the address specific to the master of those addressed, ﷺ, and the meaning would be: "Did you not know that by revelation?" Even so, the condition of carrying the verse on what was mentioned is not hidden.

Close to what has been said is what az-Zamakhshari reported concerning the verse from some people: that every water in the earth comes from the sky, descending from it to the rock, and then God Most High distributes it among the regions. But what we have chosen is opposed by the apparent meaning of what Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas, who said about the verse: "There is no water in the earth except what God Most High sends down from the sky, but there are veins in the earth that alter it. Whoever wishes that salt become sweet, let him ascend." He transmitted something similar from Sa'id ibn Jubayr and ash-Sha'bi. If this report is sound, and we say that it has the ruling of a report traced to the Prophet ﷺ, then there is nothing against us in saying according to its apparent meaning. Reason does not reject it, and God Most High is powerful over all things.

Furthermore, it is permissible that "springs" (yanabi') be the plural of yunbu', in the sense of "gushing", for just as it is applied to the source, so it is applied to what has been mentioned. In that case it would be in the accusative as a state (hal), and the meaning would be: "He made it waters gushing in the earth." This is not free from difficulty, because if this were intended the apparent wording would be "from the earth". According to the well-known view, "springs" is accusative by removal of the preposition, as we have indicated.

The possibility that it is accusative as a verbal noun (masdar) in either of its two senses, namely that the original is "He made it flow a flowing in springs, i.e. channels", so the verbal noun was deleted and what is in the position of a qualifier was put in its place; or that the original is "He made it flow the flow of springs, i.e. gushing waters", so the first noun was deleted and the noun in the genitive was put in its place, is far-fetched, as is not hidden.

﴿ثُمَّ يُخْرِجُ بِهِ﴾ "then He brings forth by it", i.e. by means of it, out of consideration of wisdom, not because bringing forth depends on it in reality. The Ash'aris said: that is, He brings forth with it, without any influence on its part in any respect except concomitance, ﴿زَرْعًا مُخْتَلِفًا أَلْوانُهُ﴾ "crops of varying colors", i.e. its kinds and varieties, such as wheat, barley, and others; or its qualities perceived by sight, such as green, red, and others; or its qualities in general, including colors, tastes, and others, as has been said. It includes both the crop that is eaten and other crops. ﴿ثُمَّ﴾ "then" indicates succession in rank or in time. The present tense of the verb is to bring the image before the mind. ﴿ثُمَّ يَهِيجُ﴾ "then it dries up", i.e. withers. The apparent statement of the lexicographers is that this is the literal meaning of "hayaj"; but some commentators' statements imply that yahiju means "to stir" (yathur). Its use in the sense of "drying up" is a metaphor of approach, because when the crop dries and its dryness is complete, it is about to stir and depart from its roots. ﴿فَتَراهُ مُصْفَرًّا﴾ "then you see it yellow", after its greenness and freshness. It is also read as "musfarran". ﴿ثُمَّ يَجْعَلُهُ حُطامًا﴾ "then He makes it debris", crumbled and broken fragments, as if it had not flourished the day before. Because this state is among the powerful effects, it is linked to God Most High's making, just as the bringing forth is. Abu Bishr read ﴿ثُمَّ يَجْعَلَهُ﴾ with the accusative. The author of al-Kamil said: this is weak, and he did not explain the basis of the accusative. It is apparently the elision of "an" (that), as in the line of poetry: "Indeed I, and my killing Sulayk, then paying its blood-money" (innī wa-qatlī Sulaykan thumma a'qilahu). The weakness of this here is not hidden.

﴿إِنَّ فِي ذَلِكَ﴾ "Indeed in that", a reference to what has been mentioned in detail. The sense of distance in "that" serves to announce the remoteness of its rank in strangeness, and to indicate what its explanation intends. ﴿لَذِكْرى﴾ "is surely a reminder", a great reminder, ﴿لِأُولِي الْأَلْبابِ﴾ "for people of understanding", for those with intellects pure of defects, and an alert to them concerning the truth of the matter, by which they remember the state of the worldly life and the swiftness of its passing, so that they are not deceived by its splendor nor tempted by its allure. Or they are certain that whoever is able to send down water from the sky and to dispose of it in the best manner is able to make rivers flow beneath those chambers. It seems the first is preferable, so that what came before is an encouragement toward the Hereafter, while this is a warning against the world. It has been said that the meaning is: indeed in that there is a reminder and an alert that such a thing necessarily requires a wise maker, and that it is in accordance with a plan and management, not by neglect or idleness. This is far from what the context requires. Moreover, the more fitting reading for that intention is to mention the effects without attributing them to Him, glorified is He. Since they are mentioned attributed to Him, glorified is He, the apparent reading is that the object of the reminder and alert is His affairs, mighty and majestic, or the affairs of His effects, as indicated, not His existence, exalted is He.

Al-Alusi's commentary on Surah 39, verse 22:

Allah's words, ﴿Is one whose breast Allah has opened to Islam...﴾ and so on, form a resumptive clause (istinaf) that functions as a justification for what precedes it, namely the restriction of the admonition to people of understanding. Sharh (opening, expanding) originally means spreading out and stretching flesh or the like, and it is used as a metaphor for widening. Here it is used figuratively for Allah's creating the rational soul (al-nafs al-natiqa) in a state of complete readiness to accept, because it does not resist acceptance and attainment is easy. This requires first a metaphorical use of "breast" (al-sadr), with the rational soul intended by it insofar as it is the seat of the heart. In its cavity there is a subtle vapour formed from the purest of foods. The soul is first attached to it, and through it is attached to the rest of the body in the manner of governance and direction. It is this soul that is characterised by Islam and faith. Some eminent scholars took "whose breast Allah has opened" to be an allegorical metaphor (isti'ara tamthiliyya). The interrogative hamza (alif al-istifham) is for denial and enters upon an elided element, according to one of the two opinions mentioned just above. The fa' is for conjunction with that elided element. The predicate of man (the relative "one who") is elided, the context after it indicating it. The estimated meaning is: "Are all people equal? So one whom Allah the Exalted has opened the breast of, and created ready for Islam, [remains upon the original nature (fitra)] and has not been altered by acquired accidents that corrupt it, [is] by virtue of that, settled [ fa-huwa mustaqirr ], ﴿upon light﴾ great, ﴿from his Lord﴾, which is the divine gentleness shining upon him from the towers of mercy when witnessing the created and revealed signs, and the granting of success to be guided by them to the truth. [This is] like one whose heart has hardened and whose breast has become constricted through altering Allah's fitra by his own bad choice, and whom the darkness of error and misguidance has overcome, so that he turns away from those signs entirely, so that he neither remembers by them nor takes advantage of them." The expression was turned away from "'indahu" or "fa-lahu nur" to the sublime wording used in the verse, to indicate the continuity of that state and its stability within the light. The "light" here is a metaphor for gentleness and the granting of success to be guided. It may also be said that it is a divine matter other than gentleness and success, by which the truth is perceived.

It is transmitted in the narration of al-Tha'labi in his tafsir, al-Hakim in his al-Mustadrak, al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman, and Ibn Mardawayh, from Ibn Mas'ud, that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited this verse, ﴿Is one whose breast Allah has opened...﴾ and so on. We said: 'O Messenger of Allah, how is the expansion of the breast?' He said: 'When the light enters the heart, it expands and widens.' We said: 'What is the sign of that, O Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'Turning penitently to the abode of eternity, withdrawing from the abode of delusion, and preparing for death before it descends.'"

This raises a difficulty: the apparent meaning of the verse is that the entry of the light follows the expansion, since expansion is the readiness to receive it, whereas the noble hadith states the reverse. Apparently the question was about what is in the verse, and the answer explains its manner. It has been answered that guidance has degrees, some preceding and some following, and the expansion of the breast is according to natural disposition and character, and according to what occurs to it after the overflow of divine gentleness upon it. Between them there is mutual implication. The expansion of the breast in the hadith means what occurs after it has become firmly established within it, while in the verse it means what has been mentioned before. The light should be judged by the same reasoning. The answer belongs to the category of the wise approach (al-usluub al-hakim), so reflect.

﴿Woe then to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of Allah﴾, that is, because of His remembrance, may He be glorified, which by right should soften hearts. That is, when Allah the Exalted is mentioned in their presence, or His signs, Mighty and Majestic is He, they recoil from that and their hearts grow even harder. It has been read as "'an dhikr Allah" (against/away from the remembrance of Allah). The widely transmitted (mutawatir) reading is more eloquent, because one who is hardened on account of a thing is more intensely resistant to accepting it than one who is hardened away from it for another reason. And for the sake of emphasis in describing those as accepting and these as refusing, he mentioned the expansion of the breast, because its widening and making it a place for Islam, rather than the heart in which it is located, indicates the intensity of the one and the excess of its abundance, which overflowed until it filled the breast, let alone the heart. Ascribing it to Allah the Exalted is apparent in that it is in the most complete manner, since it is the act of the All-Powerful, the All-Wise. He contrasted it with hardness, although the contrast would seem to call for expressing it with narrowness (dayq), because hardness, as in a solid rock, requires that nothing be accepted, unlike narrowness, which implies that something little may be accepted. He departed from expressing it in a way that indicates that hardness is made by Him and created by Him, to indicate the extreme degree to which it is inseparable from them, as though even if it were not made, it would have been realised in them by the necessity of their essences. As for ascribing it to the hearts rather than the breasts, this is to specify the corruption of this organ, which when corrupted corrupts the whole body. The plural was observed for these disbelievers and the singular for those believers, where He, glorified be He, said: ﴿Is one whose breast Allah has opened﴾, rather than "whose breasts," to indicate that the believers, though they are many, are like one man, whereas the disbelievers are not like that.

﴿Those﴾, the distant ones characterised by the hardness of heart mentioned, ﴿are in manifest error﴾, clear, such that it is evident to everyone that it is error.

The verse was revealed concerning Ali and Hamza, may Allah be pleased with them both, and Abu Lahab and his son. Ali, may Allah honour his face, and Hamza, may Allah be pleased with him, are among those whose breasts Allah the Exalted has opened to Islam, while Abu Lahab and his son are among those whose hearts are hardened.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 39, verse 23:**

﴿Allah has sent down the best of speech﴾. This is the Noble Qur'an. That it is "speech" (ḥadīth) means that it is speech that is "narrated" (muḥaddath bih), not that it is the opposite of the eternal (qadīm). As for those among the Ash'ariyya (the followers of al-Ash'ari) who held the necessary implication (talāzum) of the createdness of the verbal speech, they took the descriptions that indicate its createdness to refer to that speech. He also allowed that the application of the term "speech" (ḥadīth) here to the Qur'an is by way of *mushākala* (a rhetorical device in which a word is used because of its association with another word).

From Ibn Abbas: some of the Companions said, "O Messenger of Allah, relate to us some fine narratives and accounts of the ages," and so this was revealed.

From Ibn Mas'ud: the Companions grew weary of something, so they said to him (ﷺ), "Relate to us," and so this was revealed.

That is, it is a guidance for them toward what removes their weariness, which is the recitation of the Qur'an and hearing it from him (ﷺ) fresh and new. In placing the name of Allah, exalted is He, as the subject (mubtada') and in the construction of ﴿sent down﴾ upon it, there is an exaltation of "the best of speech" and an evidence of its excellence, and an emphasis on its being attributed to Allah, glorified and exalted is He, and that the like of it cannot be spoken by anyone other than Him, glorified is He. As for the exaltation, it is because it is of the type of "the caliph in the presence of so-and-so." As for the evidence of its excellence, it is because it comes from One than whom no greater can be conceived; indeed, nothing has any perfection in comparison with Him in any respect. As for the emphasis on its attribution to Him, exalted is He, it is from piety (taqwā). As for the claim that the like of it cannot be spoken by anyone other than Him, glorified is He, it is because of the appropriateness (tanāsub), for the most perfect speech can only come from the most perfect speaker by necessity. The position of al-Zamakhshari is that such a construction (tarkīb) conveys restriction (ḥaṣr), and that there is no contradiction between this and piety when combined, so understand this.

﴿A Book﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿the best of speech﴾, or a circumstantial state (ḥāl) from it, as al-Zamakhshari said. It is not based on the view that the annexation of the elative form (*ism al-tafḍīl*, the comparative/superlative form such as *afḍal* and *aḥsan*) makes it definite, as Abu Hayyan supposed; for mere annexation is sufficient for the validity of its being a circumstantial state, as is not hidden from anyone with even a little familiarity with Arabic. Its occurring as a circumstantial state while being a noun rather than an adjective is either because it is described by His saying, exalted is He, ﴿similar (mutashābihan)﴾, or because it has the force of "written" (maktūban).

The meaning of its being "similar" here is the similarity of its meanings in soundness, firmness, being founded on truth and sincerity, bringing the benefits of creation in the Hereafter and in this life, and the harmony of its words in eloquence and the correspondence of its arrangement in inimitability. This is similar to the Arabic saying about a face that is complete in beauty: "a face that is balanced (*mutanāṣif*)", as though part of it were just to another part in its share of beauty. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿oft-repeated (mathānī)﴾ is another attribute of ﴿a Book﴾, or another circumstantial state from it. It is the plural of *muthannā*, with a *ḍamma* on the *mīm* and a *fatḥa* on the doubled *nūn*, contrary to analogy, for its analogical plural would be *muthannayāt* in the sense of "repeated" and "reiterated," for what has been repeated and doubled of its rulings, admonitions and stories. It was also said that it is because it is recited in pairs (yuthannā) in recitation.

It is also allowed that it is the plural of *mathnā* (with a *fatḥa*), lightened from *al-tathniya*, in the sense of repetition and reiteration, just as His saying, exalted is He, ﴿then return the gaze twice (karratayn)﴾ means one repetition after another; and likewise *labbayka* and *sa'dayka*. The meaning is that it is a plural for the sense of repetition and reiteration, just as the dual is used for that purpose, but the use of the dual in this sense is more common, because it is the first degree of repetition. It may also be meant that *mathnā* in the sense of repetition and reiteration is like the clear dual in such as "*karratayn*," and then it was made plural for emphasis. It was also said that it is the plural of *mathniyya*, because its verses include praise (thanā') of Allah, exalted is He, or because it praises by its eloquence and inimitability the one who speaks it. It is not hidden that observing the correspondence with ﴿similar﴾ makes this less preferred, and that it is good if it is taken to mean praise in respect of its inimitability. In *al-Kashf*: the most analogical reading according to the wording is that ﴿mathānī﴾ is derived from *al-thanā'* (praise) or *al-thany* (reiteration), being the plural of *muthannā*, *mufa''al*, from either of them: either as a verbal noun, its plural being used for what has become an attribute, or as a place-noun originally, transferred to the attribute for emphasis, like *ard ma'sada* (a land full of lions). For the place of praise falls by way of metaphor on the second, and the one praised, and likewise the place of reiteration. End of quotation. Its being an attribute of *Kitāb* is in respect of its details, and the details of a thing are its totality and nothing else. Do you not see that you say, "The Qur'an consists of sevenths and fifths, and of suras and verses"? So likewise you say, "It consists of rulings, admonitions and stories, *mathānī*." Its parallel is your saying, "The human being consists of veins, bones and tendons," except that you have left the qualified noun for the attribute, the original being: a book similar, in sections, oft-repeated. It may also be a specifying accusative (*tamyīz*) transferred from the agent, the original being: "similar in its *mathānī*," and it was transferred and made indefinite, because the more common usage is indefiniteness, and this is like your saying, "I saw a man good in features (*shamā'il*)." Hisham and Abu Bishr read *mathānī* with a *sukūn* on the *yā'*. This may be the predicate of an omitted subject, or it may be in the accusative. The *yā'* was made quiescent according to the dialect of those who make it quiescent in all cases, because what precedes it is kasra, finding the vowel on it burdensome.

﴿The skins of those who fear their Lord shiver therefrom﴾. It was said that this is an attribute of ﴿a Book﴾, or a circumstantial state from it, because it is specified by the attribute. Some said: the more apparent view is that it is a resumptive sentence (isti'nāf), brought to explain its outward effects upon its hearers after explaining its attributes in itself, and to establish that it is the best of speech.

*Al-iqshi'rār* is contraction. It is said: the skin "shivered" (iqsha''arra al-jild) when it contracted very tightly. Its root is from *al-qashc*, which is a dry hide, and the letter *rā'* was added to it to make it quadriliteral and to indicate an additional meaning. It is said: "his skin shivered," meaning his hair stood up, when a great fear befell him from a terrible matter that came upon him suddenly. The purpose is to depict their fear by mentioning its perceptible concomitants, and it is also called an illustration (tamthīl), though it is of the type of metonymy (kināya).

It was also said: it is a depiction of fear by mentioning its effects and the comparison of one state with another, so it would be a true illustration. The first is better, because comparing one story with another by way of metaphor here is not free of artificiality. It was preferred that the intent is to explain the occurrence of that state and its onset upon them in a real manner. The meaning is: when they hear the Qur'an and its striking verses of warning, fear and dread seize them, and their skins shiver from it; and when they remember the mercy of Allah, exalted is He, upon hearing the verses of His promise and His kindnesses, their dread turns into hope and their fear into desire. This is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿then their skins and their hearts soften to the remembrance of Allah﴾, that is, they become calm and at rest in remembering His mercy, exalted is He. He did not state "mercy" explicitly as an indication that it is the first thing that comes to mind when His name is mentioned, because of its originality, as the report ("My mercy has preceded My wrath") points to. The mention of the hearts is because of the precedence of fear, which is one of its accidents. Perhaps the reason it was not mentioned there in the same manner as here is that the hearts are not described as shivering, but are described as softening. In the verse there is nothing more than the description of His friends by the shivering of the skins from the Qur'an, then their tranquillity in His mercy, glorified and exalted is He. There is no description of them as falling unconscious, ecstasy, or clapping, as some people do.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Asakir reported from Abd Allah ibn Urwa ibn al-Zubayr who said: I said to my grandmother Asma': How did the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) behave when they recited the Qur'an? She said: They were as Allah, exalted is He, described them: their eyes shed tears and their skins shivered. I said: Some people here, when they hear that, are seized by a swoon. She said: I seek refuge in Allah, exalted is He, from Satan.

Al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar reported in *al-Muwaffaqiyyat*, from Amir, from Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr who said: I came to my mother and said: I have found a people whom I have never seen better than, who mention Allah, exalted is He, and one of them trembles until he faints from the fear of Allah, exalted is He. She said: Do not sit with them. Then she said: I saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) reciting the Qur'an, and I saw Abu Bakr and Umar reciting the Qur'an, and this does not befall them. Do you think they feared Abu Bakr and Umar more?

Ibn Umar, when he saw someone collapse from hearing the Qur'an, said: We fear Allah, exalted is He, and we do not fall down. These people, Satan enters into the belly of one of them.

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Qatada that he said about the verse: This is the description of the friends of Allah, exalted is He. He said: Their skins shiver, their eyes weep, and their hearts become tranquil in the remembrance of Allah, exalted is He. Allah, glorified is He, did not describe them as losing their minds and falling unconscious; that is only among the people of innovations, and it is only from Satan.

Ibn Abi Shayba reported from Ibn Jubayr: The swoon is from Satan. Ibn Sirin said: Between us and those who are struck down when the Qur'an is recited, let one of them be placed against a wall with his legs outstretched, then the whole Qur'an be recited to them; if he throws himself down, then he is truthful. These reports are a censure of some of the Sufis for their swooning, their ecstasy, and their striking their heads against the ground when they hear the Qur'an. Their shaykhs say that this is because of the weakness of the hearts in bearing the incoming state, and that those who do such things are not in perfection like the Companions, the people of the first generation, in strength of endurance. So it is nothing but a sign of deficiency, by the evidence that when the wayfarer (*sālik*) reaches perfection, his heart becomes firm and strong, and nothing of that proceeds from him. They say: the verse contains nothing more than the affirmation of the shivering and softening; and it contains no negation that some other state may befall them. Rather, the verse implies that what is mentioned is the state of the firmly established, perfected ones, since He, glorified is He, said: ﴿those who fear their Lord﴾, using the relative pronoun. The presupposed knowledge of the relative clause implies that they have a firm establishment in fear, such that they are known by it. Therefore it does not follow, from the fact that their state is what is mentioned, that the state of others is not so; and the claim that it is only so is only if the verse is taken to indicate restriction. Furthermore, when a matter is involuntary, like sneezing, there is no objection to the one who is characterized by it; and in Ibn Sirin's words there is something that supports this. This is the furthest that can be said in this field. We ask Allah, exalted is He, to bestow upon us what He bestowed upon the Companions of His Prophet (ﷺ).

﴿That is the guidance of Allah﴾: the reference is to the Book whose states it has explained. ﴿He guides by it whom He wills﴾, that is, whom Allah, exalted is He, wills to guide by enabling him, glorified is He, to reflect upon the evidences of truth within it and the signs that it is from His presence, mighty and majestic is He. It is also allowed that the pronoun in ﴿wills﴾ refers to *man* (whoever), and the meaning would be: Allah, exalted is He, guides by it whom He wills, with the guidance of Allah, exalted is He; but this is not the intended meaning.

﴿And whomever Allah sends astray﴾: that is, He, glorified is He, creates straying in him because of his turning away from what would guide him to the truth, through his poor readiness. ﴿For him there is no guide﴾ to rescue him from the snare of error. It was also said: the reference in *dhālika* is to what was mentioned of shivering and softening, and the meaning: that which was mentioned of fear and hope is the effect of His guidance, exalted is He. By that effect He guides whom He wills of His servants, and whoever He sends astray, that is, whoever is not affected by it because of the hardness of his heart and his persistence in his wickedness, for him there is no guide, that is, no one who affects him with anything at all. And this, as you see, is weak.

**Al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, on Surah 39, verse 24:**

﴿Is one who shields his face from the terrible punishment on the Day of Resurrection [equal to one who is safe]?﴾ This is a resumptive sentence (*istinaf*), functioning as a justification (*ta'lil*) for what precedes it, namely the difference between the state of the one who is guided and the one who is astray. The discussion of the interrogative hamza, the *fa'* (the conjunction linking the clause), and the predicate (*khabar*) is as was discussed for its parallels. It is said, according to one of the two opinions, that the implied meaning here is: "Are all people equal? Rather, one whose condition is that he shields with his face, which is the noblest of his limbs, on the Day of Resurrection from the evil, severe punishment, because his hand with which he used to shield himself from hardships is chained to his neck, [is not equal to] one who is secure, from whom no harm comes and who has no need to shield himself by any means." According to this, the face is taken in its literal sense. It may also be taken figuratively, without needing to say that the hand is chained, to depict the perfection of his protecting himself with it, and this is more eloquent. In this context, the verse of the poet applies:

*He meets the swords with his face and his chest,*
*and sets his head in place of a helmet.*

It is also permitted that "face" means the whole person (*al-jumlah*), and the emphasis (*mubalaghah*) then lies in this sense rather than in the preceding one. It has been said that shielding with the face is a metonymy (*kinayah*) for the absence of anything with which one could shield oneself, since shielding with the face has no real "face" to it, because it is not something one can shield with, and it is not free of scratches. The annexation of "evil" to "punishment" is the annexation of an attribute to the thing it describes. "On the Day of Resurrection" is the object (*ma'mul*) of "shields," as we have indicated. It is also permitted that it is part of the phrase "evil punishment," meaning: "Is one who shields himself from the punishment of the Day of Resurrection like one who persists in his disbelief?" This is a good interpretation, and the face in this case, as in the previous interpretation, is either the whole person, for the sake of emphasis regarding his piety, or literal, depicting the perfection of his piety by his use of it, which is more eloquent. The meaning that comes first to mind is the previous one.

It has been said that the verse was revealed concerning Abu Jahl. ﴿And it will be said to the wrongdoers﴾ is coordinated (*'atf*) with "shields," meaning: and it will be said to them, from the direction of the keepers of the Fire. The past tense form is used to indicate certainty and settledness. It has also been said that the *waw* is for the circumstantial (*hal*), and the clause is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "shields," with *qad* implied or not implied. The explicit noun is placed in the position of the pronoun in order to record their wrongdoing against them and to indicate the reason for the command in the Almighty's words: ﴿Taste what you used to earn﴾, that is, the consequence of what you used to earn in the world continually, of disbelief and sins.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 39, verse 25:

﴿Those before them denied, so the punishment came upon them from where they did not perceive.﴾ This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) brought to explain what befell some of the disbelievers of the worldly punishment, following the explanation of what befalls all of them of the punishment of the Hereafter.
