That is: those before them of the earlier nations denied, ﴿so the punishment came upon them﴾ — the punishment decreed for each nation among them — ﴿from where they did not perceive﴾, from a direction they did not expect, and it did not occur to their minds that it would come from it, because that is more severe upon the soul.

﴿So Allah made them taste the disgrace﴾, that is, the humiliation and abasement, ﴿in the life of this world﴾, such as being transformed (maskh), swallowed up by the earth (khasf), killed, taken captive (sabi), and expelled (ijla'), and other kinds of punishment. The **الفاءُ** (al-fa') here is explanatory (tafsiriyyah), like its use in His saying: ﴿So We answered him and delivered him﴾. ﴿And the punishment of the Hereafter﴾ prepared for them ﴿is greater﴾ because of its severity and its perpetuity, ﴿if only they knew﴾, meaning: if they were the kind of people who could know anything, they would have known this and taken warning from it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 39, verse 27:

﴿And indeed We have set forth for mankind in this Qur'an﴾ [the Qur'an] of great dignity, ﴿every kind of example﴾ that the one who reflects needs concerning the matters of his religion, ﴿that they may remember﴾. That is, so that they may remember and take admonition; or, [the verb can be read as expressing] that their remembering and taking admonition is hoped for. The hope (al-raja') with regard to other than God, the Exalted, is [understood as] the case, and the [reading of the particle as expressing] cause (al-ta'lil) is more apparent.

﴿Qur'anan 'Arabiyyan﴾ (an Arabic Qur'an) is a ḥāl (circumstantial qualifier, describing the state of the noun it refers to) of ﴿this﴾. The reliance here is on the attribute (ṣifah), namely ʿarabiyyan. Otherwise, qur'anan would be a rigid noun (jāmid) that is unfit to serve as a ḥāl. Moreover, it is the same as the one it describes (dhū al-ḥāl), so its state would not become apparent. Therefore, the ḥāl in reality is ﴿ʿarabiyyan﴾, and qur'anan serves as a tamhīd (preparatory introduction). A parallel is: "Zayd came as a righteous man." It has been said that this is equivalent to "an Arabic one in truth."

It is also permitted that it be in the accusative by an implied verb, whose estimate is: "I mean," "I specify," "I praise," or the like. It is also permitted that it be the object of ﴿yatadhakkarūn﴾ (they may remember). But this, as you see, is weak.

﴿Ghayra dhī ʿiwajin﴾ (without any crookedness) means there is no defect in it in any respect. It is more eloquent than "mustaqīm" (straight), because ʿiwajan is an indefinite noun (nakira) placed in the context of negation, due to what the word ghayr carries of that meaning. Straightness may be from one aspect but not another, whereas the negation of the accompaniment of crookedness from it entails the negation of its being characterized by it by a stronger implication. Therefore it is more eloquent than "ghayr muʿawwaj." The ʿiwaj (with a kasra) is said of what is perceived by thought and insight, while the ʿawaj (with a fatha) is said of what is perceived by the senses. The former is used to indicate that it has reached a level where the intellect does not perceive crookedness in it, let alone the senses. The full discussion has passed in Surat al-Kahf.

It has been said that the intended meaning of ʿiwaj is doubt (shakk) and confusion (labs). This was narrated from Mujahid, and they cited the verse of the poet:

"And there has come to you a certainty free of crookedness from God, and a word that is not false."

There is no proof in this that ʿawaj means doubt, because the crookedness of certainty is, without doubt, doubt. The argument regarding how this is a proof is that the poet understood this meaning from the verse, since it is a quotation (iqtibās). When an eloquent speaker understands it along with the soundness of the figurative usage, it is an obvious forced interpretation (taʿassuf), because it is not clear that he derived it from the verse. Even if it is granted, it would be capable of what the crookedness bears in the arrangement that has no crookedness in it. It may be said that the intent of whoever said it is: that is, there is no confusion in it, and no doubt, is a negation of some types of defect. Upon this is what is narrated from Uthman ibn Affan, that he said: that is, not inconsistent and not contradictory. And what has been said: that is, not containing any grammatical error (laḥn).

Al-Daylami, in Musnad al-Firdaws, narrated from Anas that "the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Ghayr dhī ʿiwaj, ghayr makhlūq' (without crookedness, not created)."

Perhaps, if the report is sound, it is an explanation by necessary implication (tafsīr bil-lāzim), so reflect.

﴿La-ʿallahum yattaqūn﴾ (so that they may be mindful of God) is another cause (ʿillah), consequent upon the first.

God has struck a parable: a man in whom are partners disputing with one another. This is the introduction of one of the Qur'anic parables, after the explanation that the wisdom in striking such parables is remembrance, taking warning from them, and attaining taqwa (God-consciousness). What is meant by striking a parable here is applying a striking state to another similar state and making it like it. ﴿مَثَلا﴾ (mathalan) is the second object of ḍaraba, and ﴿رَجُلا﴾ (rajulan) is its first object, placed after the second for the sake of creating suspense toward it, and so that what completes it, which is the core of the comparison, may be joined to it. Alternatively, ﴿مَثَلا﴾ is the object of ḍaraba, and ﴿رَجُلا﴾ and what follows is a substitute (badal, a substitution of the whole from the whole) for it.

al-Kisa'i said: ﴿رَجُلا﴾ is in the accusative by the omission of the preposition, i.e., "a parable concerning a man." It has been said otherwise, and the discussion of its parallel has already preceded.

﴿فِيهِ﴾ (fihi) is the predicate placed first, ﴿شُرَكاءُ﴾ (shurakā') is the subject, and ﴿مُتَشاكِسُونَ﴾ (mutashākisūn) is its attribute. An indefinite noun, even when qualified by an attribute, may have its predicate placed first.

The sentence is an attribute of ﴿رَجُلا﴾, and the connecting element is the pronoun hā' (in fīhi) or the prepositional phrase, which occupies the position of an attribute to it. ﴿شُرَكاءُ﴾ is in the nominative as the agent, because it depends on the qualified noun. It has been said that ﴿فِيهِ﴾ is a complement of shurakā', and that the subject is the predicate-bearer, with mutashākisūn as its predicate. The objection to this is that there is no clear rhetorical purpose in fronting it.

The meaning: God struck a parable for the polytheist according to what his doctrine leads to, namely the claim of each of his deities to the worship of his servant, a servant in whom a group of quarrelsome people share, because of the badness of their characters and the evil of their natures, pulling him in different directions and passing him between them in their divergent affairs, so that he is bewildered and his heart is scattered. ﴿ورَجُلا﴾ (wa-rajulan), that is, and He struck for the monotheist the parable of a man, ﴿سَلَمًا﴾ (salaman), that is, wholly devoted, ﴿لِرَجُلٍ﴾ (li-rajulin), to one single man, to whom no one else has any access at all. So he is at ease, free of bewilderment and of a scattered heart. The man was chosen as the parable because he is more perceptive of what makes him wretched or happy, for a boy and a woman may be heedless of that.

ʿAbd Allah, Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿIkrima, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Zuhri, al-Hasan according to one report from him, al-Jahdari, Ibn Kathir, and Abu ʿAmr read ﴿سالِمًا﴾ (sālimā) as an active participle from salima, meaning wholly free for him from partnership. Ibn Jubayr read ﴿سِلْمًا﴾ (silman) with a kasra on the sin and sukun on the lam, and it was also read ﴿سَلْمًا﴾ (salman) with a fatha and then sukun. Both are verbal nouns (maṣdar), and they were used as attributes to emphasize the exclusivity from partnership.

It was also read ﴿ورَجُلٌ سالِمٌ﴾ (wa-rajulun sālimun) with both in the nominative, meaning and there is a man who is wholly free. It was permitted that nothing be supposed (as omitted), and that rajulun be the subject with sālimun its predicate, because this is a place of detail, since what indicates it has already preceded. It is then like the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"When she weeps from behind her, she turns to him with one side, and the other side with us is not turned away."

God's saying ﴿هَلْ يَسْتَوِيانِ مَثَلا﴾ (Are the two equal in likeness?) is a denial and a declaration of improbability of their equality, and a negation of it in the most eloquent and emphatic manner, and an announcement that this is so clear and manifest that no one can utter that they are equal, or hesitate in judging that they differ, since it is necessarily so that one of them is in blame and hardship, and the other in ease of mind and contentment. It has also been said: since one of them is in the highest of the ʿIlliyyin and the other in the lowest of the lowest. Whichever it is, the secret of leaving the superior and the inferior unspecified is to point to the full clarity of the matter for whoever has even a slight awareness.

The accusative of ﴿مَثَلا﴾ is a tamyīz (specificative accusative) transferred from the agent, since the underlying sense is: "Are their likeness and their state equal?" Restricting the tamyīz to the singular is to show the genus, and it was restricted to it first in God's saying ﴿ضَرَبَ اللَّهُ مَثَلا﴾. It was also read ﴿مَثَلَيْنِ﴾ (mathalayn), meaning: Are their two likenesses and their two states equal? It was put in the dual although the intended purpose of the tamyīz is achieved by the singular without ambiguity, for the purpose of indicating an additional meaning, namely the difference of kind. It was also permitted that the pronoun in yastawiyān refer to the two parables, because the implied sense in what preceded is "the likeness of a man" and "the likeness of a man", meaning: Do the two likenesses equal two likenesses? This is like the saying "Sufficient are the two of them as two men," which is of the type "May God give him blessing as a horseman." It returns to: Are the two equal as two men with respect to the example that has been struck? And since the parable carries the meaning of the striking attribute that is like a parable, the meaning is: Are the two equal in what pertains to their attribute?

God's saying ﴿الحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ﴾ (Praise be to God) is a confirmation of what preceded, namely the negation of equality, by way of parenthetical insertion (iʿtirāḍ), and an admonition to the monotheists that the excellence they have is by God's grace, and that it is a magnificent blessing that requires continual praise of Him and worship of Him. Or it is on the basis that His explanation through the striking of parables, that for them is the highest likeness and for the polytheists is the likeness of evil, is a beautiful act and a complete kindness from Him, the Mighty and Majestic, which requires His praise and worship.

God's saying ﴿بَلْ أكْثَرُهم لا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ (But most of them do not know) is a transition (iḍrāb) from the explanation of non-equality in the stated manner to the explanation that most people, who are the polytheists, do not know this despite its full clarity, or they are not among those possessing knowledge, so they do not know it and remain in the pit of polytheism and error. It has been said that the meaning is that they do not know that the whole is from Him, and that praises belong only to Him, the Mighty and Majestic, so they associate others with Him, glory be to Him. Thus the speech is a continuation of ﴿الحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ﴾ and not a parenthesis. But it is not hidden that building the speech on the parenthetical reading, as you have heard, is preferable.

[Page 263]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 39, verse 30:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, you will die, and indeed, they will die﴾ is a preparation for what follows of disputing on the Day of Resurrection. In al-Bahr: when they did not turn to the truth and did not benefit from the striking of the parable, He, glorified is He, informed that the destiny of all is, by death, to Allah, Exalted is He, and that they will dispute on the Day of Resurrection before Him, and He, Mighty and Majestic is He, is the Just Judge, so the one who is right and the one who is wrong will be distinguished there.

And some of the eminent scholars (ajillah) said: when, from the beginning of the surah until here, there were mentioned the decisive proofs cutting off the root of the associationism (shirk) that had been firmly established, due to the extreme ignorance of the polytheists and their not returning despite his ﷺ great effort in turning them back to the truth and his eagerness for their guidance, the question turned from him, peace and blessings be upon him, after what he had endured from them, to the effect of saying: what is my state and their state? So it was answered: indeed you are dying, and indeed they are dying, and so on.

And Ibn al-Zubayr, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Ibn Muhaysin, Isa, al-Yamani, Ibn Abi Ghawth, and Ibn Abi Abla read: ﴿Indeed, you are mā'it (about to die), and indeed they are mā'itun﴾. The difference between mayyit and mā'it is that the first is an adjectival noun (sifah mushabbahah), which indicates permanence, so it implies that their life is itself a kind of death, and that death is a constant, inescapable necklace. The second is an active participle (ism fa'il), which indicates occurrence, so here, with the context, it conveys no more than that death will befall them. The pronoun of address, as you have heard, refers to the Messenger ﷺ. Abu Hayyan said: the believers of his community also enter with him, peace and blessings be upon him. The plural absent pronoun refers to the disbelievers. The emphasis of the sentence in ﴿indeed they will die﴾ is to indicate that they are in a great heedlessness, as if they deny death. The emphasis of the first is to repel the improbability of his, peace and blessings be upon him, death. It was said: it is for conformity (mushakalah). It was also said: death is among the things that souls dislike, and they naturally dislike hearing news of it, so it was likely that information about it would not be attended to, or that its occurrence would be denied, even out of obstinacy, so the judgment was emphasized with its occurrence for this reason. The absence of dislike in some [individuals] does not harm this, due to a particularity in them, such as the Master of the Worlds ﷺ,

[Page 265]

﴿Then indeed you﴾ is said with the second person given precedence over the third person (ghalab al-mukhatab 'ala al-ghayb).

﴿On the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord﴾, i.e., the Owner of your affairs, ﴿you will dispute﴾. You will argue against them, claiming that you conveyed to them what you were sent with, including the rulings and admonitions, among which are those contained within these verses. You strove in calling them to the truth with the utmost striving, while they persisted in obstinacy and stubbornness, and they will make excuses with falsehoods, such as: ﴿We obeyed our leaders﴾, and ﴿We found our fathers [doing so]﴾, and ﴿Our wretchedness overcame us﴾. The combining of ﴿on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord﴾ serves to increase the awe, by showing that their disputing takes place on a great day, before the Owner of their affairs, whose judgment is binding upon them. Had he (Allah) limited himself to the first (phrase), it would have been possible that the disputing among them would occur without a tribunal and with a tribunal. However, the Owner of their affairs is not with them. Restricting it to the second (phrase), on the assumption that it is understood that this is the Day of Resurrection with Him, without ambiguity, does not substitute for mentioning both, because the explicit statement of what is virtually a known matter carries the awe that it does. 

A group (of scholars) said: The intended meaning of this disputing is the general disputing that occurred in the world among mankind, not specifically the disputing between him (ﷺ) and the arrogant disbelievers. The narrations contain what rejects the aforementioned specificity.

‘Abd al-Razzaq, ‘Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn ‘Asakir narrated from Ibrahim al-Nakha‘i, who said: When this verse was revealed, ﴿Indeed you will die, and indeed they will die﴾, etc., (the Companions) said: "What is our dispute, when we are brothers?" Then when ‘Uthman ibn ‘Affan was killed, they said: "This is the dispute among us."

Sa‘id ibn Mansur narrated from Abu Sa‘id al-Khudri, who said: When there was revealed, ﴿Then indeed you, on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord, will dispute﴾, we used to say: "Our Lord is One, and our religion is one." But when the Day of Siffin came, and some of us attacked others with swords, we said: "Yes, this is it."

‘Abd ibn Humayd, al-Nasa’i, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ‘Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: We remained for a period of our lives, while we thought that this verse was revealed concerning us and the People of the Two Scriptures before us: ﴿Indeed you will die, and indeed they will die﴾ ﴿Then indeed you, on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord, will dispute﴾. We said: "How will we dispute, when our Prophet is one and our Book is one?" Until I saw some of us striking the faces of others with the sword, and I knew that it was revealed concerning us. In another narration from him, in these words: The verse was revealed to us: ﴿Then indeed you, on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord, will dispute﴾, and we did not know concerning what it was revealed. We said: "There is no dispute among us." Then there was no disputing until the Fitnah occurred, and I said: "This is what our Lord promised us, that we would dispute about it."

Ahmad, ‘Abd al-Razzaq, ‘Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sound), Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu‘aym in al-Hilyah, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba‘th wa al-Nushur narrated from al-Zubayr ibn al-‘Awwam, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "(When there was revealed: ﴿Indeed you will die, and indeed they will die﴾ ﴿Then indeed you, on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord, will dispute﴾), I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, will what occurs between us in this world be reproached to us, along with the particular sins?' He said: 'Yes, it will be reproached to you, until every possessor of a right is given his right.' Al-Zubayr said: 'By Allah, the matter is indeed severe.'"

Al-Zamakhshari claimed that the aspect indicated by the speech of Allah the Exalted is the one mentioned first, and he cited His saying: ﴿Who then is more unjust﴾, etc., and His saying: ﴿And he who has brought the truth﴾, etc., as evidence that these two are the ones between whom the dispute will be, and similarly what preceded of His saying: ﴿Allah presents an example: a man﴾, etc. Al-Taftazani (?) (note: this name is not in the text; omit) — rather, this was criticized in al-Kashf, which said: I say: It has been transmitted from the foremost of the Companions and the Successors, may Allah be pleased with them, what indicates that they understood the second aspect, i.e., the generality. Indeed, the apparent meaning of al-Nakha‘i's statement ﴿the Companions said: "What is our dispute, when we are brothers?"﴾ indicates that it is the saying of all of them. So the preferable aspect is that.

Its verification is that His saying the Exalted, ﴿And We have certainly presented to the people in this Qur'an﴾, is a speech addressed to the whole community, both its monotheists and its polytheists. Similarly His saying the Exalted: "Allah presents an example: a man," and "a man, and a man," or rather "most of them," are as an explicit text on that. So when it is said: "Indeed you will die," it must be in the manner of ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women﴾ (65:1), i.e., "Indeed you, O Prophet, and the believers," and it is made general so that it encompasses both groups. The composition is not contradictory, for from the beginning of the sura up to this point, the opposition between the two parties has been observed, not between him (ﷺ) alone and the disbelievers. Then, when it is said: ﴿Then indeed you﴾ with the second person given precedence, it is a giving precedence of the addressees over all people. This is from the standpoint of the wording and the apparent context. Then, when death is a matter that encompasses him and all people, the meaning is upon it also. As for the narration of the disputing and the antithesis that he mentioned, it is worth nothing, because by its generality it includes it in a primary way, as this meaning has been verified many times. 

The concluding statement with His saying, ﴿Who then is more unjust﴾, is to draw attention to it being the target of the purpose, and that the intended aim is the climbing up to that dispute. I do not deny that His saying, ﴿before your Lord﴾, indicates that the disputing is on the Day of Resurrection, but I deny that it is specific to the disputing of the Prophet (ﷺ) alone with the polytheists. Rather it includes him first, and likewise the disputing of the believers and the polytheists, and the disputing of the believers among themselves, like the disputing of ‘Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, on the Day of Resurrection with his killers. This is what those (scholars) went to, and they are (the foremost), may Allah be pleased with them all. End of quote.

It seems that by his saying "I do not deny, etc.," he meant the refutation of what is said: that ﴿before your Lord﴾ indicates that the disputing is on the Day of Resurrection, and this has been clearly stated in the sublime composition, so it is an emphasis implying attention to the matter of that disputing. It is therefore nothing but the disputing of His beloved (ﷺ) with his arrogant enemies. The refutation is that, even if it is granted that the benefit of the combining is what has been mentioned, we do not grant that this requires taking the specificity into account. Rather, for the attention it is sufficient that the disputing of the Beloved with his enemies (ﷺ) is included. So reflect on it. Then you know that even if there were in this context nothing but the authentic, elevated hadith, it would suffice for the intended meaning to be the generality of disputing. So the truth is to say its generality, and it has many kinds.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn ‘Abbas that he said regarding the verse: The truthful disputes with the liar, the wronged with the wrongdoer, the guided with the astray, and the weak with the arrogant.

Al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated with a chain that is not objectionable (la ba’s bihi), from Abu Ayyub, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The first to dispute on the Day of Resurrection will be a man and his wife. By Allah, her tongue will not speak, but her hands and feet will testify against her concerning what was (owed) to her husband, and his hands and feet will testify concerning what was (owed) to her. Then the man and his servant will claim the same. Then the people of the markets will claim, and there will not be found there a dānaq nor a qīrāṭ. Rather the good deeds of this one will be given to this one who wronged him, and the evil deeds of this one who wronged him will be placed upon him. Then the tyrants will be brought in iron fetters, and it will be said: 'Drive them to the Fire.' By Allah, I do not know whether they will enter it, or as Allah said: ﴿And there is none of you but will come to it﴾ (19:71)."

Al-Bazzar narrated from Anas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'The unjust ruler will be brought, and his subjects will dispute against him.'"

Ahmad and al-Tabarani with a fair chain narrated from ‘Uqbah ibn ‘Amir, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'The first two adversaries on the Day of Resurrection will be two neighbours.'"

Perhaps the "first" (in these reports) is relative, in view of the earlier hadith of Abu Ayyub.

There has also come from Ibn ‘Abbas the disputing of the soul with the body. Indeed, Ahmad narrated with a fair chain from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Every thing will certainly dispute on the Day of Resurrection, even the two sheep concerning what they butted each other.'"

"The Twenty-Third Part is complete, and it is followed, if Allah the Exalted wills, by the Twenty-Fourth Part, whose beginning is: ﴿Who then is more unjust﴾."

[Page 2]

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Who does greater wrong than one who lies against Allah﴾ by attributing to Him, exalted is He, a partner or a son, ﴿and denies the truth﴾, i.e., the matter which is the very essence of truth and the reality of truthfulness, namely what the Prophet (ﷺ) brought, ﴿when it has come to him﴾, i.e., at the very first coming of it, without reflection or deliberation. ﴿Fa-idha﴾ (then, suddenly) is a sudden-occurrence particle (fuja'iyyah), as Zamakhshari stated explicitly. However, Ibn Hisham in al-Mughni stipulated that it occurs after bayna or baynama, and he transmitted this from Sibawayh, so this is perhaps the predominant usage. It may be said that this meaning is required by the context without depending on idhā being a sudden-occurrence particle. Then the intended meaning is that this liar who denies the truth is the greatest wrongdoer of every wrongdoer. ﴿Is there not in Hell an abode for the disbelievers?﴾, i.e., for those who fabricated against Allah, exalted is He, and hastened to deny the truth. The apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun in order to record disbelief against them. The plural is according to the meaning of "man" (who), just as the singular in the preceding pronouns is according to its wording, or it refers to the genus of disbelievers, so it includes the People of the Book, and these are included in the ruling by way of priority. In any case, the meaning is that Hell is sufficient as a recompense for them, as if it were said: Is not Hell sufficient as an abode for the disbelievers? Like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Hell is sufficient for them; they will burn in it﴾ [al-Mujadila: 8], i.e., it suffices as a punishment for their disbelief and denial. The sufficiency is understood from the context, as you say to someone who asks you for something: "Did I not bestow favor upon you?", meaning: my previous favor to you suffices you. The verse was cited as evidence for declaring the people of innovations (ahl al-bid'ah) to be disbelievers, because they deny what is known to be true.

It was objected that "man kadhdhaba" (whoever denies) is specific to those who denied the prophets directly at the time of their conveying the message, not in general, based on His saying: ﴿when it has come to him﴾. And even if its generality is granted, they, because they interpret (their denial as interpretation), are not deniers; and what they negated and denied is not known to be true by necessity, for if it were known from religion by necessity, its denier would be a disbeliever, like one who denies the obligation of prayer and the like.

Al-Khafaji said: The more evident view is that what is intended is the denial of the prophets, peace be upon them, after the manifestation of miracles, regarding their having come from Allah, exalted is He, not mere denial in general. It seems to me you would choose that the one who interprets is not a denier, but there is no excuse for an interpretation that negates what is known from religion by necessity.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 39, verse 33:

﴿And he who brought the truth and believed in it﴾. The relative pronoun (al-mawsul) refers to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), as reported by Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat from Ibn 'Abbas. He interpreted "the truth" (al-sidq) as "There is no god but Allah." The believers are included by the indication of the context, and the ruling of subordination (hukm al-tab'iyyah) is like the inclusion of the troops in your saying: "The commander has descended at such-and-such a place." This is not at all a combination of the literal (haqiqah) and the figurative (majaz), because the second is not intended from the very wording (haq al-lafz), and it does not harm this that bringing the truth is not a description of the believing followers, as is not hidden. On this view the relative pronoun is singular in wording and meaning. The plural in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Those are the God-fearing (al-muttaqun)﴾, is by considering the inclusion of the followers as subordinates. The degrees of God-fearing (taqwa) vary, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) has the highest of them.

It is also permitted that the relative pronoun be an attribute of an omitted noun, i.e. "the group which" or "the party which"... etc. It would then be singular in wording and plural in meaning. It was said: the discourse then is on the basis of distribution (tawzi'), because bringing the truth in its literal sense belongs to him, upon him be prayers and peace, and believing in what he brought belongs to the followers, though it includes him and his followers (ﷺ) as well, but it is more apparent in them. So it should be understood this way for the sake of antithesis (taqabul). In al-Kashf: the more correct view is that it should not be understood as distribution; the most that can be said is that one of the two attributes is more apparent in one of the two described persons. On this basis is to be understood the statement of al-Zamakhshari which seems to suggest distribution. Some scholars understood the relative pronoun as generic (li'l-jins), since its definiteness is like the definiteness of the one with the article (dhu'l-lam), which may be generic or specific (al-'ahd). The intended meaning then is the Messengers and the believers.

In support of the intended meaning mentioned is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: (wa'alladhina ja'u bi'l-sidqi wa-saddaqu bihi) ("those who brought the truth and believed in it"). Some claimed that the intended reading was "wa'alladhina", with the nun dropped, as in the verse:

Indeed those whose blood was spilled at Fulj, they are the people, all of the people, O mother of Malik.

Abu Hayyan refuted this, saying it is not sound, because the pronoun in the relative clause must then be plural, as in the line. Do you not see that if the nun is dropped from (alladhani), the pronoun is dual, as in His saying:

O sons of Kulayb, indeed my uncles who (alladha) killed the kings and loosened the shackles.

'Ali'yah, Abu'l-'Aliyah and al-Kalbi, and a group said: (alladhi ja'a bi'l-sidq) is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and (alladhi saddaqa bihi) is Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him). This was reported by Ibn Jarir, al-Bawardi in Ma'rifat al-Sahabah and Ibn 'Asakir through the chain of Usayd ibn Safwan, who had companionship (suhbah), from 'Ali (may Allah ennoble his face). Abu'l-Aswad, Mujahid in one narration, and a group from the People of the House and others said: the one who believed in it is 'Ali (may Allah ennoble his face). Ibn Mardawayh reported it from Abu Hurayrah, traced to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Suddi that he said: (alladhi ja'a bi'l-sidq) is Jibril (peace be upon him), and (wa-saddaqa bihi) is the Prophet (ﷺ). It is said: on all three views the relative pronoun requires an implied ellipsis (idmar alladhi), which is not permitted according to the soundest view of the grammarians, namely that it is not permitted to omit the relative pronoun while retaining its clause absolutely, i.e. whether it is conjoined to another relative pronoun or not.

It is also weakened by the predicate being given in the plural. It was answered that there is no need for ellipsis, and by alladhi is meant the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and al-Siddiq, or 'Ali (may Allah ennoble both their faces together), with the relative clause being distributive; or by alladhi is meant Jibril (peace be upon him) and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) together in the same way, and a plural pronoun may refer to two, and they may be meant by alladhi. The stretch involved in this is not hidden. Allah knows best the state of the reports. Perhaps the mention of Abu Bakr, for example, if the report is sound, is by way of restricting to some individuals of the general for a particular point, which in Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) is that he was the first man to believe and affirm, and in 'Ali (may Allah ennoble his face) that he was the first of the boys to believe and affirm. Something similar is said if the report of al-Suddi is sound, though it hardly is sound, given His words, Exalted is He, afterwards: ﴿that He may expiate﴾, etc. By what has been mentioned the reports, if sound, may be reconciled, and none of them is taken as restricting. So reflect.

Abu Salih and Ikrimah ibn Sulayman read "wa-sadaqa bihi" with a light form (mukhaffafan), meaning: he conveyed it to the people and did not lie to them about it, i.e. he delivered it to them as it was revealed to him without distortion. The object is then omitted, because the discourse concerns the one who is characterized by it as truthful; and in the hadith "truthfulness" (al-sidq) is mentioned. The discourse is general rather than specific to him, upon him be prayers and peace, for the Companions memorized the whole of the Qur'an from him, upon him be prayers and peace, and conveyed it as it was sent down. It was said: the meaning is "he became truthful by it", i.e. by means of it, because the Qur'an is a miracle (mu'jiz), and a miracle indicates the truthfulness of the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace. On this view the description is specific. The verb "sadaqa" has been used figuratively in the sense of "became truthful by it", and there is no metonymy (kinayah) in it, as has been said. Abu Salih said: i.e. he acted by it, and this, as you see, is weak.

Ṣafḥa 4
It was also read "wa-ṣaddaqa bihi" in the passive voice with the doubled form.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 39, verse 34:

﴿For them is whatever they wish with their Lord﴾ is an explanation of what belongs to those described as having brought the truth. The confirmation of this in the Hereafter is among the good of the final return, after the explanation of what they have in this world of good deeds. That is, for them is everything they wish for of attracting benefits and warding off harms in the Hereafter, not in Paradise alone, because some of what they wish for, such as the expiation of their misdeeds, security from the Greatest Terror, and the rest of the horrors of the Resurrection, occurs before entering Paradise. ﴿That﴾, which has been mentioned, namely the attainment of everything they wish for, ﴿is the recompense of the doers of good﴾, that is, those who did good in their deeds. What is meant by them are those who were spoken of, but the apparent noun was put in place of the pronoun to draw attention to the cause of attaining the recompense. It was also said: what is meant is something that encompasses them and others, and they enter it in the first instance.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 39, verse 35:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That Allah may expiate from them the worst of what they did﴾ .. and so on. It is connected to an omitted element, meaning: "That Allah may expiate from them and reward them." He, glorified is He, singled them out with what He singled them out with, or with what precedes it, based on its overall sense (fahwa), as has been said. That is, Allah promised them everything they desire of the removal of harms and the attainment of pleasures, so that by the requirement of that promise He would expiate from them the worst of what they did, and so on. The meaning is not far from the first. It is also permitted that it be connected to His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And that is the recompense of the good-doers﴾, meaning, by what this indicates of established reward, or by "the good-doers," as Abu Hayyan said. It is as if it were said: "And that is the recompense of those who did good in their deeds, so that Allah, exalted is He, may expiate from them the worst of what they did, ﴿and reward them with their best reward﴾, that is, give them their reward, ﴿for the best of what they used to do﴾." The expiation is mentioned before the giving of reward because warding off harms is more important than attracting benefits.

The Majestic Name is placed in the position of the pronoun referring back to (their Lord) to show the utmost care for the content of the statement. The annexation of (worst) (أسوأ) and (best) (أحسن) to what follows them is the annexation of the elative form (af'al al-tafdil) to something other than the thing it is compared with, for clarification and explanation, as in: "al-Ashajj is the most just of the Banu Marwan," and "Yusuf is the best of his brothers." The comparison, according to what al-Zamakhshari said, serves to indicate that the lapse that is expiated in their view is the worst, because they greatly regard disobedience in every form due to the intensity of their fear. And the goodness they do is the best in the sight of Allah, exalted is He, because of the sincerity of their devotion in it.

This, according to what was established in al-Kashshaf, is because the comparison here is of the type of absolute excess, without regard to a thing compared against, looking at its reaching the furthest limit of perfection. Then, since they were God-fearing, of complete piety, there was no worst in their deeds except by supposition and assumption.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿for the best of what they used to do﴾, rather than "the best of what they used to do," indicates that their goodness in the sight of Allah, exalted is He, is of the best, because it indicates that all of their reward proceeds in that manner. So if they had done only the best, the comparison would be according to the matter itself. But if their deeds included the best and the good, and the recompense was according to the best, by looking at the best of their deeds and then the rest of the recompense proceeding by analogy with it, this indicates that the good in the sight of the one who recompenses is like the best. So on both suppositions it is correct that their goodness in the sight of Allah, exalted is He, is the best. And it is known from this that there is no Mu'tazilism in what al-Zamakhshari stated, as Abu Hayyan imagined. As for his statement in objecting to him, that he used (worst) (أسوأ) in comparison according to their belief and (best) (أحسن) in comparison according to what is in the sight of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, and that this is a distribution within the elative form, which is contrary to the apparent meaning: this may be granted when there is nothing in the statement that signals difference. Since in this verse there is that signal, according to what was established, it is not granted that distribution is contrary to the apparent meaning.

It has been said: (worst) (أسوأ) is according to what is common in the elative form, and the intended meaning is not that they had an evil deed and a worse deed, with the expiated one being the worst. For they are the God-fearing, and although they may have evil deeds, their evil deeds are not of the great major sins, and mention of them does not fit the context of praising them. Rather, the statement is a metonymy (kinaya) for the expiation of all their evil deeds by a demonstrative method (tariq burhani), for when the worst is expiated, the others are more deserving of expiation. It is not that this proceeded from them. And we do not grant
Page 5
the necessity of realizing the literal meaning in a metonymy, and that is, as you see, [unconvincing]. Other than one has said: the elative here is as is common, and the worst is the disbelief that preceded piety and goodness, and the intended meaning is the expiation of all that had passed from them of sins before faith, by a demonstrative method.

According to this, it cannot be easily interpreted as ﴿and confirmed it﴾ referring to Ali, may Allah honour his face, since he had no original disbelief preceding it, and one hardly expresses subsequent disbelief (al-kufr al-tab'i) by the worst of deeds. It has also been said: af'al is not at all for comparison, so (worst) (أسوأ) means "evil" (al-sayyi'), whether small or great, as is also one view regarding "al-Ashajj is the most just of the Banu Marwan." It is supported by the reading of Ibn Muqsim and Hamid ibn Yahya, from Ibn Kathir, through a transmission of al-Bazzi from him, "asw'a" (أسواء) in the pattern af'al, the plural of su' (evil). According to most people of these sayings, (best) (أحسن) is on its usual pattern, in the sense that He, exalted is He, looks at the best of their acts of obedience, and then recompenses the rest by analogy with it, out of gentleness and generosity. Al-Tabarsi claimed that the best is the obligatory and the recommended, and the good is the permissible, and recompense is only for the first two and not for the permissible. It has been said: the intended meaning is that He recompenses them with a better thing than their deed, which is Paradise, and there is much to be said about this. The combination of the past and present verb forms in the relative clause of the second relative pronoun, but not the first, is to indicate their continued practice of righteous deeds, unlike the evil deed.

[Page 6]

*Is not Allah sufficient for His servant?* This is a denial and negation of His being insufficient, in the most emphatic form, as if sufficiency were so manifest that no one could utter its opposite or hesitate in answering that it exists. By "His servant" is meant either the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), as related from al-Suddi, and this is supported by the words of Allah, *"And they threaten you with those besides Him"*, that is, the idols which they took as gods. The address then is to the Messenger (ﷺ), whether the sentence is a resumptive new statement (*isti'naf*, a sentence beginning a new thought) or a circumstantial clause (*hal*, a clause describing the state of the subject) relating to him (ﷺ). It has been related that "Quraysh said to him, peace and blessings be upon him: 'We fear that our gods will drive you mad, and that their harm will befall you because of your reviling of them.' So this was revealed." In another narration: "They said: 'You must desist from insulting our gods, or some madness will surely afflict you.' So this was revealed." Or "servant" refers to the category that includes him (ﷺ) in the first instance. This is supported by the recitation of Abu Ja'far, Mujahid, Ibn Thabbab, Talha, al-A'mash, Hamza and al-Kisa'i, reading *"'ibadahu"* (His servants) in the plural, which is interpreted as the prophets, peace be upon them, and the believers. On the first interpretation, the followers are also intended, as you have heard in the words of Allah, *"And the one who came with the truth and confirmed it"*. *"They threaten you"* includes them also, according to what has preceded. The coherence of the discourse with the words *"Who is more unjust"* up to this point lies in its indication that Allah suffices His Prophet (ﷺ) in the matters of his religion and his worldly life, and suffices his believing followers in both matters. In this there is also that He, glorified is He, suffices them against the evil of the disbelievers in two ways: by way of contrast, and because it is included in the sufficiency granted to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and his followers. This is what Qur'anic eloquence requires, and it accords with the theme on which the noble surah is built, namely the mention of the two groups and their conditions, as an emphasis on what was commanded at the beginning concerning worship and sincere devotion.

It has also been read *"bikafi 'ibadihi"* (with the genitive, "sufficient for His servants"), and *"yukafi 'abdahu"*, as the present tense of *kafa* with *"'abdahu"* in the accusative. This may be a *mufa'alah* form (a verbal pattern of reciprocal or intensive sense) from sufficiency, like your saying *yujari* from *yajri*, and it is more emphatic than *kafa* because it is built on the form of intensification. This is the apparent reading, given how often this meaning recurs in the Qur'an, such as *"So Allah will suffice you against them"* [al-Baqarah: 137]. It may also be *mahmuz* (with a hamza), derived from *mukafa'ah*, which means recompense. The connection is that when Allah mentioned the condition of the one who lied against Allah and denied the truth, and his recompense, and the condition of his counterpart, namely the one who came with the truth and confirmed it, and his recompense, and alluded by His words, glorified is He, *"That is the recompense of the good-doers"*, that what has preceded is the recompense of the disbelieving evildoers, as is known from the function of building upon the demonstrative noun, then He, mighty and majestic is He, followed this with His words, *"That He may expiate for them"*, etc., in the sense of: that He may expiate for them and recompense them. He singled them out with what He singled them out with, thereby alerting to the counterpart also, from the necessity of specification and causation. In it there is also what indicates the ruling on the counterpart, taking the object of the relation to be other than what was mentioned, as becomes apparent upon slight reflection. It was followed by His words: *"Is not Allah sufficient for His servant?"* Since the aim of those who look toward the servants is the Master, the beloved (ﷺ), the meaning is: Allah recompenses His servant and His Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, with this recompense mentioned. In it is also that He is the One who definitely recompenses him. The words *"And they threaten you"* accord with this, for since it was in response to their condemnation of their gods, as you have heard in the occasion of revelation, it was a warning of the retribution of the gods. So there is no flaw in the lack of accord. Indeed, we do not deny that the meaning of sufficiency is more emphatic, as the widely known recitation requires. So know this, and may Allah, exalted is He, take charge of your guidance.

*"And whomever Allah leaves astray"*, until he becomes heedless of the sufficiency of Allah, exalted is He, and frightens himself with what neither benefits nor harms at all, *"then he has no guide"* who would guide him to any good.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 39, verse 37:

﴿And whoever Allah guides﴾ — he makes the fact that He, exalted is He, is sufficient (kafiyan) ever before his eyes, acting in accordance with its requirement. ﴿Then there is none to mislead him﴾ — none who would turn him away from his aim, or afflict him with harm that disrupts his conduct, since there is no repelling of His act and no opposing of His will, glorified and exalted is He, as His saying, exalted is He, expresses: ﴿Is not Allah Mighty (ʿAziz), Owner of Retribution?﴾ — the Victorious who is not overcome, the Invincible who is not hindered or contested — ﴿Owner of Retribution (dhu intiqam)﴾ — He takes vengeance upon His enemies on behalf of His friends. And the placing of the Exalted Name in the position where a pronoun would be expected serves to establish the meaning of the statement and to instill awe (al-mahabah).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 39, verse 38:

﴿And if you were to ask them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "Allah."﴾ This is because the proof is manifest and the path is clear, for it has been established in the intellects that contingent beings must terminate in the Necessarily Existent (wajib al-wujud, that which necessarily exists). The noble Name (al-ism al-jalil, "Allah") is the subject (fa'il) of a verb that has been omitted, meaning: "Allah created them." ﴿Say﴾ as a rebuke to them: ﴿"Have you considered what you invoke besides Allah? If Allah should intend for me some harm, are they removers of His harm?"﴾ That is, since the Creator of the upper and lower worlds is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, as you have acknowledged, then inform me: if Allah, glorified is He, intends for me some harm, can those (idols) remove that harm from me? The fa' (then) here falls in the response to an implied conditional clause. Some of them said: the implied sense is, "If there is no creator besides Him, exalted is He, then is it possible for anyone other than Him to remove the harm that He intends?" It has also been permitted that the fa' be a conjunction (ataf) upon an implied element, meaning: "Have you reflected, after you have acknowledged, and so have you seen what you claim...?" etc.

﴿Or if He intends for me mercy﴾, that is, or if He intends for me some benefit, ﴿can they withhold His mercy?﴾ so that He would withhold it from me, glorified is He.

Al-A'raj, Shayba, Amr ibn Ubayd and Isa (with a variant from him) read "kashifatun" and "mumsikatun" [in some transmissions]. Abu Amr and Abu Bakr read "kashifatun" and "mumsikatun" with tanwin in both and the following words in the accusative, and they attach the intention of harm and mercy to His own precious self, upon him be blessings and peace, to repel [the charge] back upon their necks, since they had threatened him with the disgrace of the idols; and because of what it implies of sincere counsel [given purely]. He placed harm first because repelling it is more important. It has also been said that "kashifat" and "mumsikat" [are used] in accordance with the feminine attribute they ascribe to them, as an alert to the complete weakness of these (idols).

﴿Say: "Allah is sufficient for me"﴾, the Sufficient, exalted is His majesty, in all my affairs, in attaining good and repelling evil.

It is narrated from Muqatil that when he (ﷺ) asked them, they fell silent, and so this was revealed.

﴿Upon Him do the reliant rely﴾, not upon anyone else, in everything, ﴿the reliant﴾, because they know that everything other than Him is under His dominion (malakut), exalted is He.

﴿Say, "O my people, act according to your standing."﴾ That is, according to your condition in which you are, the enmity that has become firmly established in you. The word *makānah* (standing, position) has been transferred from a sensible place to the condition in which a person is, and it is used for it as a metaphor (*isti'ārah*) of the sensible for the intelligible. This is like how *ḥayth* (where) and *hunā* (here) are used for time, through the common element of comprehensiveness and encompassing. It is also permissible that the meaning is: act according to the extent of your ability and capacity.

It is narrated from ʿĀṣim (in a recitation reading) *makānātikum* (in the plural), and the command is for threat. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, I am working﴾ is a warning to them. Its being unrestricted is for increasing the warning, because if it had been said, "according to my standing," it would have appeared that he, upon him be blessings and peace, was in a single state that does not change and does not increase. So when it was stated without restriction, it indicated that for him, may God exalt him and grant him peace, every time has a different standing, and that he continues to grow in strength through the victory and support of God, exalted is He. This is supported by His saying, exalted is He, ﴿but you will come to know﴾, for it indicates that he, may God exalt him and grant him peace, will be victorious over them in this world and in the Hereafter, by the evidence of

[p. 7]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 39, verse 40:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever will receive a punishment that will disgrace him, and upon him will descend a lasting punishment﴾. The first (ʿadhāb, punishment) is an indication of the worldly punishment, and it befell them on the Day of Badr, while the second is an indication of the otherworldly punishment, for the lasting punishment is the punishment of the Fire. Had it been said, "Indeed I am acting according to my position," while at that time he was not the one prevailing, but rather the matter was the reverse, it would not have suited the intended meaning. (Man, "whoever") may be interrogative or relative. The clause (yukhzīhi, "that will disgrace him") is an attribute of (ʿadhāb, "a punishment"). The meaning of (muqīm, "lasting") is "perpetual." In the speech there is a metaphor (majāz) either in the adverbial expression (ẓarf) or in the predication (isnād), and its original form is "muqīm fīhi ṣāḥibuhu," meaning "its companion abides in it."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 39, verse 41:

﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book for mankind﴾ for their sake, for it is the measure (manat) of their welfare in this life and the Hereafter. ﴿with the truth﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) either from the object of "sent down" or from its subject, meaning: We have sent down the Book as one that is bound up with the truth, or as [two parties] bound up with the truth. ﴿So whoever is guided﴾ by acting upon what is in it, ﴿it is for his own self﴾, since he benefits his own self thereby. ﴿And whoever goes astray﴾ by not acting in accordance with its requirement, ﴿then he only goes astray to its detriment﴾, because the harm of his straying is confined to himself. ﴿And you are not a guardian over them﴾ because of their arrogance towards guidance. Your duty is only to convey (al-balagh), and you have indeed conveyed it, and how excellent a conveyance it was.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 39, verse 42:

﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death﴾, i.e., He seizes them from the bodies by severing their connection, the connection of control (tasarruf) over them, from them, ﴿at the time of their death﴾, i.e., at the time of their dying. ﴿And those that have not died﴾, i.e., and He takes the souls that have not died ﴿in their sleep﴾. The phrase ﴿in their sleep﴾ is connected to "yatawaffa" (He takes), i.e., He takes them at the time of their sleep, on the basis that manam is a noun of time. It is also permissible that it be a mimi verbal noun (masdar mimi), meaning that He, glorified is He, severs their connection to the bodies, the connection of control over them, from them as well. Thus the taking of souls at the time of death and their taking during sleep both mean seizing them from the bodies and severing their connection to them, the connection of control. However, their taking at the time of death severs their connection to them, the connection of control, outwardly and inwardly, whereas their taking during sleep severs that only outwardly. It seems that the taking that occurs at death, being one thing at the first moment of death and after the passing of days from it, was said as ﴿at the time of their death﴾; and the taking that occurs during sleep, since it varies in strength and weakness at the beginning of the time of sleep and after the passing of a period from it, was said as ﴿in their sleep﴾, i.e., at the time of their sleep. This is what was said, so ponder it. The path of the sound intellect has room (for interpretation). The attribution of death and sleep to the souls is said to be a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli), because they are states of their bodies, not states of the souls themselves. al-Tabarsi claimed that the speech is on the elision of a modifier, namely "the bodies." al-Zamakhshari made "the souls" an expression for the whole person (al-jumla), not for what stands opposite the bodies, and he took their taking to mean causing their death and removing the soundness of their parts entirely, so that they no longer remain living, sensing, perceiving, until it is as if their very essence had been stripped away. Since this meaning is not realized in the taking during sleep, because it is nothing but the removal of full soundness and what follows from it of voluntary movements and others, he said regarding His saying, ﴿and those that have not died in their sleep﴾, i.e., He takes them when they sleep, likening sleepers to the dead. From this is His saying, ﴿And it is He who takes you at night﴾ [al-An'am: 60], where you do not discern and do not act freely, just as the dead are likewise. What seems to be a combination of the literal and the metaphorical in this is removed by reflection. The placing of the glorious Name first and the construction of (yatawaffa) upon it is for restriction (hasr), or for emphasis (taqwa), or for both. Considering restriction is more fitting to the context than considering emphasis alone; that is, Allah takes the souls in truth, not any other, mighty and majestic is He. ﴿Then He withholds those﴾, i.e., the souls ﴿upon which He has decreed﴾ in eternity ﴿death﴾, and He does not return them to their bodies, but keeps them in the state they were in. To this is added the severing of the connection of control inwardly. He expressed this by "withholding" to correspond with "taking."

Page 8
Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, 'Isa, Talhah, al-A'mash and Ibn Wththab read "qudiya" in the passive voice with "al-mawt" in the nominative. ﴿And He sends back the others﴾, i.e., the other souls, which are the sleeping ones, to their bodies, so that they become, as in the state of wakefulness, connected to them with the connection of control, outwardly and inwardly. He expressed it as "sending" in observance of the contrast. ﴿For a specified term﴾ is the time appointed for death in reality, and it is the limit of the genus of sending that occurs after withholding, not of an individual instance of it, for that is instantaneous with no extension, so it does not have a limit. Some have considered the limit to be for the genus, lest it follow that no sleep occurs after the first waking at all, and that is good. It was also said: "sends back" carries the meaning of "preserving," and the meaning is: He sends back the others, preserving them from real death, for a specified term. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that in the son of Adam there is a soul (nafs) and a spirit (ruh), between which is like the ray of the sun. The soul is that by which there is reason and discernment, and the spirit is that by which there is the soul and movement. Both are taken at death, while at sleep only the soul is taken. This is a view that distinguishes between soul and spirit, and some have attributed it to the majority. The soul is called the rational soul (al-nafs al-nathiqah), the commanding spirit (al-ruh al-amriyyah), and the divine spirit (al-ruh al-ilahiyyah); and the spirit is called the animal spirit (al-ruh al-hayawaniyyah), and likewise the animal soul (al-nafs al-hayawaniyyah). The second is like a throne to the first. Some of the theosophist philosophers said that the pineal heart (al-qalb al-sanawbari) contains a subtle vapour which is a throne for the animal spirit, a guardian of it, and an instrument upon which its effects depend. The animal spirit is a throne and mirror of the divine spirit, which is the rational soul, and an intermediary between it and the body, through which the governing command of the soul reaches it. A group went to non-difference (between them), and this is the view of Ibn Jubayr and one of the two opinions of Ibn 'Abbas. What was narrated from him at first regarding the verse agrees with what we have mentioned, in that the soul according to it is not the meaning of the whole person, as al-Zamakhshari said, and he claimed that the correct view is what he mentioned, not this narrated one, on the evidence of "its death" and "its sleep"; and the pronoun refers to the souls, and what is meant by them is not characterized by death and sleep, but rather the whole person is what is characterized by them.

Al-Kashshaf said: Because the distinction between the two souls is an opinion refuted by proof, and the application of "istifa'" (taking in full) also needs interpretation, one should not turn away from the well-known and suitable view, meaning the interpretation of taking as causing to die. Its origin is taking a thing from the one from whom it is taken in full and complete, and removing it from him entirely; then it was transferred to causing death because it is present in it, until it became what is immediately understood from it. In this there is some unease. What many sound reports attest is that the one taken is the souls that stand opposite the bodies, not the whole person.

Al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) in their Sahihayn related from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "When one of you goes to his bed, let him shake it out with the inner edge of his waist-wrap, for he does not know what has fallen upon it. Then let him say: O Allah, in Your name, my Lord, I lay down my side, and in Your name I raise it. If You take my soul, then have mercy on it, and if You send it back, then protect it with what You protect Your righteous servants." Ahmad, al-Bukhari, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Abi Shaybah related from Abu Qatadah that the Prophet ﷺ said to them on the night of the valley: "Indeed Allah took your spirits when He willed, and returned them to you when He willed." Ibn Mardawayh related from Anas ibn Malik who said: "I was with the Prophet ﷺ on a journey, and he said: Who will keep watch for us tonight? I said: I will. So he slept, and the people slept, and I slept, and we did not wake except by the heat of the sun. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: O people, indeed these spirits are lent in the bodies of the servants; Allah takes them when He wills and sends them when He wills."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh related from Sulaym ibn 'Amir that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said: "I am amazed at the dream of a man: he spends the night and sees a thing that never occurred to his mind, so his dream is like a grasp by the hand; and a man sees a dream and his dream is nothing." 'Ali, may Allah honour his face, said: "Shall I not inform you of that, O Commander of the Faithful? Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that have not died in their sleep. Then He withholds those upon which He has decreed death, and sends back the others for a specified term﴾. So Allah takes all the souls, and what they see while they are with Him, glorified is He, in the heaven, is the true dream; and what they see when they are sent back to their bodies is the false, for when they are sent back to their bodies the devils meet them in the air and deceive them and inform them of falsehoods, so they lie in them." 'Umar marvelled at his saying, may Allah be pleased with both of them. The apparent meaning of this report is that the sleeping soul that is taken remains in heaven until it is sent back, and similar things must be interpreted on the view of the soul's immateriality, but need not be on the other view. Indeed, perhaps you choose it, and it is as if you say: The soul is noble and exalted, descended from the highest station and sent forth from a protected sanctuary, and occupied with managing its dwelling in its day and its night, and it never ceases to await the opportunity of return to that sanctuary and the lofty, most exalted station; and at sleep it seizes that opportunity, and that sorrow becomes in some measure easy for it; so there arises for it a kind of turning toward the world of light and the place of joy free of evils, such that it prepares in some degree to receive some of its effects and to be illumined by something of its lights. Making it so is its taking, and by my life, by it is its spreading and its taking. So when it sees, while returning in that state and drawing from that world described with perfection, a dream, it is true; and when it sees while going backward to what it was tried with of managing a dwelling in which devils of illusions roam and crowd in any manner of crowding, its dream is false. Then, in both states, it varies in individuals in what preparation occurs, and the standing upon the reality of the state is not completed except by unveiling, not by saying and hearsay.

﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who reflect﴾. The indication is to what was mentioned of taking, withholding and sending back; the singular is for its interpretation as what was mentioned or similar; the form of the distant is in regard to its origin, or the passage of its mention, or the remoteness of its rank. The tanwin in "ayat" is for multiplicity and magnification, meaning: in what was mentioned are many great signs indicating the perfection of His power and wisdom and the comprehensiveness of His mercy, glorified is He, for a people who reflect on the manner of the connection of souls with bodies, and their taking from them at times entirely at death, and their being kept remaining, not perishing with its perishing, until Allah restores creation, and what befalls them of happiness and misery; and at other times only from their outward aspects, as in sleep, and their being sent back from time to time until the end of their appointed terms.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 39, verse 43:**

﴿Or have they taken﴾: meaning, rather, the Quraysh have taken. Here *am* is disjunctive (*munqati'a*, meaning "rather"), and the implied interrogative (*istifham*, a question) is for denouncing their taking [of intercessors]. ﴿intercessors besides Allah﴾: who intercede for them with Allah, the Exalted, in lifting the punishment. It has also been said that it concerns their worldly and otherworldly affairs. It is permissible for it to be connected (*muttasila*, conjunctive) with an implied counterpart (*mu'adil*), as Ibn al-Shaykh mentioned in the margins of al-Baydawi's commentary, but this is an unnecessary strain. The meaning of ﴿besides Allah﴾ is: besides His approval or His permission, because He, glorified is He, does not intercede with Him except for one whom He permits, from among those with whom He is pleased. Such lowly inanimate objects are neither approved nor permitted. Even if this were not taken into account, it would imply that Allah, the Exalted, is an intercessor, and this term is not applied to Him, glorified is He. Or the implied meaning is: "Or have they taken gods other than Him, the Exalted, to intercede for them," and this is interpreted in the light of what has been mentioned.

﴿Say: Even though they possess nothing and do not understand?﴾: meaning, will they intercede while they are in the state of not possessing anything of things and not understanding them? The summary of this is: will they intercede while they are inanimate objects that have no power and no knowledge? Thus the interrogative particle (*hamza*) enters upon an omitted element, the *waw* indicates a circumstantial state (*hal*), and the clause is a circumstantial clause from the subject of the omitted verb. Some scholars have held that it is for coordination (*'atf*) upon a conditional clause that has been omitted, indicated by the phrase ("even though they do not possess...") ... etc., upon it, i.e., will they intercede if they possessed something and understood? And even if they do not possess anything and do not understand? The meaning on the circumstantial reading is also: as if it were said, "Will they intercede in every state?"

Some of the grammarian-scholars (*muhaqqiqin min al-nuhat*) said: it is a parenthetical clause (*i'tirad*). By a parenthetical clause they mean that which occurs between parts of speech, connected to them in meaning while being separate in wording, by way of a shift (*iltifat*), as in the poet's saying:

*"You are divorce, and divorce is an oath."*

And in his saying:

*"You see everyone in it perishing, and far be it from you (to perish)."*

It may also come after the completion of the sentence, as in the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "I am the master of the descendants of Adam, and I say this without boasting."

Regarding whether the conditional particle in such a construction requires an answer (*jawab*), there is disagreement. According to the view that it requires one, the answer is omitted, indicated by what precedes it. The detailed positions are found in the books of Arabic grammar.

It is also permissible that the object of the omitted interrogative particle here is the taking (*al-ittikhadh*), i.e., say to them: "Do you take them as intercessors, even though they possess nothing of things, let alone possessing intercession with Allah, the Exalted, and do not understand?"

[Page 10]

**"Say: To Allah belongs all intercession."** Perhaps, as the Imam said, this is a rebuttal of their claim, which is that the intercessors are not the idols themselves but rather exalted persons whose statues these are. The meaning is that He, exalted is He, is the owner of all intercession (*shafa'a*). No one can obtain any intercession except when the one being interceded for is approved and the intercessor is authorized, and both conditions are absent here. This verse may be cited as evidence for the existence of intercession on the Day of Resurrection in general, because the possession, namely the exclusivity indicated by the *lam* here, requires existence. So using it to deny intercession absolutely is extremely weak.

His, exalted is He, saying: **"To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth."** This is an explanatory resumption (*istinaf ta'lili*) for the fact that all intercession belongs to Him, Mighty and Majestic. It is as if it were said: it belongs to Him because He, Exalted and Majestic, is the owner of all dominion, so no one may dispose of anything of it without His permission and approval. "The heavens and the earth" is a metonymy (*kinaya*) for everything other than Him, glorified is He.

His, exalted is He, saying: **"Then to Him you will be returned"** is coordinated (*atf*) with His saying: **"To Him belongs the dominion"**, etc. It seems to be an explicit statement of His ownership in the Hereafter, in which lies the greater part of the benefit of intercession, and an allusion to the cessation of apparent dominion of anything other than Him, Mighty and Majestic.

It has also been permitted that it be coordinated with His saying: **"To Allah belongs intercession."** Al-Bahr (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*) takes it as a threat to them, as if it were said: then to Him you will be returned, and you will know that they will not intercede for you, and your effort in worshipping them will be in vain. The placing of **"to Him"** (*ilayhi*) first serves the verse-ending (*fasila*) and indicates restriction (*hasr*), since the meaning is: to Him, exalted is He, and not to anyone else, glorified is He, you will be returned, neither independently nor in partnership.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 39, verse 45:

﴿When God alone is mentioned﴾, meaning singled out for mention, with their gods not mentioned alongside Him. It was also said: meaning, when it is said, "There is no god but God." ﴿the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter recoil﴾, meaning they contract and shrink away, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when you mention your Lord alone in the Qur'an, they turn their backs in aversion﴾ [al-Isra' 76]. ﴿And when those other than Him are mentioned﴾, singly or alongside the mention of God, Exalted and Majestic is He, ﴿behold, they rejoice﴾, because of their excessive infatuation with them and their forgetting of God's right, Exalted is He. The description of their ugly state has been intensified by stating the extreme in both: for istibshar (rejoicing) means that the heart is filled with joy until the brightness of the face opens up because of it, and ishmi'zaz (recoiling) means that one is filled with rage and grief, so that the skin of the face contracts from it, as is seen in the face of the frowning, sorrowful person.

The first ﴿إذا﴾ (idha, "when") is conditional (shartiyyah); its place is accusative as an adverb of time (zarfiyyah), and its governing element, according to most grammarians, is the answer (jawab), which is ﴿اشْمَأزَّتْ﴾ (ishma'azzat, "recoiled"); or, according to Abu Hayyan and a group, it is the verb that follows it, which is ﴿ذُكِرَ﴾ (dhukira, "was mentioned"). According to them, it is not in construct with the clause that follows it. Likewise the second ﴿إذا﴾: the element governing it is either ﴿ذُكِرَ﴾ after it, or ﴿يَسْتَبْشِرُونَ﴾ (yastabshirun, "rejoice"). The third ﴿إذا﴾ is a sudden-occurrence particle (fuja'iyyah), connecting the clause of the apodosis to the clause of the protasis like the fa' (fa, "then"). On the view that it is a particle, nothing governs it; on the view that it is a noun and an adverb of time or place, its governing element here is the predicate of the subject after it. Al-Zamakhshari said: its governing element is an implied verb derived from the word of suddenness (mufaja'ah), its estimated form being "they suddenly came at the time of rejoicing," so it is the object (maf'ul bih). It is permitted that it be the subject (fa'il), in the sense of "it suddenly overtook them at the time of rejoicing." This implied verb is the answer of the second ﴿إذا﴾, so it is connected to it, on the basis of the view of most grammarians that the governing element of idha is its answer. It does not follow that two adverbs are governed by one governing element, because the second of them is not accusative as an adverb.

Yes, it has been said against al-Zamakhshari that he has no precedent for what he held, and you know that a man in Arabic does not imitate others. It is strange that al-Hawfi said the third ﴿إذا﴾ is adverbial, brought in as a repetition and emphasis of the ﴿إذا﴾ before it, and its protasis has been omitted, the estimated meaning being "when that is the case, they rejoice." It should not be paid any attention at all. The verse concerns the polytheists in general. Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn Abbas that he explained ﴿those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾ as Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, al-Walid ibn Uqba, Safwan, and Ubayy ibn Khalaf, and he explained ﴿those other than Him﴾ as al-Lat and al-Uzza. This seems to be a specification of some individuals of the general term. Ibn al-Mundhir and others transmitted from Mujahid that the verse relates what the polytheists did on the day the Prophet (ﷺ) recited ﴿By the star﴾ [al-Najm 1] near the door of the Ka'bah. This too does not contradict the generality, as is clear.

We have seen many people in the same manner as this description with which God, Exalted is He, described the polytheists: they are delighted at the mention of dead persons whom they call upon for help, petition, and from whom they seek things, and they are enraptured by hearing false stories about them that agree with their desires and their beliefs about them. They honor whoever recounts these things to them, and they recoil from the mention of God, Exalted is He, alone, and from attributing the independent exercise of disposal to Him, Exalted and Majestic is He, and from reciting what indicates the greater magnificence and majesty of Him. They shun whoever does such things with the utmost aversion, and they attribute to him what they dislike. I once said to a man who was calling for help in distress to some of the dead, crying, "O so-and-so, help me," "Say, 'O God,' for He, Glorified is He, has said: ﴿And when My servants ask you about Me, indeed I am near. I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾ [al-Baqarah 186]." He became angry, and it reached me that he said, "So-and-so denies the saints." I heard from some of them that he said, "The saint is quicker to respond than God, Exalted and Majestic is He." This is a position of great disbelief. We ask God, Exalted is He, to protect us from deviation and transgression.

[p. 11]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 39, verse 46:

﴿Say: "O Allah, Originator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, You judge between Your servants concerning that over which they have been differing."﴾ This is a command to supplicate and to seek refuge in Allah, the Exalted, because of what he (ﷺ) had suffered in the matter of their call and what he had endured from the severity of their obstinacy in arrogance and stubborn opposition. For He, the Exalted, is the One capable of all things in their entirety and the One who knows all circumstances in their totality. The purpose of the command to say this is to explain their condition and to warn them, and to console His beloved, the most noble (ﷺ), and to make known that his effort and striving are recognized and appreciated by Him, Mighty and Majestic; and to teach the servants to seek refuge in Allah, the Exalted, and to supplicate by His Supreme Names. How excellent is the saying of al-Rabi' ibn Khaytham, for when he was asked about the killing of al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with him, he sighed and recited this verse. So when something of what took place among the Companions is mentioned to you, say: ﴿O Allah, Originator of the heavens﴾ ... and so on. For this is among the etiquettes that ought to be observed.

The placing of the subject (the pronoun "You") in ﴿You judge﴾ serves to restrict: meaning, You alone judge between the servants concerning that over which their disagreement has persisted, a judgment that every stubborn obstinate person will accept and to which every rebellious tyrant will submit, namely the worldly or the otherworldly punishment. The purpose of the judgment between the servants is the judgment between him, upon him be blessings and peace, and these disbelievers.

ﷻ"And if those who did wrong possessed everything on earth and the like of it with it, they would surely offer it as ransom from the evil of the Day of Resurrection..." (39:47). Al-Alusi's commentary follows.

It has been said that this is a resumed clause (mustanaf), brought to explain the consequences of the judgment that the Prophet (ﷺ) had invoked, and the extent of its severity and dreadfulness. That is: if they possessed all that is in the world of wealth and treasures, ﴿and the like of it with it, they would surely offer it as ransom from the evil of the Day of Resurrection﴾. That is, they would make all of that a ransom for their own souls from the wretched, severe punishment. It has also been said that the clause is conjoined (ma'tuf) to an implied element, the sense being: "So I will judge between them and punish them; and even if they knew that, they would not have done what they did." The first view is more apparent. The intent is not to affirm a conditional (shartiyyah) but to depict their state by likening it to that of one who tries to escape and ransom himself from his situation with what has been mentioned, and it would not be accepted from him. Its upshot is that the punishment is inescapable, and they will not be freed from it; and even if this impossible supposition were granted, there is in it such a degree of threat and despair as is not hidden.

As for the words of the Most High: ﴿And there will appear to them from Allah what they had not reckoned﴾, that is: there will become apparent to them, from among the varieties of punishments, what was not in their calculation, an intensification of the threat. A parallel to this in the promise is the words of the Most High: ﴿No soul knows what has been hidden for them of comfort for the eyes﴾ [As-Sajdah: 17].
