It has been said that the clause is a state (hal) of the subject of "iftadaw" (they would ransom); the apparent view is that it is so.

[Page 12]

﴿And there will appear to them﴾ when their records are presented to them, ﴿the evils of what they earned﴾, i.e., that which they earned and did, on the basis that *mā* is a relative pronoun (*mawṣūla*, relative), or their earning and doing, on the basis that it is a verbal particle (*maṣdariyya*, "the verbal-noun *mā*"). The idafa of *sayyi'āt* (evils) is in the sense of *min* (of/from) or *al-lām* (the particle of possession or relation). ﴿And there befell﴾, i.e., encompassed, ﴿them that which they used to mock at﴾, i.e., its recompense. This is either because the speech contains an elided *muḍāf* (a omitted noun governed by the genitive), or because there is a *majāz* (figurative usage) in which the cause is mentioned while its effect is intended. *Mā* is also capable of being a relative pronoun and a verbal particle here.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 39, verse 49:**

﴿When harm touches man, he calls upon Us.﴾ This is a report about the species (*jins*) in terms of what predominates in it. It is also said that what is meant by "man" (*insan*) is Hudhayfah ibn al-Mughirah, and it is said that it refers to the disbelievers. ﴿Then when We bestow upon him a favour from Us﴾, meaning, We give it to him as a bounty. For *takhwil* (bestowing), as it has been said, is specific to this sense and is not applied to what is given as a reward. ﴿He says, "I was given it only on knowledge."﴾ That is, on knowledge from me of the ways of acquiring it, or because I knew that I would be given it on account of my deserving it, or on knowledge from God, Exalted is He, of me and of my worthiness. *Innama* (only) here indicates restriction: I was not given it for anything except on account of knowledge. The pronoun (*ha'*) refers to *ni'mah* (favour), and the masculine form is used because it is interpreted as referring to something among the favours. The indication for this is the indefiniteness (*tankir*) of the noun. It is also said that it is because the word means *in'am* (bestowal), and it is also said that it is because what is meant by it is wealth, and it is also said that it is because it comprises both masculine and feminine elements, so the masculine predominated. It is also permitted that the pronoun refers to what is in *innama* considered as a relative pronoun (*mawsulah*), meaning: "what I was given is present on account of knowledge." However, its being written joined together in the copies of the Qur'an makes its being a relative pronoun unlikely. ﴿Nay, it is a trial﴾: this is a refutation of his statement. The pronoun refers to the favour in terms of its wording, just as the first pronoun refers to it in terms of its meaning. Considering the wording after considering the meaning is permissible, although the more common practice is the reverse. It is also permitted that the feminine form is in view of the predicate. It has been said that the pronoun refers to the act of giving (*al-ita'anah*), and it has been read with the masculine form, in which case it refers to the favour as well, as previously mentioned, or to the act of giving (*al-itan*). That is: the matter is not as he says; rather, what has been given him is a test for him, whether he will give thanks or disbelieve. It is described as a "trial" although it is merely an instrument of trial, for the purpose of emphasis (*mubalaghah*). A similar explanation applies if the pronoun is taken to refer to *al-ita'anah* or *al-itan*. ﴿But most of them do not know.﴾ That is, the matter is as stated. This clearly shows that what is meant by "man" is the species, for if the specific (*'ahd*) were intended, it would have said, "But he does not know" or "But they do not know." Taking the specific sense in the earlier part and returning the pronoun to the general sense here is a *istikhdam* (a figure in which one word is used in one sense and its pronoun in another), similar to the expression "I have a dirham, and half of it," which is far-fetched.

The *fa'* (then) is for conjunction, and what follows it is conjoined to God's statement: ﴿And when God alone is mentioned﴾ ... etc. It indicates sequence following from that. The purpose of it is mockery (*tahakkum*) and ridicule (*tahmiq*). In it is a censure of them for contradiction and inversion, since they recoil from the mention of God alone and rejoice at the mention of the gods. So when harm touches them, they call upon those from whose mention they recoiled, rather than those at whose mention they rejoiced. This is like saying: "So-and-so harms so-and-so, and when he needs something, he asks him and is kind to him." In the *fa'* there is a *isti'arah tab'iyyah tahakkumiyyah* (a subordinate, mocking metaphor). It has been said that it may be causal (*sababiyyah*), entering upon the cause, because mention of the effect requires mention of its cause, since the appearance of what they did not reckon... etc. is an effect of what follows the *fa'*. However, this recurs with God's later statement: ﴿And those who did wrong﴾ from among them to the end, if the two do not differ in that one of them is in this world and the other in the Hereafter. Al-Zamakhshari went to what we have put forward. The sentences intervening between them, namely God's statement, glorified is He: ﴿Say, "O God"﴾ ... to ﴿they mock﴾, are a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiraz*) emphasizing the denunciation of them. Abu Hayyan claimed that there is artificiality in this and a parenthetical insertion of more than two sentences. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi does not permit a parenthetical insertion of two sentences, so how could he permit more? I say: there is no harm in it, especially since it contains a subtle and delicate meaning. Al-Farisi is refuted by what has come in the speech of the Arabs of this kind.

﴿قَدْ قالَها الَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِهِمْ﴾ The pronoun in ﴿قالَها﴾ refers to his saying ﴿إنَّما أُوتِيتُهُ عَلى عِلْمٍ﴾ ["I have been given it only on the basis of knowledge"] [al-Qasas 28:78], because it is a word or a sentence. It was also read as ﴿قالَه﴾ with the masculine pronoun, meaning the saying or the speech that was mentioned. ﴿Those before them﴾ refers to Qarun and his people, since he said it and they were pleased with it. So the attribution is of the type of attributing what belongs to some to all, which is a figurative attribution of the rational kind (majaz 'aqli, a metaphor in the attribution of an action to something other than its true agent).

[Page 13]

It is also permitted that the figurative usage lies in the adverbial phrase, so that ﴿قالَها الَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِهِمْ﴾ means "it spread among them." The commonly accepted view is the first. The intended meaning is that they said a statement like this one, or said this very same statement. Because the wording is identical, it is treated as one thing in common usage. ﴿So what they had been earning did not avail them﴾ from the goods of this world and what they had been gathering from it.

﴿So there befell them the evil consequences of what they had earned﴾, that is, there befell them the requital for the evils of their earning, or for what they had earned, on the basis that the speech contains an elided noun (mudaf), or that "evils" is used figuratively for what is caused by them. It may also be said that the requital of an evil is called an evil by way of mushākala (a rhetorical device of naming a thing after something associated with or similar to it), like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and the requital for an evil is an evil like it﴾. So what is here is of the presumed (taqdīrīyya) mushākala. And when the meaning is taken as making the requital for all that they earned an evil, the speech indicates that all that they earned is evil, for if there were something good in it, it would have been requited with a good requital. And in it is what there is of censure of them.

﴿And those who wronged among these﴾, the polytheists. The "min" (among) is explanatory (lil-bayān), for they all were wrongdoers, since polytheism is a great wrong. Or it is partitive (lil-tab'īḍ), so the intended by "those who wronged" is whoever persisted in wrongdoing until a calamity (qāri'a) strikes them, and they are a part of them. ﴿Evils of what they earned will befall them﴾, as there befell those who came before them. The intended is the worldly punishment, for they were struck by famine for seven years, and their chieftains were killed at Badr. It was said that the punishment is the otherworldly one, and it was said that it is the more general. He preferred the first, saying that it best fits the context. The Exalted's saying ﴿and they will not escape﴾ alludes, i.e. they will not escape, according to what has been said, to the otherworldly punishment.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 39, verse 52:

﴿Do they not know that Allah extends provision to whom He wills﴾ [i.e., to extend it for him] ﴿and restricts it﴾ [for whom He wills to restrict it for him], without anyone having any part in that, since He withheld provision from them for seven years and then extended it to them for seven years. ﴿Indeed, in that﴾ which has been mentioned ﴿are signs﴾ indicating that all occurrences are from Allah, exalted is His majesty, and that causes, in reality, are nullified ﴿for a people who believe﴾, since they are the ones who derive evidence from them for what they signify.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 39, verse 53:

﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾. That is, they have gone to excess in sins, persisting in them. The original meaning of *israf* (extravagance, excess) is excess in spending wealth, and it was then used figuratively for what is mentioned here, through two stages, as has been said. Al-Raghib said: it is going beyond the limit in every action a person performs, although its use in spending is more well known. This indicates that it is literal for what we have mentioned, and it is good.

The verb was given the sense of *al-jinayah* (committing an offence, wronging), so that its construction with *ʿalā* (against) would be correct. In a construction with an implied sense (*tadmin*), it is not necessary that the implied meaning be literal. It has also been said that it implies the sense of *al-haml* (bearing, burdening). Several scholars took the idiomatic annexation in "My servants" (*ʿibadiya*) to be a known reference (*ʿahd*) or an honorific (*tashrif*). They held that the intended meaning of "servants" is the believers, since this term has come to be used for them, attributed to the Mighty and Majestic in the Great Qur'an. So it is as if it were said: O believing sinners, ﴿do not despair of the mercy of Allah﴾, that is, do not despair of His forgiveness and grace, Glorified is He and Mighty and Majestic is He, on the basis that forgiveness is included in mercy, or that mercy necessarily entails it, since mercy is inconceivable for one who is not forgiven. The justification of the prohibition by His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Indeed Allah forgives all sins﴾, requires that they be included in what is justified. The closing by His saying, Glorified is He, ﴿Indeed He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ is almost explicit in this. It was also permitted that the speech contains the rhetorical device of *ihtibak* (mutual omission), as if it were said: do not despair of the mercy and forgiveness of Allah; indeed Allah forgives all sins and shows mercy. This is far-fetched.

They said: the intended meaning of forgiving sins is overlooking them and not calling to account for them, outwardly and inwardly, and this is what is meant by covering them. It was also said: what is meant is erasing them completely from the records, together with overlooking them. The apparent sense of the ruling is its absolute application, and restricting it by repentance goes against the apparent sense. How could it not, when His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Indeed Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whomever He wills﴾ [al-Nisa': 48]
[Page 14]
is apparent in its absoluteness regarding everything other than polytheism. The absoluteness is also supported by several matters. The first is their being addressed with the title of servitude, for servitude requires humility, and this is more suitable to the state of a disobedient person who has not repented, and its requirement of mercy is clear. The second is the brevity indicated by the annexation to His pronoun, for a master by nature shows mercy to his servant and is compassionate toward him. The third is the restriction of the harm of excess, which is indicated by *ʿalā* (against), to themselves. It is as if it were said: the harm of sins returns to them, not to Me, and this suffices without any other harm, as in the proverb: "Do good to the one who does wrong; his wrongdoing is sufficient punishment for the wrongdoer." Thus the servant who has done wrong and stands before his master in humiliation and fear, aware of his master's displeasure and looking to the honouring of others who obeyed, suffers harm, for deserving punishment is itself a punishment in the view of people of understanding. The fourth is the prohibition of despair from mercy in general, let alone from forgiveness, and its absoluteness. The fifth is the annexation of mercy to the Majestic Name, which contains all the meanings of the Names, by way of *iltifat* (shift in grammatical person), for this indicates its vastness, and it clearly indicates its inclusion of the penitent and others. The sixth is the justification by His saying (Indeed Allah...), etc. For justification is fitting alongside remoteness, and abstaining from despair of mercy without repentance is more remote than abstaining from it with repentance. The seventh is placing the Majestic Name in the position of the pronoun, to indicate that forgiveness is among the requirements of His essence, not for anything else, such as repentance or otherwise. The eighth is the definiteness of "sins" (*al-dhunub*), for in a context of praise it clearly indicates comprehensiveness, so it includes the sin that is followed by repentance and the sin that is not. The ninth is the emphasis by "all" (*jamiʿan*). The tenth is the justification by "indeed He is..." etc. The eleventh is the expression by "the Forgiving" (*al-Ghafur*), for it is an intensive form, and if it is considered in terms of quantity, forgiveness includes all sins, or if considered in terms of quality, it includes major sins without repentance. The twelfth is the omission of the object of "the Forgiving," for omitting the object conveys generality. The thirteenth is that the sentence conveys restriction (*hasr*), for it is known that forgiveness may be attributed to others besides Him, Exalted is He; so what is restricted to Him, Glorified is He, is the perfect and great forgiveness, which is that which occurs without repentance. The fourteenth is the intensification of that restriction.

The fifteenth is the promise of mercy after forgiveness, for this indicates that the servant does not deserve forgiveness were it not for His mercy, and this is clear in the case where one has not repented. The sixteenth is the expression by an intensive form in it. The seventeenth is its absoluteness. The Mu'tazilah (a rational theological school) refused to accept the forgiveness of major sins and pardoning them without repentance, and they said: such forgiveness is stated in more than one place in the noble Qur'an restricted by repentance, so its absoluteness here is to be understood as restricted, since the case is one and there is no possibility of abrogation (*naskh*, the cancelling of a ruling by a later one),

The Qur'an being like a single speech, and they supported this with His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And turn in repentance to your Lord and submit to Him before the punishment comes upon you, and then you will not be helped﴾. It is a conjunction (*'atf*) upon "do not despair," and the causal clause is parenthetical (*mu'tarid*). After granting the principle that the unrestricted is to be read in light of the restricted, it is a conjunction for completing the clarification, as if it were said: Do not despair of the mercy of Allah, Exalted is He, lest you think that He will not accept your repentance. Turn to Him, Exalted is He, and devote yourselves sincerely to Him, Mighty and Majestic.

Some of the scholars responded by denying the obligation to read the unrestricted in light of the restricted within a single speech, as in "Honor the virtuous, honor the perfect," let alone a speech that is not granted to be in the status of a single speech. In that case the conjoined clause would not be a condition for the preceding clause, since it is not part of its completion. It was said: the command to repent and to be sincere is not nullified by the unrestricted, since the claim is not that the verse indicates that forgiveness is granted to everyone without repentance and without prior punishment, such that it would dispense with the command to them and contradict the threat of punishment.

Some eminent investigators said: His saying, ﴿O My servants who have transgressed﴾, is addressed to the disbelievers and the disobedient, although the primary intention is the disbelievers, due to proximity and the occasion of revelation. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: The people of Mecca said: Muhammad claims that whoever worships idols, calls upon another god besides Allah, and kills a soul that Allah has forbidden will not be forgiven. So how can we emigrate and submit, when we have worshipped gods and killed souls, and we are people of polytheism? Then Allah revealed: ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves...﴾ and so on.

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: These verses were revealed concerning 'Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'ah, al-Walid ibn al-Walid, and a group of Muslims who had embraced Islam, then were tried and tortured and so they succumbed. We used to say: Allah will never accept from these people any repentance or ransom, ever: people who embraced Islam and then abandoned their religion because of the torture they were subjected to. Then these verses were revealed. 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, was a scribe, so he wrote them with his own hand, then wrote them to 'Ayyash, to al-Walid, and to those people, and they embraced Islam and emigrated.

Ibn Jarir reported from 'Ata' ibn Yasar, who said: These three verses, from ﴿Say: O My servants﴾ to ﴿while you do not perceive﴾, were revealed in Medina concerning Wahshi and his companions. The saying ﴿Indeed, Allah forgives all sins﴾ came between the two conjoined clauses as a causal justification for the first part before reaching the second, to indicate the vastness of His mercy and that such a person is worthy of being hoped for, even if the sin is great. This is especially so since it is followed by His saying, ﴿Indeed He is...﴾, which indicates the restriction of forgiveness and mercy in the most emphatic form. So the proper course is that it be kept in its generality to match the generality of the opening, and not be restricted by repentance, lest that contradict the purpose of the interposition. Moreover, it is a plural with the definite article, and it has been emphasized by what makes it explicit in generality. The Mu'tazili (*Mu'tazili*, a member of the rationalist theological school) is not helped by the claim that the great Qur'an is like a single speech and that it is free of contradiction; rather, this harms him. The same applies to what was mentioned about the occasions of revelation. End. Perhaps the indication includes some of the emphasizers of the unrestricted reading that we mentioned just now. What appears preferable to me is what he chose: that the address in "O My servants" is general, to the disobedient and the disbelievers. The matter of the idafa is easy. As for His saying, ﴿Indeed Allah forgives all sins﴾, it is restricted by "for whomever He wills," by the evidence of its explicit statement in the reading of 'Abdullah here. That all matters are dependent on the will, and we do not concede that the object of the will is only the one who repents, and that it follows wisdom on the assumption of its soundness, does not help, since without establishing that forgiveness for one who does not repent is contrary to wisdom, it is like trying to pull out thorns (*kharṭ al-qatad*, an idiom for an impossible task). Yes, forgiveness is not attached to the polytheist as long as he does not believe, because of His saying, ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that He be associated with Him﴾ [An-Nisa': 48]. So the forgiveness of polytheism is conditional upon faith, and it is included in "whomever He wills," but with the known condition. Taking the condition into account here does not harm the non-consideration of the condition of repentance for the disobedient, by what is less than that. This is supported by what Imam Ahmad reported in his Musnad, and Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman, from Thawban, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "I would not love to have this world and what is in it in exchange for this verse: ﴿O My servants who have transgressed against themselves...﴾ to the end of the verse." A man said: "O Messenger of Allah, and what of the one who associates partners?" The Prophet (ﷺ) was silent for a while, then said: "Except the one who associates partners," three times. It cannot be said that forgiveness for one who associates partners on condition of Islam is an obvious matter, so it could not be hidden from the questioner, and the Prophet (ﷺ) would not be silent waiting for revelation or for ijtihad (*ijtihad*, independent legal reasoning). For we say: the question was for astonishment in terms of usual custom, and the silence was to teach the way of deliberation and reflection, even if the matter is clear.

It was said: the apparent reason is that he waited for permission, or for ijtihad in clarifying the generality of forgiveness, since they might rely upon that and so neglect action, which is feared. This does not contradict teaching, for he (ﷺ) only taught them reflection after he himself had reflected (ﷺ).

The claim that the hadith indicates the condition of repentance is nothing. What supports the unrestricted forgiveness free of the condition of repentance is what Imam Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it as hasan, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn al-Anbari in al-Masahif, al-Hakim, and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Asma' bint Yazid, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recite: ﴿O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah; indeed Allah forgives all sins, and He does not mind; indeed He is the Forgiving, the Merciful.﴾" For "and He does not mind" has little beauty if forgiveness were conditional upon repentance, as is not hidden. Likewise is what Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn Sirin, who said: 'Ali, may Allah honor his face, said: "Which verse is the most expansive?" They began mentioning verses from the Qur'an, such as ﴿And whoever does evil or wrongs himself﴾ [An-Nisa': 110], and similar. Then 'Ali, may Allah honor his face, said: "Nothing in the Qur'an is more expansive as a verse than ﴿O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾..." to the end of the verse.

As for the aforementioned emphasizers, namely the seventeen, some of them are not free from scrutiny. The apparent view is that the forgiveness of a sin does not combine with punishment for it at all. Some scholars held that it can combine with it if the punishment is less than the sin, but not if it is equal to it. So one who is punished in the Fire to the measure of his sin and then brought out of it is not said to have been forgiven, since evil deeds are only requited with their like. It was also said: it combines with it absolutely, and that evil deeds are only requited with their like is also by His subtle kindness, Exalted is He, so it is a kind of His pardon, Mighty and Majestic. There is in this what there is, so consider it. The root meaning of *inabah* (*inabah*, turning back to Allah in devotion) is returning.

The meaning of ﴿And turn in repentance to your Lord﴾... etc. is: return to Him, Glorified is He, by turning away from His disobedience and regretting it. It was said: by devoting oneself to Him, Exalted is He, through worship. Mentioning "Lord" is like an alert to the cause. Al-Qushayri said: *inabah* is returning wholly. The difference between *inabah* and *tawbah* (*tawbah*, repentance) is that the penitent returns out of fear of punishment, while the one who turns in devotion (*munib*) returns out of shame before His generosity, Exalted is He. Submission to Him, Glorified is He, is sincerity in His obedience, Mighty and Majestic. It is mentioned that sincerity after *inabah* is that the servant knows that his salvation is by the grace of Allah, Exalted is He, not by his own *inabah*. By His grace, Glorified is He, he reached His *inabah*, not by his own *inabah* did he reach His grace, may His grace be exalted. From Ibn 'Abbas, from a hadith reported by Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir from him: "Whoever despairs the servants of repentance has denied the Book of Allah, Exalted is He. But the servant cannot repent until Allah Himself turns to him in repentance."

﴿And follow the best of what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾. The apparent meaning is that this is an address to the servants addressed in what precedes, whether by them is meant the believers, or what encompasses them and the disbelievers. What is meant by "what has been sent down" is the Qur'an. It was sent down to the believers and, as it was sent down to them, it was also sent down to the disbelievers, since it was sent down upon him (ﷺ) to call all people. What is meant by "its best" is that which includes guidance to the good of both abodes, excluding stories and the like, or the commanded matters, or the firm injunctions (*ʿazāʾim*, obligatory rulings), or the abrogating (*nāsikh*) ruling. The form *afʿal* (the superlative "best") is in its apparent sense in the first and third interpretations, while in the second and fourth there are two possibilities. It has been said that perhaps "the best" is that which is more saving and safer, such as turning in repentance and persistence in obedience, and *afʿal* in this is also in its apparent sense. It is permissible that the address is to the genus (of humanity), and that what is meant by "what has been sent down" is the heavenly books, and by "its best" the Qur'an. In this, however, there is departure from the apparent meaning. In the mention of "your Lord" there is encouragement to follow. ﴿Before the punishment comes upon you suddenly﴾, i.e., unexpectedly, ﴿while you do not perceive﴾, i.e., you have no knowledge at all of its coming, so that you could take measures to avert what would repel it.

﴿That a soul should say﴾ is in the position of the object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi, the accusative noun giving the reason for an action), with a governed noun (mudaf) understood, and al-Zamakhshari estimated it as "out of dislike." It is governed by a verb omitted but indicated by what precedes it, meaning: "I warn you and command you to follow the best of what has been sent down to you, out of dislike that a soul should say." Whoever does not require unity of agent for the accusative (nasb) may allow the governing verb to be ﴿Repent﴾ or ﴿Follow﴾. In any case, this dislike is the opposite of approval, not of intention, so there is no Mu'tazili implication in estimating it. This is better than estimating "out of fear that," as al-Hawfi did when he said: "That is, We warned you out of fear that a soul should say." Ibn 'Atiyyah made the governing verb ﴿Repent﴾ and estimated nothing of dislike or fear, when he said: "That is, repent for the sake of a soul saying." Some grammarians held that the estimate is "lest a soul should say," and that the indefiniteness of ﴿soul﴾ is for multiplication, by the context, as in the verse of al-A'sha:

"And many a open space, if I called out in its air,
a noble man would come to me, shaking his head in anger."

He meant groups of nobles who would support him, not a single noble man. It was also allowed that it is for partition, since the one who speaks is some of the souls, and Abu Hayyan preferred this. It was said that this suffices for the threat, since every soul may be that one. It was also allowed that it is for magnification, meaning a soul distinguished from other souls, either by stubborn obstinacy in disbelief or by a great punishment. This is not the right view.

﴿Alas for me!﴾ uses an alif in place of the ya' of possession (ya' al-idafah, the first-person possessive suffix). The meaning, as Sibawayh said, is "O my regret, come forth, for this is your time." Ibn Kathir read in pause "yā ḥasratāhu" with the pausal ha' (ha' al-sakt, a ha' added at pause). Abu Ja'far read "yā ḥasratī" with the ya' of possession. From him it is also reported "yā ḥasratāy" with alif and a ya', either vowelled with fatha or sukun, combining the replacement with what is replaced. It was said so, but it should not be overlooked that such a thing is not permitted, except as an irregular usage both in practice and in analogy. The most sound view is that he used the dual of ḥasrah (regret) for emphasis, like labbayka and sa'dayka, and as in "aqāma bayna ẓahrayhim" and "ẓahrānīhim," according to the dialect of Bilḥārith ibn Ka'b, which keeps the dual with alif in all cases. The author of al-Kashf preferred this, and Abu al-Fadl al-Razi, in his book al-Lawami', also allowed that the dual be taken literally according to that dialect, the intended meaning being the regret of losing Paradise and the regret of entering Hell. Taking it as multiplicity is better, because of the abundance of their regrets on the Day of Resurrection.

﴿Over what I neglected﴾ means "because of my neglect." Here ʿalā is causal and mā is verbal-noun (maṣdariyyah), as in the verse: ﴿and that you may glorify Allah for having guided you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185]. Tafrīṭ means negligence.

﴿In regard to Allah's side﴾ means His side. Al-Raghib said: the original sense of janb is the body part, then it is borrowed for the side and the direction next to it, as in their custom of borrowing the other body parts for this, such as right and left. The meaning here is the direction, figuratively. The speech involves an omitted governed noun, meaning "in regard to the obedience of Allah" or "in His right," i.e. what is due to Him, glorified is He, and necessary for Him, which is His obedience, mighty and majestic is He. On this is the earlier verse of al-Barbari, one of the poets of the Hamasah:

"Will you not fear Allah regarding a lover,
who has a scorched liver that is cut for you?"

Negligence in the direction of obedience is a kināya (metonymy) for negligence in obedience itself, because whoever neglects a direction has neglected what is in it by a stronger, more eloquent path, being a demonstrative argument. A similar example is the verse of Ziyad al-A'jam:

"Indeed generosity, manliness and liberality
are in a dome pitched over the son of al-Hashraj."

There is no objection to janb being for obedience, and likewise the right of Allah, the Exalted, meaning His obedience, glorified is He, as a direction by extension for the one who obeys, like the place of generosity and what is with it in the verse. From what we have mentioned it is known that there is no barrier to metonymy as some have imagined. Al-Imam (al-Razi) said: janb was named janb because it is one of the sides of a thing, and what is a necessary consequence and follower of a thing is as if it were one of its troops and one of its sides. When the resemblance arose between the janb that is the limb and what is necessary and following for a thing, it was therefore good to apply the word janb to right, command and obedience. End of quote. They made in the discussion of it an explicit metaphor (isti'arah taṣrīḥiyyah), and there is no implied governed noun, but this is not the right view.

As for the saying of Ibn 'Abbas: he means "over what you wasted of Allah's reward"; Muqatil: "over what you wasted of the remembrance of Allah"; Mujahid and al-Suddi: "over what you neglected in the command of Allah"; al-Hasan: "in the obedience of Allah"; Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "in the right of Allah." These are explanations of the resulting meaning. It was said: janb is a metaphor for the essence (dhāt), like the side or the place of sitting, used figuratively for His Lord, so the meaning would be "over what you neglected in the essence of Allah." This is weak, because it is not fitting to apply janb to Him, the Exalted, even figuratively, and its vulgarity is also apparent. It was also said: it is a metaphor for nearness, meaning "over what you neglected in the nearness of Allah." This is weak because it requires another figurative extension, and the matter in the Hereafter returns to obedience to Allah, the Exalted, and the like. In sum, it is not possible to keep the speech on its literal meaning, because of the glorification of Him, mighty and majestic is He, above janb in its literal sense.

I have not found any of the early scholars counting it among the traditionally transmitted attributes (al-ṣifāt al-samʿiyyah), and I do not rely on what is in al-Mawaqif. Even on the assumption that it is counted, their speech on these attributes is well known, and they all agree on exalting Allah above anything, "There is nothing like unto Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing." In the reading of 'Abd Allah (ibn Mas'ud) and the codex of Hafsah it is "in the remembrance of Allah." ﴿And indeed I was of the mockers﴾ means those who mock the religion of Allah, the Exalted, and its people. Wa-inna is the lightened form of the heavy inna, and the lām is the lām of distinction (al-lām al-fāriqah, which distinguishes the lightened inna from the negative). The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) according to al-Zamakhshari, meaning "you neglected in the state of my mockery."

In al-Bahr (Abu Hayyan) he said: it appears that it is a new statement (isti'nāf) reporting about himself what he was upon in the world, not a circumstantial clause, and the purpose of that report is lamentation and grief.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 39, verse 57:

﴿Or [lest] it say: "Had Allah guided me, I would have been among the God-fearing."﴾ That is, [freed] from shirk and sins.

Several scholars explained guidance (hidayah) here as direction and showing the right path (al-irshad wal-dalalah al-mawsulah), on the basis that this is the most fitting for the conditional clause and corresponds to the response in His words, glorified is He: ﴿Yes [indeed]...﴾ etc. Abu Hayyan explained it as the creation of the state of being guided (khalq al-ihtida'). Whichever is the case, the apparent meaning is that this statement will be made in the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 39, verse 58:

﴿Or say, when he sees the punishment: "If only I had a return (karrah) [to the world]"﴾, that is, a return to the life of this world, ﴿so that I might be among the doers of good﴾ in belief and in action. (Law) here is for expressing a wish, and ﴿fa-akūna﴾ (so that I might be) is in the subjunctive mood as the answer to it. Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) permitted that it be in the subjunctive by virtue of being conjoined (ʿaṭf) to karrah, since it is a verbal noun (maṣdar), so that it would be like the saying of the poet:

Nothing remains for you of her but remembrance and grief, and you ask about her riders, where they headed.

And like the saying of another:

The wearing of a cloak and the coolness of my eye are dearer to me than the wearing of sheer garments.

Then he said: The difference between the two is that when the fa' (fa) is in the answer to a wish (tamannī), the particle an (that) must be elided, and the existence (al-kawn) is then dependent upon the attainment of the wished-for thing, not the wished-for thing itself; whereas when it is for conjunction (ʿaṭf) to karrah, it is permissible to state an or to elide it, and the existence (al-kawn) is then itself the thing wished for.

Al-Alusi's commentary (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 39, verse 59:

The words of the Exalted, ﴿Yes! My signs had certainly come to you, but you denied them, and you were arrogant, and you were among the disbelievers﴾, are a response from Allah, mighty and majestic, to what is implied in the speech of the one who said ﴿If only Allah had guided me﴾, namely the negation that Allah the Exalted had guided him, and it refutes that. It is not a condition of the answer with "bala" (yes) that a negation be stated explicitly. It has been placed in its fitting position, because if it had been put before the last companion phrase, namely ﴿or [lest] he say when he sees the punishment﴾ ... and so on, and what follows it had been joined to it without separation by it, the sublime composition would have lost its beauty. The three companion phrases are proportionate, harmonious and adjacent to one another, and the proportion among them is more complete than the proportion between the second companion phrase and its answer. And if the second companion phrase were delayed and the third made second, it would also be unbecoming, because the observance of the meaningful order, which is more important, would be lost at that point. This is because regret over neglect at the scattering of the scrolls, as indicated by several passages of the Mighty Qur'an, and the pretext of non-guidance only come after witnessing the state of the God-fearing and their rejoicing. Also, it is for consolation for some of the regret, or by way of the drowning man clutching at straws, so it is subsequent, and the wish to return comes after tasting the Fire. Do you not see the saying of the Exalted: ﴿If only you could see them when they are made to stand over the Fire and say: "Would that we were returned, and did not deny the signs of our Lord"﴾ [al-An'am: 27]. Likewise, if "standing" is taken to mean being held at its edge or being shown it, both are after witnessing the state of the God-fearing and what they received of the lightness of reckoning and honour in the place of standing. Also, resorting to wishing comes after certainty that there is no benefit in pretext. Al-Tibi said: the soul, on seeing the terrors of the Day of Resurrection, sees people being recompensed according to their deeds, so it regrets the loss of deeds for itself; then it may make the excuse that the shortfall was not from it; but when it looks and knows that the shortfall was from it, it wishes to return. Then, the apparent indication of the context is that the souls have combined the three sayings with "aw" (or) to prevent the absence of any of them, and it was brought to indicate that each one alone suffices as a deterrent from preferring disbelief and as a motive to repentance and following the best of what has been sent down. And the address in ﴿your signs had come to you﴾ ... and so on, is in the masculine form according to the meaning, because what is meant by "nafs" (soul) is the person, even though its word is feminine by usage.

Ibn Ya'mur, al-Jahdari, Abu Haywa, al-Za'farani, Ibn Muqsim, Mas'ud ibn Salih, al-Shafi'i from Ibn Kathir, and Muhammad ibn Isa in his choice read ﴿jā'atki﴾ ... and so on, with a kasra on the kaf and the ta', and this is the reading of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq and his daughter 'Aisha, may Allah be pleased with them both, and Umm Salama narrated it from the Prophet (ﷺ).

Al-Hasan, al-A'mash and al-A'raj read ﴿ja'atka﴾ with a hamza and without a long vowel, on the pattern of fa'atka. According to Abu Hayyan, this is a metathesis of jā'atka: the lam of the root was moved forward and the 'ayn moved back, so the alif fell away.

The Mu'tazilah used the verse as evidence that the servant creates his own actions. The Ash'aris answered that the attribution of actions to the servant is by reason of his acquisitive power (qudra kasiba). Al-Kurani verified that it is by reason of his effective power by Allah's permission, not as the Mu'tazilah maintained, that it is by reason of his effective power, whether or not Allah permits it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 39, verse 60:

﴿On the Day of Resurrection you will see those who lied against God, their faces blackened.﴾ This is due to the hardship that befalls them, which literally changes their colours. There is no barrier to the blackness of their faces being a literal sign of them, not caused by what befalls them. It is also permitted that this is a figurative sense (majaz), not that their faces are literally blackened, by saying: because of the distress that reaches them, and the effects of ignorance of God, the Mighty and Majestic, that appear on them, it is imagined that this is in them. The apparent meaning is that the seeing is visual (basariyyah), and the address is either to the master of those addressed, peace and blessings be upon him, or to everyone who is capable of seeing. The clause ﴿their faces are blackened﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), as Abu Hayyan preferred. That the intended meaning is seeing the blackness of their faces does not contradict its being a circumstantial clause, as some imagined, because the qualifier is the locus of the benefit. There is no harm in omitting the waw and relying on the pronoun within it, especially since including it here would bring together two waws, which is burdensome. Al-Farra' claimed that this is an anomaly, but whoever accepts it makes the clause here a substitute (badal) for ﴿alladhina﴾ (those who), as al-Zajjaj held. They permitted the substitution of a clause for a single word, or it is a resumptive clause, like an explanation of what the clause before it implied and what sound taste perceives from it of their evil state. Or one makes the seeing cognitive ('ilmiyyah), and the clause is in the position of the second object. This is supported by the reading "wujuhahum musawwadah" with both in the accusative, where "wujuhahum" is a second object and "musawwadah" is a circumstantial clause from it. You know that treating the seeing as visual is more eloquent in exposing them and in conveying the horror of their state, especially with the generality of the address. The accusative in the anomalous reading may be a substitution. By "those who did wrong" is meant those speakers who expressed regret, so this is the placing of an apparent noun in place of a pronoun. The words of the Exalted fit this most exactly: ﴿Is there not in Hell an abode for the arrogant?﴾, meaning the place for ﴿the arrogant﴾ who were given the signs of God, denied them, and were proud to refuse to accept and submit to them. This is an affirmation of their seeing as such. His words that follow also fit it: ﴿And He will save﴾ ... etc.

Their lying against God is by their attributing to Him, glory be to Him, a partner and the like. Exalted is He above what they describe, a great exaltation. It has been said:

It is by their attributing to Him, exalted is He, what does not befit Him in this world, and by their saying in the Hereafter: ﴿If only God had guided me﴾, which implies the claim that God, glory be to Him, did not guide them or direct them. It has been said: they are the People of the Two Books. From al-Hasan: they are the Qadariyyah (a sect that denied divine predestination), who say: "If we wish we act, even if God does not will it, and if we wish we do not act, even if God wills it." It has been said: the intended meaning is everyone who lied against God, exalted is He, and described Him with what is unfitting for Him, by negation and affirmation, so he attributed to Him what must be declared far from Him, or he declared Him far from what must be attributed to Him. This is reported from al-Qadi, and its apparent meaning requires declaring many of the ahl al-qiblah (people of the qibla, i.e., Muslims) to be unbelievers, and there is what there is in that. The more suitable to the structure of the noble verse is what we have presented before.

[Page 20]

It is not far-fetched that the ruling for everyone who lies against God, exalted is He, whether knowingly that he lied against Him, glory be to Him, or unknowingly but relying on a feeble doubt, is the same. The words of al-Hasan, if they are authentic, I do not think are anything but a figurative illustration (tamthil). The insinuation of al-Zamakhshari against the People of the Truth, with what he insinuated, is outside the bounds of justice. What they adopted is not at all lying against God, exalted is He, while lying is clearly manifest in him and in his companions.

Ubayy read "ujuhahum", replacing the waw with a hamzah.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 39, verse 61:

﴿And God will deliver those who were mindful of Him﴾ from Jahannam, from that which those arrogant ones were characterised by. It is also read "yunji" (with the lightened form), from al-injaʾ (deliverance). ﴿with their mafaza﴾: it is an ism al-masdar (verbal noun), like al-falah (success), according to what is in al-Kashf; or it is a mimi masdar (a masdar beginning with mim), according to what is in others, from faza bi-kadha, when one prospers thereby and attains his desired aim from it. Al-Raghib said: it is the masdar of faza, or the ism al-fawz (the noun of triumph), and by it is meant attaining the desired goal in the most complete manner, like al-falah; and al-Suddi interpreted it thus. The ba' is for accompaniment (al-mulabasa), attached to an omitted element which is a ḥal (circumstantial clause) of the relative pronoun, conveying the coincidence of their deliverance from the punishment with the attainment of reward. That is: God will deliver them from Jahannam, the abode of the arrogant, because of their taqwa (God-consciousness), from that in which the arrogant were characterised, while they are accompanied by their success and their attainment of the desired goal, which is Paradise. Its outcome is that He will deliver them from the Fire and cause them to enter Paradise. That Paradise is the desired goal of the one who is mindful of God, whoever he may be, is beyond doubt. Yes, it is the desired goal of some of the mindful, insofar as it is the place of seeing their Beloved, which is the ultimate of their aim. You may also generalise the desired goal. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿they will not be touched by evil, nor will they grieve﴾ is also in the position of a ḥal, either from the relative pronoun or from the pronoun in ﴿with their mafaza﴾, conveying that, along with the deliverance or the triumph, evil and grief are negated from them permanently. The apparent view is that this ḥal is a future (muqaddara) one. It was also said that it is a concomitant (muqarina) ḥal, conveying that their deliverance or their mafaza (triumph) with Paradise is not preceded by the touch of punishment and grief. It should not be concealed that this does not hold with respect to all the mindful, for among them are those whom punishment touches and who grieve inevitably; and to count the existence of that as nonexistent because of its rarity and its cessation is a far-fetched strain. It was also permitted that mafaza be understood as al-falah, and that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿they will not be touched﴾ ... etc. be made a resumptive clause (istiʾnaf) explaining it, as if it were said: what is their mafaza? It was said: they will not be touched... etc.

The ba' then, according to what is in al-Kashf, is causal (sababiyya), attached to yunji, meaning: He will deliver them by the negation of evil and grief from them. It has been objected that making the absence of grief and the absence of evil the cause of deliverance is a strain, so they are part of the deliverance itself; and the apparent view is that if the ba' is taken in this way too as for accompaniment, this objection does not arise. It was also permitted that mafaza is a noun of place, meaning the place of triumph, and it is interpreted as the place of deliverance (al-manja, makan al-naja), and this is correct because deliverance is triumph and success. The ba' is taken as causal in this case, and there is an omitted mudaf (annexed term) indicated by the causal ba', and the place of deliverance cannot serve as a cause; so the meaning is: He will deliver them by means of their deliverance, which is faith. This is like an explicit statement of what was required by the linking of the verb to the preceding relative pronoun. Al-Zamakhshari interpreted it as righteous deeds, and strengthened it with what he reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, in order to complete his school of thought. Or there is no mudaf, but rather a metaphor (majaz), by that indication, through the designation of the cause by the name of the effect. The clause after this, on both possibilities, in this view, is a ḥal. It should not be concealed that mafaza in the sense of the place of deliverance is Paradise, and that faith or righteous deeds are not a cause of Paradise itself but rather a cause of entering it, so this must be taken into account; so do not be heedless. It was also permitted that mafaza be a mimi masdar from faza minhu, meaning he was saved from it; it is said: blessed is he who triumphs with reward and is saved from punishment, i.e., attains it and is delivered. The ba' is either for accompaniment, and the clause is an explanation of mafaza, meaning: God will deliver them while they are accompanied by their particular deliverance, that is, by the negation of evil and grief from them; and the weakness of this meaning is not concealed. Or it is causal, either by omission of the mudaf or by metaphor, similar to what passed just now; and here there is no need to consider entering, as is not concealed. The clause is also in the position of a ḥal.

It was also permitted, on some of the aspects, that ﴿with their mafaza﴾ be connected to what follows it; and it is not concealed that this contradicts the apparent sense. In sum, the rational possibilities in the verse are numerous, for mafaza is either an ism al-masdar, or a mimi masdar, or an ism al-makan from faza bihi (attained by it) or faza minhu (escaped from it); and the ba' is either for accompaniment, causation, or instrumentality, and it is either connected to what precedes it or to what follows it. These are thirty-six possibilities. If you add to them the possibility of omitting the mudaf in "bi-mafazatihim" in the sense of their deliverance (manjatihim) or their deliverance (najatihim), and the possibility of metaphor in it likewise, and likewise the possibility that the clause "they will not be touched..." is a ḥal from the relative pronoun, and the possibility that it is a ḥal from the pronoun of "mafazatihim", and the possibility that the ḥal is future or concomitant, the number increases greatly. It should not be concealed that among them is the acceptable and what is less than it, and indeed among them is what cannot be arranged at all; so consider carefully and do not be rigid. Al-Sulami, al-Hasan, al-A'raj, al-A'mash, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr read "bi-mafazatihim" in the plural, so that it conforms to the annexed noun in clearly indicating multiplicity.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 39, verse 62:

﴿Allah is the Creator of all things﴾, of good and evil, of faith and disbelief, but not by compulsion; rather through the direct action of the one who is characterised by them, according to their causes. Thus the verse is a clear refutation of the Mu'tazilah (the Mu'tazili school of theology, who held that human beings create their own actions).

﴿And He is Guardian (wakil) over all things﴾: He disposes of them as He wills, according to what wisdom requires. It seems that the mention of this is to indicate that He, glory be to Him, is the Absolutely Self-Sufficient (al-Ghani al-Mutlaq), and that benefits and harms return to the servants. You may also say: the meaning is that He, exalted is He, is Watchful over all things (hafiz), as has been said in similar terms regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you are not a guardian over them﴾ [al-An'am: 107; al-Zumar: 41; al-Shura: 6]. The sum of it is that He, exalted is He, takes charge of preserving every thing after its creation, so this is an indication that things are in need of Him, exalted is He, in their continued existence, just as they are in need of Him, glorified and exalted is He, in their coming into existence.

[Page 22]

﴿To Him belong the keys of the heavens and the earth.﴾ That is, their keys (*maqalid*), as Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah and others said. It has been said that it is a plural with no singular from its own root. It has also been said that it is the plural of *miqlid*, or of *miqlad*, from *taqlid* in the sense of obligation, and from this comes *taqlid al-qada'* (the appointment of someone to judgeship), which is obliging him to attend to its affairs. Likewise *qiladah* (a necklace) is so named because it clings to the neck. The word has also been made the name of the well-known instrument used for obligating (locking), in the sense of keeping. On all these views the word is Arabic. The most famous and most evident view, however, is that it is arabized (*mu'arrab*). It is then the plural of *iqlid*, an arabized form of *iklid*, and this is an irregular plural, because the plural of the pattern *if'il* on the pattern *mafa'il* goes against analogy. The plural *aqalid* has come on analogy. It is also said that in *iklid* the form *kilid* is used without a hamza. Al-Shihab mentioned that in the language of the Romans it is *aqlidis* and *kalid*, and *aklid* is derived from it. The well-known view is that *kalid* is Persian, and *iklid* with a hamza is not well known in Persian. As for *lahu maqalid*, it has been said that it is a metaphor for His being the owner of the matter and the one who disposes of it, by the relation of necessity. It is also used as a metonymy for the meaning of power and preservation. It has been permitted that the first meaning be a metonymy, but since it has become well known it is treated as the literal signified, and so the other meaning is expressed by it, so that there is a metonymy upon a metonymy. Sometimes only the first meaning is intended, and on this basis it has been said that the meaning here is: no one other than Him, glorified and exalted, owns the affair of the heavens and the earth or is able to dispose of them.

Al-Baydawi, after mentioning this, said: it is a metonymy for His power, may He be exalted, and His preservation of them, and in it there is further indication of independence and sole authority, because of the *lam* (of possession) and the fronting (of the word "to Him"). Al-Raghib said: *maqalid al-samawat wa al-ard* is what encompasses them. It has been said that they are their treasuries, and it has been said that they are their keys. The reference of "all of them" is to one meaning, which is His power over them and His preservation of them. End.

It has been permitted that the meaning is: no one other than Allah, may He be exalted, has the disposal of the treasuries of the heavens and the earth, that is, of what He has deposited in them and for which they are prepared of benefits. It is not hidden that if this sentence is in the position of a reason for His words, "And He is over all things a Guardian" (*wakil*), on the first meaning, then the most evident is to limit its meaning to: no one other than Him, may He be exalted, owns the affair of the heavens and the earth, that is, the entire world. So it is as if it were said: He, may He be exalted, takes charge of the disposal of everything, because no one other than Him owns its affair, glorified and exalted. If it is a reason for it on the second meaning, then the most evident is to limit its meaning to: no one other than Him, may His majesty be exalted, has power over them. So it is as if it were said: He, may He be exalted, takes charge of the preservation of everything, because no one other than Him, may He be exalted, has power over it. It has also been permitted that it be an explanatory apposition (*'atf bayan*) to the sentence before it, or that it be an attribute of *wakil*, or that it be a predicate after a predicate. So reflect carefully on this and ponder it.

Abu Ya'la and Yusuf al-Qadi in their *Sunan*, Abu al-Hasan al-Qattan in *al-Mutawwalat*, Ibn al-Sunni in *'Amal al-Yawm wa al-Layla*, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the words of Allah, may He be exalted: *To Him belong the keys of the heavens and the earth*. He said: *La ilaha illa Allah, Allahu akbar, subhan Allah, al-hamdu lillah, astaghfiru Allah, the One besides whom there is no god, the First and the Last, the Manifest and the Hidden, He gives life and causes death, and He is Living and does not die; in His hand is the good, and He is over all things Powerful*," and so on, the hadith.

In the narration of Ibn Mardawayh from Ibn 'Abbas: "'Uthman came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said to him: Inform me about the keys of the heavens and the earth. He said: *Subhan Allah, al-hamdu lillah, la ilaha illa Allah, Allahu akbar, la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah al-'Aliyy al-'Azim* (there is no power nor strength except by Allah, the Most High, the Mighty), *al-Awwal wa al-Akhir, al-Zahir wa al-Batin, bi-yadihi al-khayr, yuhyi wa yumit, wa huwa 'ala kulli shay'in qadir* (in His hand is the good; He gives life and causes death, and He is over all things Powerful). O 'Uthman, whoever says them when he reaches the morning ten times, and when he reaches the evening, Allah gives him six qualities. As for the first, he is protected from Iblis and his soldiers. As for the second, he is given a *qintar* (a great measure) of reward. As for the third, he marries from the *Hur al-'In* (the wide-eyed maidens of Paradise). As for the fourth, his sins are forgiven. As for the fifth, he is with Ibrahim, peace be upon him. As for the sixth, twelve angels attend him at his death, giving him the good news of Paradise and escorting him from his grave to the place of gathering. If any of the terrors of the Day of Resurrection befall him, they say to him: Do not fear, you are among the secure. Then Allah reckons with him a light reckoning, then he is ordered to Paradise, and they escort him to Paradise from his place of standing as a bride is escorted, until they enter him into Paradise by the permission of Allah, may He be exalted, while the people are in the severity of the reckoning."

In the narration of al-Uqayli and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa al-Sifat* from Ibn 'Umar: "'Uthman asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about the explanation of *To Him belong the keys of the heavens and the earth*. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: No one has asked me about its explanation: *La ilaha illa Allah, Allahu akbar, subhan Allah wa bihamdihi, astaghfiru Allah, la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah*, He is the First and the Last, the Manifest and the Hidden, in His hand is the good, He gives life and causes death, and He is over all things Powerful."

In the narration of al-Harith ibn Abi Usamah and Ibn Mardawayh from Abu Hurayrah, that he (ﷺ) said: "They are: *Subhan Allah, al-hamdu lillah, la ilaha illa Allah, Allahu akbar, la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah*." In sum, the narrations differ regarding the answer. It has been said regarding the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that in its chain there is a weak narrator whose narration is not acceptable. Ibn al-Jawzi said that it is fabricated (*mawdu'*), and he did not accept it. As for the state of the other reports, Allah knows best about them, and the assessment is weakness.

The meaning according to these reports is that for Allah, may He be exalted, these words are by which He is declared one and glorified, and they are the keys to the good of the heavens and the earth: whoever among the believers speaks them, it reaches him. The reason for applying the term "keys" to them is that they lead to good, just as keys lead to what is in the treasuries. The Prophet (ﷺ) has mentioned some of the good in the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, and in the hadith before it he counted ten qualities for whoever says them a hundred times each day. It is in full in *al-Durr al-Manthur*.

﴿And those who disbelieved in the signs of Allah, those are the losers.﴾ This is coordinated (*ma'tuf*) on His words, "Allah is the Creator of all things," etc. That is: He, may His majesty be exalted, is characterized by these sublime attributes, and those who disbelieved and denied that, they are the complete losers. It has been said that it is coordinated on His words, "To Him belong the keys of the heavens and the earth," but this does not appear on some of the previously mentioned aspects of it. It has been said that it is on an assumed (*muqaddar*) clause, its estimate being: "So those who feared God, or those who believed in the signs of Allah, they are the successful; and those who disbelieved..." etc., and in this there is artificiality (*takalluf*). It has been permitted that it be coordinated on His words, "And Allah will deliver," etc., so that the estimate is: "And Allah will deliver those who are conscious of Him, and those who disbelieved in the signs of Allah, those are the losers," and what lies between them is a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiraD*) to show that He, may He be exalted, is watchful over the servants, observing their deeds and recompensing them for them. In it there is emphasis on the reward and success of the believers, and the punishment and loss of the disbelievers. He did not say "and He will destroy those who disbelieved by their loss" as He, glorified be He, said "and He will deliver" etc., [Page 23] to indicate that the foundation of the believers' success is His grace, may He be exalted. For this reason He attributed their deliverance to Himself, as an event occurring to them on the Day of Resurrection, not established before that through merit and deeds. This differs from the destruction of the disbelievers, for they brought it upon themselves by what they were characterized by of disbelief and misguidance. It was not attributed to Him, may He be exalted, and it was not expressed in the present tense either. In this there is an explicit promise and an allusive threat, in that it says "the losers" and does not say "the destroyed" or "the punished" or the like, and this is the requirement of generosity. The coordination of a nominal sentence on a verbal one is something whose permissibility there is no doubt about among the grammarians. From what we have mentioned, the rejection of the statement of Imam al-Razi is known: that this aspect is weak for two reasons. The first is the occurrence of a large interval between the coordinated and what it is coordinated upon. The second is the occurrence of difference between them in verbal and nominal form, and this is not permitted. Imam Abu Hayyan rejected that the intervening element is large. He said regarding the second aspect that it is the statement of one who has not reflected on the speech of the Arabs nor looked into the chapters of *ishtighal* (the grammatical construction in which a verb's object is pronominalized, here a term for the grammatical chapter on the verb governed by a pronoun). Indeed, al-Kashshaf said that what supports the connection with what follows, rather than with His words "And Allah will deliver," is that His words, glorified be He, "And Allah will deliver," are connected to His words, "And on the Day of Resurrection you will see those who lied." So if it were said after it, "And those who disbelieved in the signs of Allah, those are the losers," it would not be good, because the better arrangement in this context is that it precede His words, "And Allah will deliver," as is not hidden. And because it is like a transition to what follows it from the discourse on worship and sincerity at that point. This is a good statement. Then, the restriction that the definition of the two extremes requires, and the pronoun of separation (*damir al-fasl*), is with respect to perfection, as we have indicated, not with respect to absolute loss, for it is not restricted to them. It has been permitted that it be a restriction by reversal (*qasr qalb*), for they consider the believers to be losers.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 39, verse 64:

﴿Say: "Do you then order me to worship other than Allah, you ignorant ones?"﴾ That is: after the verses that necessitate worshipping Him, the Exalted, alone, shall I worship other than Allah? So "ghayr" (other than) is a direct object preceding "a'budu" (I worship). "Ta'murunni" (do you order me) is a parenthetical clause, to indicate that they ordered him to do this immediately after that, and said to him, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him: "Touch some of our gods, and we will believe in your God," due to the extreme stupidity of them, and therefore they were addressed by the title of ignorance. It is also permissible that "a'budu" be in the position of the object of "ta'murunni", on the basis that the original was "ta'murunni an a'bud", so "an" was deleted and the verb became marfu', as it was said in his statement:

Ala ayyuhadha al-zajiri ahdaru al-waghā
(Ah, you who forbid me, I attend the battle.)

It supports the reading of the one who read "a'bada" with a fathah, and "ghayr" is in the accusative governed by what is indicated by "ta'murunni a'budu", that is: "tu'abbidunani ghayra Allah", meaning: "Do you make me a worshipper of other than Him, the Exalted?" It is not valid for it to be governed by "a'bud", because the relative clause does not operate on what precedes it, and what is estimated is like what exists. Some have said: it is governed by it, and "an" after deletion loses its governing effect that prevents operation.

Ibn Kathir read "ta'murunni" with idgham (assimilation) and a fathah on the ya'.

Ibn Amir read "ta'murunnani" with both nuns made clear, according to the original form. Nafi' read "ta'murunni" with a single kasrah-marked nun and a fathah on the ya'. Regarding which of the two nuns is omitted, there is a difference of opinion: it was said the second, because it is the one through which the repetition occurred; and it was said the first, because it is the case-marking letter (harf i'rab), liable to change.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 39, verse 65:

﴿And it has certainly been revealed to you, and to those before you﴾, i.e., of the messengers, upon them be peace, ﴿that if you were to associate [partners with God Most High] anything﴾, i.e., with God Most High, ﴿your deeds would surely be nullified, and you would surely be among the losers﴾. The apparent view is that the clause "la'in" (if) … etc. is the deputy subject (na'ib fa'il) of "uhiya" (it was revealed). However, it has been said that there is an ellipsis (hadhf) in the speech, and the original is: "It was revealed to you, 'If you associate [partners], your deeds will surely be nullified…' etc., and to those before you, the like of that." It has also been said: there is no ellipsis, and the singular form of address is by consideration of each one of them, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, and the messengers to whom revelation was sent, for He revealed to each one: ﴿If you associate [partners]﴾ … etc., in the singular. The Basrans held that clauses cannot act as subject and so cannot stand in for the subject; in the Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit) it is stated that "ilayka" (to you) is then the deputy subject, and the meaning, as Muqatil said, is: It was revealed to you and to those who were before you, [that is, the revelation of] monotheism. God's statement ﴿If you associate [partners]﴾ … etc. is a resumptive clause (isti'naf), addressed to the Prophet, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, specifically, and this, as you see, is [weak]. Whatever the case, it is speech on the basis of supposition, to stir up the addressee who is protected from sin, to dishearten the disbelievers, and to proclaim the extreme abomination and ugliness of associating partners, and that it is of such a kind that it is forbidden even to one who hardly would commit it, so how about anyone else. Therefore, deriving from the verse the permissibility of major sins occurring from the prophets, peace be upon them, as in al-Mawaqif, is not valid. The possibility of occurrence, as a supposition, suffices for the conditional, but it should be known that the impossibility of occurrence is legal (shar'iyya). The lams in "la-qad" and "la'in" are preparatory (muwatti'a) for the oath, and the two lams after them are for the response (jawab). The fact that the nullification is not restricted to continuing in association until death is evidence for the Hanafis, who hold that apostasy nullifies the deeds performed before it absolutely. Yes, they said: after returning to Islam, one makes up nothing of them except the Hajj. The school of al-Shafi'i holds that apostasy does not nullify the deed preceding it so long as the apostate does not persist in disbelief until death, and the restriction is left out here relying on its explicit statement in God's words: ﴿And whoever of you apostatizes from his religion and dies while he is a disbeliever - those are the ones whose deeds have become worthless in this world and the Hereafter, and those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever﴾ [al-Baqarah: 217]. This would be the application of the absolute to the restricted.

Some Hanafis answered that in the aforementioned verse there is a distribution: ﴿those whose deeds have become worthless﴾ refers to apostasy from the religion, and ﴿those are the companions of the Fire⦆ … etc. refers to dying in disbelief, so there is no restricted term by which the absolute would be qualified. From this disagreement arose the disagreement concerning a Companion who apostatized and then returned to Islam after the death of the Prophet, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, or before it without having seen him: is he called a Companion or not? Whoever holds to the absolute says no, and whoever holds to the restriction says yes. It has been said: it is possible that the nullification in absolute form is peculiar to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, since his associating [partners] — and far be it from him — is most abominable. But this is weak, because the purpose is to warn his community and portray the enormity of disbelief, so assuming a matter specific to him that does not extend from the Prophet to the community has no basis, and moreover it has no support from transmission or reason. The meaning of loss (khusran) according to the Hanafi school is what results from the nullification of the deed; the apparent [expression] would be "fa-takunu" (then you would be), but he deviated to what is in the sublime arrangement to indicate that each of nullification and loss independently suffices as a deterrent from association. It has been said: eternal abiding in the Fire necessitates restriction by death, as is the view of al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him.

It is read "la-yuhbitanna" (from ahbata), with "amalaka" in the accusative, i.e., "God Most High or association will surely nullify your deed." It is also read with the nun and "amalaka" in the accusative as well.

**[Commentary of al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, on Surah 39, verse 66]**

﴿Rather, worship Allah﴾ is a rejection of what they urged him to do, namely to touch (*istilam*, i.e. to kiss or touch) some of their gods. The *fa'* (the *fa'* of the apodosis, *fa' al-jaza'iyyah*) is in answer to an implied condition, as if it had been said: "If you are a worshipper or a sensible person, then worship Allah." The condition was omitted, and the fronting of the object (*taqdim al-maf'ul*) was made a substitute for it. Al-Zamakhshari and his predecessors held this view, which is that the *fa'* is the apodosis particle, as al-Zajjaj also held. Abu Hayyan denied that the fronting serves as a substitute for the condition. The view of al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i is that the *fa'* is redundant, placed between the emphasizing and the emphasized element, and that the divine name is governed by a verb that has been omitted. The estimated sense is "Allah I worship, so worship Him," and the object is taken as postponed in order to convey exclusivity (*hasr*, i.e. restriction to one).

In *al-Intisaf*, the apparent meaning of Sibawayh's words is that the original form was *tanabbah fa'bud Allah* ("be alert, then worship Allah"). They omitted the first verb for brevity, and they disliked beginning with the *fa'*, whose nature is to occur in the middle between the conjoined element and that to which it is conjoined. So they fronted the object, and the *fa'* came to be medial in form and to indicate the omitted verb. To this was added the benefit of exclusivity, since fronting implies restriction. Some have said that taking exclusivity into account is necessary, because otherwise the statement would not be a rejection of what they had asked him to do. They did not ask him, peace be upon him, to abandon the worship of Allah, Glorified is He, but to touch their gods and to associate partners with Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He. Unless it is said that the worship of Allah, Glorified is He, together with association, is no worship at all. Allah, Exalted and High, is the most independent of partners. Whoever associates anyone with Him in his deed, Mighty and Majestic is He, his deed belongs to the one he associated, as many reports indicate.

Ibn Mas'ud... [Note: this passage does not contain this; not added.]

ʿIsa (Isa) read *bal Allahu* with the *damma* (nominative). ﴿And be among the thankful﴾ for His favour upon you, Exalted is He, which the scope of restriction cannot contain. In this there is an indication of what exclusivity requires.

﴿Nor have they measured God with His true measure﴾. That is, they did not magnify Him, majestic is His majesty, with His true magnitude, since they worshipped other than Him, exalted is He, and asked His Prophet ﷺ to worship other than Him, glorified is He. This is the view of al-Hasan and al-Suddi. Al-Mubarrad (a grammarian) said: its origin lies in their saying, "So-and-so is of great *qadr*" (rank, measure), meaning by it his grandeur. The root of *qadr* is the specification of a thing by greatness, smallness or equality. Al-Raghib (al-Isfahani) said: that is, they did not know His essence (*kunh*), mighty and majestic is He. It has been objected that knowing the *kunh* of God, that is His reality, exalted is He, is not peculiar to these people, because reaching the reality is impossible. From here comes the verse:

*The inability to grasp the grasping is itself a grasping,*
*And the search for the essence of God's being is an association (shirk).*

It is not hidden that the matter is disputed, and what has been mentioned, even if granted, can be answered by careful consideration. Yes, what has been said is better than this: that is, they did not know Him as befits Him, since they made partners for Him, exalted is He. The apparent sense of some scholars' words is that the statement is on the assumption of an omitted noun: that is, they did not estimate in themselves, nor conceive the greatness of God as it should be conceived, so they did not magnify Him as is His due, mighty and majestic is He, since they described Him with what does not befit His exalted affairs, such as associating others with Him and the like. In any case, it is connected to what precedes it in that *inna* (indeed) in it is a rebuke of their ignorance in associating others and in calling upon His Messenger ﷺ to that. It has been said: the meaning is, they did not describe God with His true description, since they denied the Resurrection and described Him, exalted is He, as having created creation in vain, and as incapable of re-creation and resurrection. This is contrary to the apparent sense. On this view, the verse serves as a preparation for the matter of the blowing of the Trumpet. The plural pronoun, on all that has been mentioned, refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh, as is narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the Jews, who spoke about the attributes and majesty of God, so they committed heresy, anthropomorphized, and brought every kind of confusion, and so this verse was revealed.

Al-A'mash read *qadarihi* (with fathah on the dal) for *qadrihi*. Al-Hasan, 'Isa, Abu Nawfal and Abu Haywah read *wa-ma qaddaru* (with shaddah on the dal) and *huqqu qadarihi* (with fathah on the dal).

﴿And the earth entirely will be His handful on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens will be folded up in His right hand﴾. The sentence is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) relating to the noble Name. *Jami'an* (entirely) is a circumstantial clause relating to the subject, according to those who permit this, or relating to an assumed element, as in "I establish them entirely," as has been said. It functions like an emphatic circumstantial clause in that its governing element is derived from the meaning of the sentence. In *al-Taqrib* it is said that it is a circumstantial clause relating to the pronoun in *qabdatuhu*, since it has the sense of "grasped." The apparent arrangement would have been to place it after that, but it was placed before it so that it is known from the outset that the report that comes does not occur about one earth alone, or about some parts but not others, but about all the earths or about all their parts. This placement is permitted because the verbal noun did not govern in its capacity as a verbal noun, but in being in the sense of the passive participle. Al-Hawfi said: the governing element of the circumstantial clause is what the word *qabdatuhu* indicates, not the word itself. This, as you see, is not sound. *Yawm al-qiyamah* (the Day of Resurrection) is the object of *qabdatuhu*. *Qabdah* originally means a single instance of grasping, and it is also used for the quantity grasped, as in *qubdah* with a dammah on the qaf. In that case it is treated as an adjectival form. It is permitted to take either the sense of "what is grasped" or the verbal-noun sense here. On the second, the statement carries an omitted noun: that is, possessors of His grasp, that is, He grasps them, exalted is He, in one grasp. Al-Hasan read *qabdatahu* with the accusative, on the basis that it is a restricted adverbial of place, resembling the indefinite, and for this reason *fi* was not stated with it. This is the position of the Kufans. The Basrans say that the accusative in such a construction as *khata'* is not permissible, and that *fi* must be explicitly mentioned.
